item.title: Apple’s new CEO, a foldable iPhone, and what I actually want to try
item.description: Apple’s new CEO, a foldable iPhone, and what I actually want to try
item.dc:creator: Taylor Arndt
item.content:encoded:
Apple’s new CEO, a foldable iPhone, and what I actually want to try

I use my iPhone for absolutely everything. Being blind, it’s a necessity, but I’m also a huge tech user. So when John Ternus opened Apple’s event talking about the iPhone as an intelligent personal hub, I thought, that’s what it is. My iPhone has been that for me for years.

Taylor’s Substack is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

This was also John’s first product launch as Apple’s new CEO. He took over from Tim Cook on September 1. The opening video had Tim pointing him out as the person to follow, and then John led the event, introducing the products and handing off to the teams who worked on them. AP’s coverage of the leadership debut

I liked that opening. Having someone new lead the event was already a change, and then we got new ideas about AI and, eventually, a “one more thing.”

I’ll be streaming later today at 3 p.m. Central to talk about all of this. Here are the announcements and my thoughts, in the order Apple presented them.

iPhone 18 Pro and Siri AI

Apple started with iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. They come in black, silver, glacier, and burgundy, with color-matched aluminum and back glass.

The phones use Apple’s latest Foundation Models, including its newest on-device model, and support larger models through Private Cloud Compute.

Apple demonstrated Siri AI finding personal information across Mail and Messages, using the camera to answer questions, and taking actions in apps. The demo involved finding a conversation about making a pie, helping choose ingredients, and adding the remaining items to a grocery list.

There’s a dedicated Siri app for revisiting conversations, with private syncing across Apple devices. Siri is also integrated into the camera, including turning information from a flyer into calendar events. You can use it to write and edit wherever you’re typing.

New on-device voices let you adjust the pace and expressivity. Apple says its on-device model also improves dictation, including punctuation, spelling, and capitalization.

This is what I want Siri to do. My phone already has my messages, calendar, and email. I want to ask about something and have it find the information without needing to explain where everything is.

I’m interested in the voices and dictation too. I use speech a lot, so I want to see how it handles the way I actually talk. I also want to know how much the phone can do locally.

More Apple Intelligence features

Safari is getting Notify Me, which monitors a webpage and tells you when something changes. Shortcuts can use intelligence to do things like update your calendar and reminders when an email arrives.

The Phone app can surface information relevant to a business call, such as a flight confirmation code. Image Playground adds more image styles, while Photos gets improved Clean Up, Extend, and spatial reframing to change a photo’s perspective after capture.

Apple said Apple Intelligence will be available in 16 supported languages with its OS releases. Siri AI is rolling out in beta in English, with French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish coming in October.

Some features that use server models will have usage limits. Increased access will be available through iCloud+ plans.

I already have iCloud+, so I want to know what my plan includes. If I’m going to use these features regularly, I need to understand the limits. I’m especially interested in the things that work with information already on my phone, because that’s where I can see myself using Siri more.

A20 Pro and on-device AI

The A20 Pro is built on two-nanometer technology. It has a six-core CPU with two supercores and four efficiency cores. Apple says the supercores are up to 20 percent faster.

The seven-core GPU offers up to 40 percent more performance. Apple also added a second Neural Engine for a total of 32 cores, doubling its Neural Engine compute power. Memory bandwidth is up 50 percent.

Apple specifically talked about neural accelerators for running third-party language models on the device. It also described improvements to graphics, gaming, and AI image generation.

The chip packaging has changed too. Memory now sits beside the silicon, allowing the silicon to connect directly to the vapor chamber.

This is a big part of what interests me about the new phones. I work with on-device AI, so I’m thinking about the models we can run and what we can build with them.

I want to see how much difference the memory bandwidth and new hardware make when I’m actually using a model. Apple gave us the performance numbers. Now I want to try it.

Cooling, battery life, and gaming

The Pro’s new vapor chamber has three times the surface area of the previous version. Apple also changed the graphite and copper materials used to move heat through the system.

Apple says the result is up to 40 percent better sustained performance than iPhone 17 Pro and up to twice the sustained performance of iPhone 16 Pro and older models.

The smaller iPhone 18 Pro now matches last year’s Pro Max for battery life, according to Apple. Video playback on the eSIM-only models is rated at up to 36 hours on the Pro and 45 hours on the Pro Max.

Apple introduced a mixed-usage estimate that includes activities such as taking photos and using AI. Those estimates are up to 24 hours on the Pro and 30 hours on the Pro Max.

Wired charging reaches up to 50 percent in around 15 minutes. Apple says a five-minute charge provides around six hours of video playback.

Apple then demonstrated Monster Hunter Outlanders, with graphics at up to 120 frames per second, MetalFX upscaling, and spatial audio. It’s scheduled for later this year.

Battery life and cooling matter to me because of how much I use my phone. I want to know how these phones hold up with VoiceOver, my apps, and AI running throughout the day. The smaller Pro matching last year’s Pro Max is something I definitely noticed.

Cameras and video

The Pro’s main camera now has variable aperture. It adjusts how much light enters the camera and affects depth of field. Apple says it can let in around 50 percent more light in darker conditions and narrow the aperture to keep more of a scene in focus.

New Pro Controls let you manually adjust aperture, shutter speed, and white balance, and check exposure with a histogram.

Apple also announced Cinematic mode effects that can be applied after recording regular video, support for 60-frame-per-second Cinematic effects, 4K Dolby Vision HDR time-lapse, and improved Audio Mix processing for voice recordings.

Smart focus tracking uses on-device AI to follow a subject, including when they leave and return to the frame. Photographic Styles adds texture and grain controls that can be changed afterward.

Apple Reference Image uses camera data signed at capture to create an unalterable reference image through Private Cloud Compute. It stays alongside the editable photo. Apple also discussed identifying images generated or edited with AI.

Since I’m streaming and making content, I want to try the video and audio features. I also want to see how accessible the new controls are. Adding more camera options is useful to me if I can get to them and use them while recording.

iOS 27, accessories, and Pro pricing

The Dynamic Island is smaller and can show three Live Activities. iOS 27 adds more parental controls, search improvements, up to 80 percent faster AirDrop transfers, and smarter transitions between cellular and Wi-Fi.

iPhone Handoff lets you use one phone number across two iPhones. The number becomes active on whichever phone you pick up. Apple said support starts with T-Mobile and Telekom Germany, with Verizon and EE joining by the end of the year.

Apple showed updated clear cases, new TechWoven and silicone colors, matching crossbody straps, and a wrist strap that works with iPhone cases and AirPods Pro.

The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199, and the Pro Max starts at $1,299. There’s a new 2TB option. Preorders begin Saturday, September 12, and availability is September 18.

In the US, Apple introduced Apple Upgrade, a leasing program with 12- or 24-month terms. Apple also announced trade-in offers of up to $1,200 for qualifying purchases and AppleCare One Family.

The phone-number feature is interesting if you use more than one iPhone. We were talking about how that could let someone switch between a regular phone and a Duo without needing separate numbers.

I also want more details about AppleCare One Family. It was mentioned pretty quickly, and I’d like to understand what’s included.

I am buying the pro

AirPods 5

AirPods 5 keep the open-ear fit without silicone ear tips. Apple announced a new acoustic design and updated Adaptive EQ, along with active noise cancellation as standard.

Apple says noise reduction is 50 percent better than the previous generation. AirPods 5 also include Transparency mode, Adaptive Audio, personalized spatial audio, Live Translation, and access to Siri AI. Apple says durability against rain, sweat, and dust has improved.

The $129 model gets up to four hours of listening with ANC and up to 20 hours with the charging case.

The $149 model adds volume swipes on the stem, a wireless charging case that supports Apple Watch and Qi chargers, and up to five hours of listening with ANC.

Both opened for preorder today and will be available September 18.

One thing I wanted to understand was what had physically changed. What do these look like compared with the previous AirPods? What is different about the fit? We talked through the open-ear design afterward, along with which version includes volume swipes.

Those are the kinds of details I need when I’m explaining a product to people during a stream.

Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4

Apple introduced a redesigned health sensing system for both watches. It includes changes to the electrodes, photodiodes, and LEDs.

Background heart-rate readings happen every five seconds, which Apple says is 60 times more frequent than before. Heart-rate variability can be measured every five minutes, or 24 times more frequently.

The updated Heart Rate app and watch complications display the more frequent data. HRV is also included in Vitals, with both overnight and daytime views.

A new readiness score uses recent activity, sleep, and vitals to estimate your capacity for the day. The score can update throughout the day and appears on the Watch and in the Fitness app.

I want to see how that information is presented and explained. There’s a lot being measured, and I’m interested in how easy it is to go through with VoiceOver.

The redesigned Health app

The Health app is getting an Insights tab with AI-generated summaries and personalized guidance. Apple also introduced health age and a longevity tab that brings together information about sleep, movement, heart health, and other areas.

You can add lab results manually or through synced medical records. In the US, Apple announced a $119 Quest panel with more than 50 biomarkers, with results brought together with your Watch data.

Apple demonstrated guided movement assessments using the iPhone camera. These include spoken and on-screen instructions and feedback during the assessment.

The redesigned Health app is coming later this year, starting in US English.

I’m glad spoken instructions were part of what they showed. I want to see how the whole process works without needing to look at the screen, including setting up the camera and understanding the results.

Audio Intelligence

Sound Recognition can run directly on Series 12 and Ultra 4, detecting sounds such as alarms, sirens, doorbells, and a baby crying, even without the phone nearby.

Live Rewind lets you double-press the Digital Crown to transcribe the previous 15 seconds. You can ask Siri about the transcript or save it.

Siri Recap creates titles, summaries, and key points from conversations. You can turn it on and off or set a schedule.

Apple says these features don’t create or store audio recordings, don’t identify individual speakers, and use end-to-end encrypted iCloud syncing for saved transcripts and recaps.

Live Rewind and Siri Recap require Siri AI and are coming in beta later this year, starting in English. A new Siri Modular watch face provides access to Siri, previous conversations, and recaps.

I can see why Live Rewind would be useful when somebody gives you several pieces of information at once. I want to try it and see how easy it is to get back to the part I missed.

With Siri Recap, I want to understand how it works around other people and how accurate the notes are. I’d want to see what it keeps from a conversation and what gets left out.

Watch performance, finishes, and battery

The new S11 chip powers the watches, with a faster CPU, GPU, and Neural Engine. Its always-on processor includes protected audio processing for Audio Intelligence.

Series 12 comes in space gray, black, light gold, and dark bronze aluminum. Titanium options are natural and radiant gold. Ceramic versions come in pearl white and night blue.

The aluminum models get Ceramic Shield 2, which Apple says is 60 percent tougher than the previous Ion-X glass. There are new band colors, Nike options, and Hermès additions.

Series 12 is rated for up to 24 hours of battery life. Ultra 4 comes in black and natural titanium and gets more than two days. Apple says it supports up to 18 hours of workout tracking with full GPS and heart rate, or up to 45 hours in the extended workout mode.

Series 12 starts at $399. Both watches opened for preorder today and will be available September 18.

The new chip came up in our discussion because of VoiceOver responsiveness. I want to know if it makes a noticeable difference. Apple didn’t give a specific VoiceOver performance claim, so that’s something we’ll have to test.

John’s “one more thing”

After the phones, AirPods, and watches, John returned to the stage and said there was “one more thing.”

He brought it back to the idea he opened with: the iPhone as your intelligent personal hub. He talked about having a larger display while still fitting the phone in your pocket. Then Apple revealed the iPhone Duo, and John was there holding it.

Having Apple’s new CEO lead the event and then introduce a completely new kind of iPhone was a big part of this keynote. There was already a lot announced before we even got to that moment.

iPhone Duo’s design

The Duo has a 5.4-inch outer display and a 7.6-inch inner display. Both use the same aspect ratio. Apple says the inner display is 50 percent larger in area than the Pro Max display and 80 percent larger than the Pro display.

It comes in star white and night sky, with a polished titanium frame and an inner FaceTime camera hidden behind the display.

Apple described a hinge designed to support the screen when open, a layered display structure, and a nanotexture finish to reduce glare and crease visibility. The display uses a custom polymer cover, glass layers, and a titanium support plate.

The phone has Ceramic Shield on the back, Ceramic Shield 2 on the outer front, and an IP68 rating for dust and water resistance. USB-C Apple Pencil support is coming later this year on both screens.

Authentication uses Touch ID in the side button. You can enroll multiple fingers and unlock the phone with an Apple Watch.

I want Face ID. Touch ID has never worked well for me on phones, and that was my immediate reaction. I understand the options Apple gave, but unlocking my phone is something I do all day.

I also wanted a better description of the colors and physical design. A name like star white doesn’t tell me enough about what the product actually looks like.

Multitasking and using the Duo

The Duo moves controls to the side, including a vertical dock. You can open two apps side by side, use two windows of the same app, swap their positions, and save app pairs.

The interface responds when the phone is folded, rotated, or flipped. You can prop it up without a stand or use it partially folded. StandBy works without charging and adds more faces and a light-based wake-up feature.

Apple showed apps adapting to the design, including Zoom, Slack, Detail, and Netflix. Detail was also shown using on-device models through Core AI.

Speakers at the top and bottom adapt their audio processing to the phone’s orientation and position.

I want to try all of this with VoiceOver. There could be advantages to having more room on the screen, but I need to understand how focus works when you fold it and how moving between apps feels.

The speaker setup is interesting too. We talked about how it might work when listening in different orientations. That’s something I’d want to hear myself.

I sometimes use a crossbody strap to help stabilize my phone for video, so I’d also want to check the accessory options before deciding how the Duo would fit into what I do.

Duo performance and battery

The Duo uses the A20 Pro, including a display engine for both screens, and a vapor chamber. Apple claims up to 35 percent better sustained performance than iPhone 17 Pro.

The C2 modem adds US millimeter-wave support. Apple says uploads are up to 50 percent faster than C1X while using 15 percent less energy, with improvements to reconnecting in low-coverage areas.

The Duo is eSIM-only worldwide. It has a battery in each half, managed together as one system.

Video playback is rated at up to 31 hours on the inner display and 44 hours on the outer display. Mixed usage with both screens used equally is estimated at up to 24 hours. Charging reaches up to 50 percent in around 20 minutes.

From the AI side, I’m interested because it has the A20 Pro. But I’d still need to decide whether I want the folding design. The regular Pro gets the new chip too, so I don’t have to buy the Duo to explore that hardware.

Duo cameras, accessories, and availability

The Duo has a 48-megapixel main camera with 2x optical-quality telephoto and a 48-megapixel Ultra Wide. It supports 4K video at 120 frames per second, updated Photographic Styles, and a Center Stage front camera, along with the inner FaceTime camera.

You can use the rear cameras for selfies while previewing on the outer screen. Duo Preview lets the person being photographed see their framing. Kid Cue displays animations to get a child’s attention.

Smart Take uses on-device AI to follow the scene and automatically take a photo when everyone is ready.

Apple also showed FaceTime sharing front and rear camera views at once, and letting another person join using the outer screen.

Accessories include a folio with an integrated kickstand and a two-part protective case. The Duo starts at $1,999, with storage from 256GB to 2TB. Preorders begin October 16, and availability is October 23.

I’m curious, but I need to use it before deciding. Touch ID is a concern for me, and I want to know how the software works with VoiceOver. At that price, those details matter.

item.title: GPT-6 Astra Is Here, But I Think AI Has a Rollout Problem
item.description: GPT-6 Astra Is Here, But I Think AI Has a Rollout Problem
item.dc:creator: Taylor Arndt
item.content:encoded:
GPT-6 Astra Is Here, But I Think AI Has a Rollout Problem

Yesterday was a very interesting day for the AI community, and I think we’re heading in a direction that I’m not too happy about.

Taylor’s Substack is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

So here’s the deal. Yesterday afternoon, around 2:30 Central, I saw OpenAI announce GPT-6 Astra. This is the newest generation of OpenAI models, and obviously I got excited. They’re talking about coding, research, computer use, cybersecurity, complex multi-step work, all this stuff. Basically, this is supposed to be a really big model.

And of course my immediate thought was, okay, new model release. You know what that means. It’s live streaming time.

I wanted to get it, throw an actual iOS project at it, see how good it was at coding, see what it could do with computer use, test accessibility, and just generally play with it. That’s what I like doing when these models come out. I don’t just want to read a model card or watch somebody else use it. I want to actually use the thing.

So I updated ChatGPT. Nothing. I checked Windows. Nothing. I checked the Mac. Nothing.

Then, of course, all my friends and I started talking about it and trying to figure out what was going on. Is Astra out? Is it not out? Does Pro have it? Do creators have it? Is it only organizations? Do I need to update something? Is it coming later today?

Meanwhile I’m seeing creators posting about Astra. I’m seeing videos about Astra. Everybody is talking about this thing, and I’m trying to figure out why I can’t find it.

Now, I want to be fair here because OpenAI did explain what was happening. In the full announcement, they said Astra was rolling out first to a limited set of organizations and would become available to Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise users over the coming days.

So yes, they said that. I’m not saying they didn’t.

Maybe part of my problem is that I first saw all of this on Twitter, where you have a limited amount of space and everything moves incredibly fast. Maybe somebody who went straight to the full blog post immediately understood exactly what was happening.

But that was not the impression I got from the marketing I saw yesterday.

The impression I got was: GPT-6 Astra is here. Then I saw all these creators posting about using it, and I was kind of like, okay, where is mine?

And actually, at least with creators, they usually tell me when they have early access. They’ll say, ‘OpenAI gave me early access to this,’ or, ‘I’ve been testing Astra for a few days.’ Fine. That makes perfect sense to me. I know immediately why they have it and I don’t. That doesn’t bother me at all.

What bothers me is when the broader marketing around a model feels like a public launch, the entire internet starts talking about it, and then normal paying customers are trying to figure out whether they are actually supposed to have it.

I think we have a problem as an industry with this.

A model can now somehow be announced, launched, rolling out, in early access, and not generally available all at the same time, depending on who you are. That is confusing.

And I think this matters because people already have a hard time trusting tech companies. We’ve seen that over and over again. People hear these huge announcements and immediately wonder what the catch is, what the fine print says, or whether something is actually going to work the way it was advertised.

I’m not saying OpenAI was deliberately trying to trick anybody. Again, they did explain the rollout. But when my friends and I are sitting there having an entire conversation trying to figure out whether a model is actually available, I think something in the communication could have been clearer.

And this isn’t just about OpenAI. I think the whole AI industry needs to get better at this.

If something is early access, say early access. If it is only available to a limited group of organizations today, make that one of the first things people see. If it’s going to start reaching individual customers over the next few days, make that really obvious.

Because I understand why there are evaluations. I understand that governments are important. I understand that cybersecurity researchers need to test a model like Astra. I understand that other organizations need to evaluate it before everything is opened up. Especially with the cybersecurity capabilities OpenAI is talking about here. I get why you have to be careful.

But I also think there is a level where we can over-evaluate these things.

And I could probably turn that into an entirely separate post about China, competition, and whether we’re going to get to a point where we’re moving too slowly while somebody else is willing to move faster. That’s another conversation.

My issue here is much simpler. This slow rollout stuff is getting annoying.

I loved when a model came out and I could use it the same day it came out. The model was announced, I opened ChatGPT, there it was, and I could start playing with it. Maybe I loved it. Maybe I hated it. Maybe I broke it in twenty minutes. Whatever. I could use it. I miss that.

And yes, I understand that this gets harder when you have millions of users and the models are getting more capable. There may be capacity issues. There may be security issues. There may be evaluations that really do need to happen.

But I would have hoped that most of that would be figured out before the big public launch. Or, if it isn’t, then call it what it is.

Say, ‘Today we’re announcing GPT-6 Astra. It is currently available to a limited group, and paid ChatGPT customers will get it over the coming days.’ Okay. That’s fine. I can handle waiting.

What I don’t like is seeing the announcement, seeing the entire AI internet explode, getting excited enough that I’m thinking about rearranging my day so I can stream it, updating my apps, checking multiple computers, and then slowly realizing, oh, okay, I don’t have it.

That was disappointing. And I think there is something a little indecent about creating all of that excitement around something when a lot of the people seeing the excitement still can’t use it.

Again, I’m not saying I deserve every model the second it exists. That’s not my point. My point is that the marketing and the actual availability should match each other better.

And I do want to give OpenAI credit for something they did after the launch. Tibo from OpenAI said that paid ChatGPT users will get one banked usage reset for every day they don’t have access to Astra.

I actually really like that. I pay $200 a month for ChatGPT Pro, so if I have to wait while the rollout happens, giving me something useful for every day I’m waiting is a good gesture. I give OpenAI credit for that.

But I would still rather have really clear communication at the beginning than have the company make it up to people afterward.

And I think the $200 a month part matters too. Individual customers matter.

Yes, governments matter. Enterprises matter. Security researchers matter. Creators matter. But so do the people paying for ChatGPT every month.

I don’t want us to get to a place where individual paying customers are always the people at the end of the line when a major model comes out.

And OpenAI, if you happen to be reading this, maybe give me early access next time. I’m just saying.

I’m a blind creator. I’m a developer. I test AI tools. I work heavily with accessibility, and when I get these models, I actually put them into real workflows.

I don’t see many blind creators getting early access to these things. Maybe there is an accessibility benefit there for you too.

If you’re building models that are supposed to use computers for people, then I think having a blind person testing those computer-use capabilities with a screen reader before everybody gets them might actually tell you some useful things.

Give me early access. Let me test it. Let me break some stuff. I’ll tell you what happened. I’m only half joking.

And yes, this is another reason I keep coming back to local AI.

When a model is actually sitting on my computer, nobody has to roll it out to me. Nobody decides whether I’m in wave one or wave four. Nobody tells me I’ll get it sometime over the next few days. I have it.

Obviously local models have their own issues. You need hardware. Some of them are a pain to set up. They aren’t always going to be as capable as the newest frontier model. But there is something really nice about knowing that the model is there and you can use it whenever you want.

Despite this entire post, I’m still really excited about GPT-6 Astra. That’s actually why I got frustrated.

I want to use it. I want to see how good the coding really is. I want to see what the computer use is like. I want to test it with accessibility. I want to put it into an actual development workflow and see whether it really feels like a new generation of models.

And whenever I get access, yes, I’m still going to stream it.

I just hope this doesn’t become the normal way every major AI model launches.

OpenAI did say ‘over the coming days.’ I want to make that very clear. I just wish ‘over the coming days’ had been as obvious to me yesterday as ‘GPT-6 Astra’ was.

Because I think people can handle waiting. Just make it clear that we’re waiting.

item.title: How I Actually Develop Apps Being Blind
item.description: How I Actually Develop Apps Being Blind
item.dc:creator: Taylor Arndt
item.content:encoded:
How I Actually Develop Apps Being Blind

People keep asking me what my development process actually looks like, so here is what I really do.

Taylor’s Substack is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

People have been asking me how I actually develop apps being blind, especially now that I use AI for so much of my development work. And I think sometimes people assume I just sit there and say, “Hey AI, make me an app,” and then somehow an app comes out. No. That’s definitely not how this works.

So I streamed myself working on Perspective Transcribe, and honestly I think that stream showed my process better than me trying to make some perfect demo. Things broke. VoiceOver talked over me. NVDA wasn’t coming through the stream correctly. Codex did weird things. My Mac fans were going crazy. I thought something was done, tested it on my iPhone, and immediately found another problem. That’s development.

I want to explain how I actually do it because being blind definitely changes my process. Having ADHD changes my process too. I have multiple disabilities, and there are things about a normal software development workflow that just do not work very well for me. AI has changed a lot of that. Not because AI magically made me a developer. I wanted to be a developer way before ChatGPT existed. AI just made a lot more of the process possible for me to do in a way that works with my brain and how I access a computer.

I wanted to make apps before AI

I’ve wanted to make apps for a long time. I got an iPod with VoiceOver when I was around eleven, and then an iPhone when I was around twelve. I remember using all these apps and thinking about how cool it was that I could actually use this device as a blind person. Then I started thinking, I want to make apps too.

By the time I was a teenager, I knew I wanted to develop iPhone apps. The problem was actually figuring out how to do it. Old iOS development was not exactly designed around a blind developer. There was a lot of visual stuff. Storyboards were a big thing. Xcode has had accessibility problems for years. And at that point I didn’t know a bunch of blind iOS developers where I could just go, “Okay, how are y’all doing this?”

I knew blind people were programming, obviously, but I didn’t have this giant group of blind Apple developers teaching me the process. Then I met Michael Doise at the National Federation of the Blind convention in Orlando, Florida in 2018. And the funny part is I met him because of a Google Home Mini. He was doing a drawing in the hotel deli, I entered it, and I won. So somehow winning a Google Home Mini led to all of this.

Michael is low vision and had already been doing app development for years. We became friends, and especially during COVID we started talking a lot more. Eventually he started teaching me Swift and iOS development. Now he’s my boss at Techopolis. So AI did not teach me the idea of software development. Michael taught me a lot of this. I had to learn Swift. I had to learn how apps work. I had to understand what state is, what views are, what models do, how data gets stored, and how an app actually gets built and shipped. That foundation matters.

Then SwiftUI came along, and SwiftUI was huge for me. SwiftUI lets you build Apple interfaces much more through code. For me that matters a lot. If my interface can be described through text and code, I can understand it a lot better than if somebody gives me a visual canvas and tells me to start dragging things around. I can understand that there’s a button, then a list, then a toggle, then a navigation link. I can read the hierarchy with VoiceOver. I can read what the code says that thing is supposed to do.

Now, does that mean SwiftUI automatically makes your app accessible? Absolutely not. You can make a horrible inaccessible SwiftUI app. I’ve seen plenty of them. But it gives me a much better starting point. Then we got AI, and that is where things really changed for me.

AI is an equalizer for me, but not in the way people think

I use the word equalizer intentionally. I’m not saying AI suddenly makes disability disappear. It doesn’t. I’m blind. I have ADHD. I have multiple disabilities. Those things still affect how I work. But there are parts of development where AI can take something that is really annoying or really difficult for me to access and put it into a form that works much better.

Code diffs are a good example. I can absolutely read code with VoiceOver. I do it. But if there are hundreds of lines of changes, added lines, deleted lines, symbols, indentation, file names and everything else, I have to process all of that through speech. That can get really annoying really fast.

So one thing I do is make Codex explain what it changed. Tell me what files you changed. Tell me what functions you changed. Tell me what the old behavior was. Tell me what the new behavior is. Tell me why you did it. Then if something doesn’t make sense, I can go deeper into the actual code. That doesn’t mean I don’t care about the code. It means I’m using AI to make the code review process more accessible to me.

Visuals are another huge one, and we’ll get to visuals because I hate visuals. ADHD is another one, and honestly the ADHD part is probably one of the biggest reasons my current process works.

ChatGPT helps keep me from adding 15 million features

My problem with ADHD is not that I can’t think of things to build. It is the exact opposite. I get too happy. I’ll be working on one thing and then I’ll think, oh, we should add this. And then, oh, we should add this other thing too. And then suddenly I have 15 million features I want to add and the original thing is not done. I love building stuff. That is also sometimes the problem.

So I started using ChatGPT projects as a way to keep myself on track. For Perspective Transcribe, I have a whole ChatGPT project for Perspective Transcribe. I gave it a technical brief. It knows what the app is. It knows how a lot of the project is structured. It knows decisions we’ve already made. It knows the accessibility expectations. It knows what I’m trying to build.

Then when I finish a Codex task, I copy that Codex conversation as Markdown and put it back into the ChatGPT project. I actually made myself a keyboard shortcut for doing this because I do it so much. That means ChatGPT keeps getting updated on what happened, and this has been really useful for me.

I can come back and say, okay, here’s the next thing that’s annoying me, and it already has context. It can also tell me when I’m trying to go crazy. That’s important. I need something that can basically say, yes Taylor, that’s a nice idea, but maybe let’s actually finish the thing we’re working on.

I also start a new chat for every task. When the task is done, I archive it. Done. Gone. Next task. I don’t want 25 different half-finished things in front of me because then my brain is going to go everywhere. This workflow has been working really well for me. Will I do it exactly this way forever? Probably not. AI changes every five seconds. But right now this is what works.

What I actually did on the stream

I was working on Perspective Transcribe. If you haven’t used Perspective Transcribe, it is our transcription app. You can record something or import something and transcribe it. You can get summaries. You can get action items. You can chat with the transcript. So I could have a transcript from the stream and ask something like, “What did Taylor say about VoiceOver?” and it can find that information.

A lot of the AI is happening on the device, which is also why my poor Mac sounded like it was preparing for takeoff during the stream. I’m working on a much bigger update to Transcribe right now. One thing I’ve been adding is speaker diarization. Basically, instead of getting one giant wall of transcript, the app can figure out that different people are speaking. Speaker 1 said this. Speaker 2 said this. And ideally, once the app actually knows the speakers, Taylor said this, Michael said this, and so on.

I also have Quick Capture on the Mac. I made Quick Capture because I needed it. That’s how a lot of my apps happen. I need something, I get annoyed that it doesn’t exist the way I want it, and then I go make it. I talk on Discord a lot. Sometimes I want to capture something from Discord without setting up some giant recording workflow. So I wanted to hit a keyboard shortcut, record what I’m doing, and have Perspective Transcribe handle it. That’s Quick Capture.

Before the stream I had been working on some stuff, got distracted, and didn’t finish it. Again, extremely normal for me. So I finished that work, and then I was looking at Settings. There was a Recording category and it had basically one setting in it: Instant Recording. Then there was an Export category that really didn’t need to be this whole separate thing either.

And I didn’t like that. Especially with VoiceOver. Every category is something I have to navigate to. Every extra screen matters. I don’t want a Settings screen where you open a category and there’s one random toggle sitting in there.

So I went into ChatGPT and basically dictated what I wanted. I didn’t sit there and write some giant engineering document myself. I basically said, we need to fix this because Recording only has this one setting, Export has the same kind of issue, clean this up.

ChatGPT already had all the project context, so it made a Codex task for me. And this is where I really like this workflow, because ChatGPT added things I probably would not have thought to say every single time. Don’t just move the setting and call it done. Check all the Settings categories. Make sure the storage key doesn’t change. Make sure existing users don’t lose their preference. Make sure VoiceOver still announces everything correctly. Check iPhone. Check iPad. Check Mac. Check the visuals. Run the tests. Don’t randomly redesign the rest of Settings while you’re there.

That last part is also very important with coding agents because sometimes you ask them to move a toggle and they decide it’s time to redesign civilization. No. Fix the thing I asked you to fix.

Why I use Codex and how I deal with visuals

Once I have the task, I give it to Codex. I use the standalone Codex app for a lot of this instead of doing everything directly inside Xcode. There are a few reasons for that. Xcode still has accessibility problems. I can use it. I do use it. But Codex gives me a workflow I like better for agent-based coding.

For example, sounds. Codex can make a sound when it needs my attention. I love that. That probably sounds like this tiny stupid feature, but I’m blind. Audio matters. I don’t want to sit there waiting for an AI agent to decide it needs permission to do something. Make a sound. Tell me. Now I can go do something else.

Codex can also work with the simulator, read and change files, run tests and use different skills. That whole system around the AI model matters. People call that the harness. Basically, the AI model is one part. The harness is all the stuff that actually lets it work. I’ve found that Codex’s harness works really well for the way I develop.

I also use Swift and SwiftUI skills with Codex. Just because an AI can write Swift does not mean it understands Swift well. Let me tell you. Swift concurrency can make these models lose their minds. They will fix one problem and create another problem, then fix that and create the first problem again. It’s really fun.

So I use more specific Swift guidance to help the model follow better patterns. Again, this isn’t just me giving one prompt to a magic model. I’m trying to give the model a good environment so it has a better chance of doing good work.

And then there are visuals. Somebody on the stream asked me what the hardest part of developing apps being blind is. Visuals. Visuals are evil. Evil, evil, evil, evil. I don’t like them. But I also care about them.

I don’t want my apps to look bad just because I can’t see them. I don’t want somebody to open something I worked on and say, “Well, obviously a blind person made this.” No. It needs to look good. The problem is there are visual things I just cannot personally verify. Is the spacing weird? Is a label cut off? Did something get shoved into the wrong place on iPad? Is the Mac version ugly? I can’t just look over at the screen and answer all of that.

So I use multiple things. First, I put visual checking into my Codex tasks. Codex can launch the simulator and inspect things. During the stream you could actually hear this happening. It launched an iPhone simulator. Then it killed that one. Then suddenly VoiceOver said iPad because Codex launched an iPad simulator. It was going through the app and testing things. That is really cool to me, and it helps me with something where I have an obvious disadvantage.

But I don’t just trust that either. I still test with VoiceOver. I still test on my physical iPhone. And I have Michael. Michael is low vision, so if I need another human to actually look at something, I can ask him. AI helps. It doesn’t mean I suddenly have sight.

Then I tested the real app and immediately found another bug

Codex finished the Settings change. It ran tests. It built on the different platforms. It checked accessibility. Great. Now I wanted the build on my actual iPhone, because I don’t care how many tests you run. I want to use the thing.

So I opened Perspective Transcribe. I went into Settings. I checked the new organization. It was better. Great. Then I made a recording, because we changed something related to recording Settings, and if recording suddenly doesn’t work, that would be a little embarrassing.

It worked. Great. Then the transcript came back. Speaker diarization ran. VoiceOver said, “Speaker 1.” Okay. So I clicked it. I went to rename the speaker. And then VoiceOver told me this name only applies to this recording.

No. No. No. We need to fix that.

That is basically what I said right there on the stream. I did not like that behavior at all. If I tell the app this person is Taylor, why should I have to do that in every single recording? And if I rename somebody on my iPhone, why wouldn’t I expect my Mac to know about it too? That’s how I want the product to work.

So now the Settings task was finished, but testing it gave me the next task. This is why I actually use my apps.

I copied the finished Codex transcript back into the ChatGPT project. Then I dictated the new issue. And I actually said Windows when I meant iOS while I was dictating because apparently words are hard. But ChatGPT knew what I meant. I basically said that speaker names should not only exist for one recording. Save them in the speaker settings. Sync them across devices. If I rename someone on my iPhone, my Mac should get it.

That was my idea. ChatGPT took that and made another Codex task. Except this one became much more complicated, because Speaker 1 in one recording is not necessarily Speaker 1 in another recording. Those are just labels the diarization system made for that particular recording. So you can’t just say Speaker 1 equals Taylor forever. Because then I could have a completely different person in another recording and suddenly the app thinks they’re me. That would be bad.

So now we had to deal with actual speaker profiles, saved identities, how a speaker in a specific recording connects to a saved speaker, syncing, CloudKit, SwiftData, exports and all kinds of stuff. All because I clicked a button and said, no, I don’t like this. This is what I mean when I say I am still making product decisions.

AI can help, but it also has to know when not to guess

When Codex started looking into the speaker system, it found that we already had more pieces of this than I thought. There were speaker profiles. There were embeddings coming from the local diarization system. An embedding is basically a numerical representation the system can use to compare something, in this case voices.

And this is where I don’t want AI to get too confident. Just because you have some numbers that say two voices might be similar does not mean I want the app deciding that somebody is Taylor and changing their name everywhere. That would be horrible.

So the work had to be conservative. Save the speaker. Give them a stable identity. Sync that correctly. But don’t just go around deciding that every voice sounds close enough and now they’re the same person. I would much rather the app say, “I don’t know who this is,” than confidently identify somebody incorrectly.

While Codex was working through this, it also found an accessibility problem in what it had made. VoiceOver could announce an unnamed local speaker in a way that made it sound like that person was already a saved speaker. It could also say Speaker 1 twice in a way that was confusing. So it went back and fixed that too.

That’s what I want. I don’t want accessibility to be something we do after the feature is finished. The VoiceOver experience is the feature too. If I add a speaker system and a blind person can’t understand whether they’re editing a detected speaker or a saved person, the feature isn’t done. That’s not an accessibility bug I’ll get to later. That’s a broken feature.

Eventually Codex got the tests passing. Then it put a new build on my phone. And I went back and tested it. Record something. Let it transcribe. Check the speakers. Try the rename. See if the thing actually does what I asked for. That’s my process.

It is a loop. I have an idea. I explain it. ChatGPT helps me turn it into a more complete task. Codex works on it. I read what it did. Automated tests run. Accessibility gets checked. Visuals get checked as much as possible. Then I use the actual app. And sometimes I immediately go, nope. We’re doing this again.

AI is not doing all my thinking

I think this is something people really misunderstand about AI coding. Yes, AI writes a lot of code for me now. A lot. I’m not going to pretend otherwise. Why would I?

But look at what happened just during this one stream. I decided the Settings organization was bad. I decided the speaker behavior was bad. I decided speaker names should sync. I decided that Speaker 1 can’t mean the same human across every recording. I questioned Codex when it started doing something weird with code signing. I had to decide whether test failures were actually caused by my changes. I found a bug by actually using the app. I decided how I expected the product to behave. I decided I don’t want the app automatically identifying people if it isn’t confident enough.

I made those decisions. The AI helps me get from the decision to a working implementation much faster. There is a difference.

There’s a lot of talk about AI replacing developers. There’s also a lot of talk about people vibe coding things when they have no idea what they’re doing. Fine. Talk about that. But I think there is another part of this story people should be paying more attention to: what does this technology mean for disabled people?

Because for me, this is a big deal. I can dictate a messy bug report and have it turned into something Codex can work from. I can have a huge code change explained in plain English. I can have an agent inspect things visually that I cannot see. I can keep my project context somewhere so when my ADHD sends my brain in twelve directions, I have something that can help pull me back to what I’m actually supposed to be doing.

I can make the computer work more like I work. That is why I keep calling AI an equalizer. It doesn’t mean everything is easy now. Xcode still has accessibility problems. AI still does dumb things. Sometimes Codex takes forever. Sometimes I have two screen readers talking over each other because I’m running Windows in Parallels on my Mac. Sometimes I say Codex when I mean Discord. Sometimes my Mac sounds like it is about to fly across the room because we’re running transcription models, language models, simulators and compilers all at the same time.

But I can build. And I can build a lot more than I could before.

I want to hear how other people are doing this

I really love making apps, even when it’s annoying. There’s something really cool about having an idea because something annoys me, then actually making the thing exist. Quick Capture exists because I wanted it. A lot of Perspective Transcribe exists because I wanted a better transcription workflow. Perspective Intelligence came from us wanting a different way to work with AI and documents.

I’m going to keep doing this, and I’ll probably change my development process again. There will be a new AI model. There will be a new Codex feature. Apple will change Swift again and probably break something. I’ll find another workflow I like better. That’s fine. This is what works for me right now.

And since people keep asking how a blind person actually develops an app, I wanted to show the real process instead of pretending it’s cleaner than it is. Because it isn’t clean. But it works.

If you’re a blind developer or another disabled developer, I’m really curious how you’re doing this. Are you using AI? Are you using Xcode directly? Do you use Codex, Claude Code, something else? What part of development is still the biggest pain for you?

And if you’re a developer who isn’t disabled, I’m curious too. Did any part of my workflow surprise you? I especially want to hear from people doing iOS development because I didn’t grow up knowing this giant group of blind iOS developers. If you’re out there building apps, tell me what you’re building.

If you’re curious about the apps I’m actually building with this process, go try Perspective Transcribe and Perspective Intelligence. And don’t just download them and never open them either. Actually use them. Record something in Transcribe. Import something. Try the summaries. Try the chat. If you’re using VoiceOver, tell me what annoys you.

Seriously. If something makes you say, “Taylor, why in the world does it do this?” tell me. That’s basically how the speaker bug in this article got found.

And if you know somebody who thinks blind people can’t develop apps, send this to them too. I think they might be surprised.

item.content:encoded:
Why We Changed Start Testing

So after all y’all’s feedback, I ended up rethinking a lot of Start Testing.

Taylor’s Substack is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

Not just one feature or one page. I mean the pricing, the plans, how businesses fit into it, how clients fit into it, and really what I want Start Testing to become.

And I think the biggest thing I realized is that we had built a lot more product than the pricing really explained.

Start Testing started from testing and issue tracking, but it has grown into project management for software teams. You can track projects, tasks, issues, app feedback, GitHub issues, releases, accessibility work, reviews, milestones, sprints, and all the other things that happen while you’re actually building software.

But the way we were packaging it still felt like we were selling pieces of the product instead of the whole thing.

So I wanted to change that.

The first thing was figuring out who the plans are actually for

One problem with the old pricing was that everybody was basically looking at the same thing.

But somebody working by themselves and somebody running an agency are not making the same buying decision.

So we split the pricing into Individual and Business.

If you’re working on your own, there’s Free, Individual at $5 a month, and Individual Pro at $15.

Then the business side starts with Team at $29 a month, Studio at $99, Agency at $250, and Enterprise is Contact Sales.

That part sounds like just changing prices, but there was more thinking behind it.

For example, Studio and Agency now have unlimited active projects.

I kept coming back to this idea that if a company is using Start Testing for project management, I don’t really want to make money by making them nervous about creating projects.

If an agency has another client project, they should be able to create the project.

That is literally what the software is for.

There are still reasonable-use rules, obviously, but the product should encourage people to use it instead of making every new project feel like another billing decision.

Then I started thinking more about how businesses actually work

This is where client collaborators became important.

If you have an agency with ten employees and five clients, the people at those client companies are not the same as the people working for the agency.

That sounds obvious, but a lot of software pricing doesn’t really treat it that way.

You invite a client because they need to see their project or give feedback, and suddenly that person becomes another paid seat.

I didn’t want that.

So on Studio, Agency, and Enterprise, external client collaborators don’t use your internal seats.

Employees and contractors working for your organization still count as internal users.

But the client who needs access to their own work doesn’t.

Studio supports up to five active client organizations, and Agency supports unlimited active client organizations.

We also added client archiving, because I don’t think finishing work with a client should mean deleting their history just to free up capacity.

That was one of those things where I started thinking less about, ‘What feature should we add?’ and more about, ‘What would make this annoying to actually run a company with?’

Lyra also needed to make more sense

Lyra is the AI side of Start Testing.

It powers AI features inside the product, and we use credits to measure that usage.

The important part is that Lyra credits are not your Start Testing usage.

They’re specifically for AI.

So Team includes 250 Lyra credits each month. Studio includes 750. Agency includes 2,000.

If you use all of those credits, your projects do not stop working.

Your issues don’t get locked.

You can still manage tasks, work with GitHub, handle releases, use accessibility workflows, and do all the normal project management stuff.

You’ve just used the included AI capacity for that billing period.

I wanted that separation to be really clear because I don’t want Start Testing to become one of those products where AI is technically ‘included,’ but then the entire product is designed around getting you to buy more AI usage.

Lyra is there to help with the work.

It is not the thing you are buying instead of the project management system.

And as we learn more about how people actually use Lyra, I’m sure those allowances will keep evolving too.

I also didn’t want every feature to become a pricing decision

This was another big part of it.

It is really easy when you build SaaS to start making a giant feature matrix.

This plan gets GitHub.

This plan gets forms.

This one gets accessibility.

This one gets API access.

And pretty soon nobody actually knows what they are buying.

I didn’t want to do that.

Paid Start Testing plans broadly include the core product.

Projects, issues, tasks, features, milestones, sprints, releases, forms, GitHub, App Store Connect and TestFlight, accessibility workflows, reviews, reporting, API, MCP.

The pricing differences are mostly around capacity.

How many people are using it.

How many projects or clients you are managing.

How much attachment storage you need.

How much Lyra you use.

That is a pricing model I can explain without needing a giant comparison spreadsheet.

Enterprise was probably the biggest change in how I was thinking

Before, Enterprise was too close to being just another plan with a bigger number.

And the more I thought about it, the less sense that made.

Enterprise companies don’t usually come to you and say, ‘We just need twenty more seats.’

They have other requirements.

They might need invoice billing.

They might need onboarding.

They might have security reviews.

They might need SSO.

They might need a DPA.

They might have audit requirements or data-retention requirements.

They might need something I haven’t even thought about.

And I don’t think the right answer is for me to sit here and invent fifty Enterprise features just because that makes the pricing page look more impressive.

So Enterprise is now Contact Sales.

Right now it gives us room for custom internal seats, unlimited projects and clients, 500 GB or more of storage, custom Lyra allowances, onboarding, invoice billing, and enhanced support.

But the bigger reason I wanted Enterprise set up this way is because I want those conversations.

If a larger organization is seriously looking at Start Testing and there is something preventing them from using it, I want to know what that thing is.

Maybe we already have an answer.

Maybe it is something we need to build.

Either way, that is a much better way for me to figure out the Enterprise side of Start Testing than guessing.

So this release is really about making Start Testing easier to understand

Yes, the prices changed.

The plans changed.

Storage changed.

Lyra changed.

Client access changed.

Enterprise changed.

But for me, the bigger change is that the pricing now matches how I think about the product.

Start Testing is project management for software teams.

I want the paid plans to give you the actual product.

Then the price should grow when your usage and your organization grow, not because you suddenly need one particular checkbox.

That feels a lot more straightforward.

And now that the new version is out, I’m especially interested in talking with agencies and larger organizations about how they’re managing projects today and what Start Testing would need to replace or simplify.

If you’re looking at Start Testing for a business or an Enterprise deployment, you can book some time with me.

I’d rather hear how your organization actually works than make assumptions about what you need.

item.title: Your Vibe-Coded App Probably Doesn't Need That Custom Control
item.description: Your Vibe-Coded App Probably Doesn’t Need That Custom Control
item.dc:creator: Taylor Arndt
item.content:encoded:
Your Vibe-Coded App Probably Doesn’t Need That Custom Control

I see so many apps now that people want me to test, especially apps being built with AI, and a lot of them are not accessible.

Taylor’s Substack is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

But here is the frustrating part.

A lot of them absolutely have the potential to be.

I will open an app and think, this is actually cool. I like what they are trying to do here. The app looks like it has been thought through, the idea is good, and then I start going through it with VoiceOver and something that should be really simple just does not work.

And one thing I keep seeing is custom controls.

Developers are obsessed with custom controls.

I understand why.

I am a SwiftUI developer. I like making things look good too. Sometimes you don’t want the default thing. Maybe you want a different-looking toggle. Maybe you want your own picker. Maybe you have some really nice cards where one of them is selected. Maybe you want a button to animate differently or you want something that fits the design of your app better.

That is fine.

I am not saying do not make custom controls.

But I think we need to talk about what you are actually doing when you decide to replace the control Apple already gave you.

What are you actually replacing?

Let’s take SwiftUI.

SwiftUI already gives us Button.

It gives us Toggle.

It gives us Picker.

It gives us Slider, TextField, TabView, and all of these other controls.

And those controls are not just what you see on the screen.

That is the part I think gets missed.

SwiftUI has accessibility support built into the framework. Apple specifically documents accessibility modifiers and representation APIs so developers can preserve or refine what assistive technology gets from an interface.

So when I use a real SwiftUI Button, I am not just getting something I can tap.

I am getting a control the system already understands as a button.

VoiceOver understands it.

The operating system understands it.

Apple has already done a bunch of work for me.

Same thing with something like a Toggle. It already has the concept that this thing can be on or off. A Picker already has a selection.

Then we come along and go:

Well, I don’t like how that looks.

And now instead of a Button, maybe we have an HStack with an onTapGesture.

Or instead of a Toggle, we make our own thing with a circle that slides across the screen.

And that might look fantastic.

But now you have to ask:

What did I just throw away?

This is what I keep finding

I will find something where there are three choices on the screen.

Let’s say:

Basic.

Pro.

Business.

You select Pro and visually it changes color.

Great.

Then I come along with VoiceOver and swipe through it.

Basic, button.

Pro, button.

Business, button.

Okay.

Which one is selected?

I have no idea.

The developer built the visual selected state. The AI built the visual selected state. Everybody looking at the screen knows exactly what is happening.

But nobody told VoiceOver.

Or I get a custom switch.

I activate it.

The little thing moves from the left to the right.

Is it on?

Is it off?

VoiceOver does not know.

Or somebody has made a really nice custom control where tapping a card does something.

Maybe VoiceOver does not even tell me it is a button.

Maybe I hear a bunch of text and have no idea that I am supposed to interact with the thing.

This is the kind of stuff I am seeing in apps people are giving me to test.

And I keep thinking, why?

Because these apps are not that far away from being accessible.

Some of them are really close.

I think vibe coding makes this easier to do

This is one of the things I worry about with vibe coding.

You tell the AI:

Make this look better.

Make me a custom toggle.

Make these options look like cards.

Make this whole row clickable.

Make this picker more modern.

And it does it.

That is what you asked for.

And I use AI to code too, so I am not saying AI coding is bad. I use it all the time.

But if what you asked for was a visual design, that is what it is going to focus on.

And if the custom thing looks right and you can tap on it, it is really easy to go:

Great. That works.

Until somebody like me comes along and actually tries to use it with VoiceOver.

The AI does not get lost.

It does not hear three buttons and wonder which one is selected.

It does not sit there trying to figure out whether your switch is on or off.

It does not get frustrated because it cannot find the control you spent all afternoon making look really good.

That is why somebody still has to test this stuff.

But I want a custom control

Okay.

Make one.

Seriously.

If the custom control makes your app better, build it.

Apple gives developers accessibility APIs for custom interfaces for exactly this reason.

But now you own more of the work.

That is the point.

You have to think about what this thing is.

What should VoiceOver call it?

What state is it in?

Can I operate it?

If the state changes, can I tell?

If something opens, where does my focus go?

If it has some special gesture, is there another way for me to perform that action?

What happens with Voice Control?

What happens with Switch Control?

And then you have to actually test those things.

Here is something else I think is really interesting in SwiftUI.

Sometimes you can still have the custom design without throwing the underlying accessibility away.

Apple’s accessibilityRepresentation API is specifically designed for cases where a custom interface can be represented to accessibility using another SwiftUI view. Apple also notes that custom styles can preserve the accessibility features of the underlying control.

That is exactly what I am talking about.

You do not always have to choose between:

boring app

and

accessible app.

Sometimes the answer is to customize the native thing instead of rebuilding the entire thing from scratch.

Do you really want to rebuild all of this?

This is the question I want vibe coders especially to ask.

Do you really want to replicate the mountain of work Apple already did?

Because Apple has been working on VoiceOver and accessibility across its platforms for years.

You get a lot of that work when you use the platform the way it was designed.

Then we sometimes throw that away because the AI can recreate the visible part of a control in thirty seconds.

Now we have to recreate the rest of it.

And maintain it.

And test it.

And make sure the next AI refactor does not break it.

And make sure when we add another state later, accessibility gets that state too.

That sounds like more work to me.

And this is not just an Apple idea.

On the web, W3C literally has what it calls the first rule of ARIA: if a native HTML element already gives you the semantics and behavior you need, use it instead of recreating the control with ARIA.

There is a reason people keep giving this advice.

Native controls have a bunch of behavior that somebody else has already built and tested.

Why take all of that work back onto yourself unless there is a good reason?

And yes, accessibility can become a legal problem too

I do want to talk about this because I think developers need to know it, but I also don’t want to scare people with bad legal information.

I am not a lawyer and this is not legal advice.

Depending on what you are building, who you are building it for, and where you are doing business, accessibility can create legal and compliance risk.

In the United States, the Department of Justice has specific accessibility requirements for web content and mobile apps from state and local governments under Title II of the ADA, using WCAG 2.1 Level AA as the technical standard.

For private businesses, the legal situation can depend on the business, the service and the jurisdiction, but the ADA does impose accessibility obligations on businesses open to the public, and DOJ publishes guidance about accessibility of businesses’ digital offerings.

And if you are offering certain covered products or services in the EU, the European Accessibility Act covers areas including e-commerce, banking services, smartphones, computers and other covered products and services.

So yes, potentially this can get bigger than one blind person being annoyed by your custom picker.

But honestly, that is not even the main argument I want to make.

I want to use your app

That is what I wish more developers understood.

When I test one of these apps and complain that I cannot use a control, it is usually because I was actually trying to use the app.

I wanted to see what it did.

I wanted to sign up.

I wanted to try the feature.

Sometimes I really like the idea.

And then I get to something that the developer probably thought was a tiny piece of the interface and I cannot continue.

That is what is frustrating.

You did all of this work.

You had the idea.

You used AI and got something built that maybe would have taken you months before.

You shipped it.

And then I cannot use it because the custom control that replaced a Toggle never tells VoiceOver whether it is on.

Come on.

We can do better than that.

Especially because SwiftUI gives us such a good place to start.

Before you tell the AI to make another custom control

Just ask yourself:

Does SwiftUI already have something that does this?

Can I style that instead?

Can I use a custom ButtonStyle or ToggleStyle and keep the underlying control?

If I really do need to build this myself, what did the native control used to do for accessibility that I now have to do?

And after you build it, turn on VoiceOver.

Actually use it.

Don’t just ask your AI:

Is this accessible?

Don’t just look through the code and see an accessibility label and assume everything is good.

Use the thing.

Try to select something.

Try to turn your switch on.

Open your custom picker.

Close it.

See where VoiceOver goes.

Do your actual app flow.

Because that is what I am going to do when you give the app to me.

And that is really why I started Taylor’s Teardowns.

I keep seeing apps with potential that are not accessible.

I don’t want to tell somebody their whole app is terrible and they need to start over.

A lot of the time they don’t.

I want to be able to say:

This is good.

This part works.

Here is where I got stuck.

Here is the custom control that is causing the problem.

Here is what I would fix first.

That is a lot more useful.

So please, make your app look great.

Make cool SwiftUI interfaces.

Use AI.

I do.

Build the custom control when you actually need the custom control.

But before you replace something Apple already gives you, remember how much work is hiding underneath that boring control.

You might be replacing a lot more than you think.

Sources and further reading

  • Apple Developer Documentation: Accessibility modifiers in SwiftUI

  • Apple Developer Documentation: accessibilityRepresentation(representation:)

  • W3C: Using ARIA - First Rule of ARIA Use

  • U.S. Department of Justice: Title II web and mobile app accessibility rule

  • U.S. Department of Justice: Guidance on Web Accessibility and the ADA

  • European Commission: European Accessibility Act

Want me to test yours?

This is exactly why I do Taylor’s Teardowns.

Give me your app, website, web app, AI chatbot, or whatever you built. I use it the way a blind customer actually would, with a screen reader and keyboard where that applies, and I tell you where I get stuck, what happened, and what I would fix first.

A written teardown is $75 during launch pricing. The teardown with a recorded screen-reader walkthrough is $175 during launch pricing. The launch pricing is limited to the first 20 teardowns.

If you built something with AI and you are not sure what VoiceOver actually gets from all those custom controls, send it to me. I would rather help you fix the app while it has all that potential than watch a blind customer hit one control and leave.
