item.title: I Keep Testing Vibe-Coded Apps. Here Are the Problems I Keep Finding.
item.description: I Keep Testing Vibe-Coded Apps.
item.dc:creator: Taylor Arndt
item.content:encoded:
I Keep Testing Vibe-Coded Apps. Here Are the Problems I Keep Finding.

Okay, so I want to talk about something I have been noticing over and over, and I want to do it the way I would if you and I were just sitting down together. Not a lecture. Not a scolding. Not a 200-page report that nobody reads. Just the pattern I keep running into, from somebody who is actually in these apps every week.

Taylor’s Substack is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

Here is the short version. I keep getting handed apps that were built with AI, I open them with a screen reader, and I keep finding the same three problems. Not different problems every time. The same three. Over and over, in app after app, from people who have never met each other and are not building anything alike.

That is what made me want to write this. When you see the same thing once, it is a bug. When you see it every single time, it is not a bug anymore, it is the tool. And if it is the tool, then I can tell you exactly what to look for before you ship, and you can fix it yourself in an afternoon.

I am a blind developer. I have been doing accessibility since 2017, so eight years now. I have tested products, trained teams, consulted, and built the tools, inside some of the biggest names in the field and at the small studio I run accessibility for now. I also build apps for Apple platforms for a living, accessible from the first line, so I am not talking about this from the sidelines. I ship it. And I use a screen reader all day, every day, still doing screen reader testing every single week. So this is not a hot take. It is a list of what actually happens when I open your app.

First, what even is vibe coding

Let me back up, because not everybody knows the term, and that is completely fine.

Vibe coding is a name Andrej Karpathy coined in early 2025. It means building software by describing what you want in plain language and letting the AI write the code for you. You steer it by prompting and trying things instead of reading every line yourself. In the fuller version of it, people do not read the code at all. Something breaks, they paste the error back in, the AI fixes it, and they keep going. You go off the vibes.

And honestly, I think it is amazing. I really do. People who could never ship software before are shipping real things now. A few years ago making an app meant opening Xcode and writing every line by hand, and it took forever, and most people just never got to have the thing they wanted to build. Now somebody can put an app together in an afternoon. That is genuinely good and I am not here to dunk on it or gatekeep it.

I will say clearly that I am not a vibe coder myself. I use AI to write my code and then I actually read it, because I know what good looks like and I know what breaks. But that is me. The wave of new builders coming in does not work that way, and we have to deal with the world as it is, not the one we wish we had.

And it is not slowing down. It got a lot more popular this year, and the part that changed things for me is that it moved onto phones. For a while this was mostly websites, and now people are shipping real mobile apps this way, into the App Store, to real customers. Which is why my list is a mobile list. These are the three things I hit in almost every AI-built app I test on a phone.

Problem one: I have no idea what went wrong

This is the one that gets me every time, and it is almost always in the very first thing you ask somebody to do, which is sign up.

I go to create an account. I type my email, except I fat-finger it, or I leave off the dot com, or I put something in that the app does not like. Then I hit the button.

And nothing happens.

That is the entire experience. Nothing happens. The form does not go through, and not one thing on that screen tells me why. No announcement. My screen reader stays silent. Focus does not move to the field that has the problem. There is no sound, no vibration, nothing.

So I press the button again, because as far as I can tell it did not register. Nothing. I press it a third time. Now I am starting to think the app is broken, or my internet is out, or I did something wrong somewhere else on the screen.

Here is what is actually happening. There is a little bit of red text under the email field that says the email is not valid. If you can see the screen, this is a solved problem. You glance down, you see red, you fix it, you move on. It takes you two seconds and you never think about it again.

I never got told. The error appeared visually and that was the whole implementation. Nobody made it announce, nobody moved focus to it, and a lot of the time the error text is not even connected to the field it belongs to, so even if I go hunting for it, it reads as some random floating sentence with no obvious relationship to anything.

And on a phone this is so much worse than on a computer. On a website I can jump around, I can pull up a list of things on the page, I have ways to go looking. On a phone I am swiping through the screen one element at a time. So finding out what went wrong means swiping through your entire form, element by element, hoping something eventually says the word email. That is if I even guess that an error exists. Most people would have assumed the app was broken and closed it. Honestly, most days, so would I.

Think about what that means for you. That is your signup screen. That is the very first thing a customer does. So the failure is not that some deep feature is hard to use. The failure is that I cannot get an account.

Problem two: my focus goes flying and I lose my place

This one is harder to explain to somebody who has not used a screen reader, so let me try to make it real.

When I am using an app, I have a spot. There is one thing on the screen that my screen reader is currently on, and everything I do is relative to that spot. It is my cursor. It is the only thing telling me where I am in your app. If you have ever lost your place reading a page, it is that, except I cannot just glance back and find it again.

So here is what keeps happening. I am somewhere in the middle of a screen, and I hit a control to do the actual thing your app is for. Save it, add it, send it, start it, whatever your app does. That is the moment that matters.

And my focus shoots straight to the bottom of the screen.

Or it jumps to the top. Or it lands on nothing at all and my screen reader just says nothing, which is its own special kind of confusing. Every so often it ends up somewhere completely unrelated, on a tab bar or a header I was nowhere near.

Now I am lost. I do not know if the thing I pressed worked. I do not know if something new appeared. I do not know where I am. So I have to swipe all the way back through the screen to find my place again and reconstruct what happened. If I have to do that every single time I press the main button in your app, using your app is exhausting, and I am not going to keep doing it.

What is actually going on is that pressing the control caused the screen to rebuild itself. The app redraws, the element my screen reader was sitting on gets thrown away and recreated, and the screen reader has to land somewhere, so it lands wherever it lands. Nobody ever told it where focus should go.

That is the real problem, and it is not really an AI problem, it is an attention problem. Focus after an action is a decision somebody has to make on purpose. When you tap the thing, focus should either stay right where I am, or move deliberately to whatever just appeared, the confirmation, the new screen, the error. Somebody has to decide that and write it down. The AI never decided anything, because it does not know focus exists. It cannot feel itself get lost.

Problem three: the selected one is only selected if you can see it

Third one, and this one is quietly everywhere.

Almost every app has a row of choices. Filter chips at the top of a list. A little segmented control for something like day, week, month. Tabs. A set of options where one of them is on.

You tap one and it turns blue. The others stay gray. Done. Obvious.

To me, every single one of those is a button. That is it. My screen reader reads down the row and says button, button, button, button. Not one of them tells me which one is currently on.

So I genuinely do not know what I am looking at. I do not know which filter is applied, so I do not know why the list below has the items it has. I do not know which tab I am on. I do not know which option I picked, or if I picked one at all. And if I try to fix that by just tapping one to be sure, sometimes I turn off the one that was already on, and now I have made it worse, and I still cannot tell.

Here is the thing that makes this one frustrating rather than just unfortunate. Both iOS and Android have this built in and free. There is a proper way to say this control is selected, and every screen reader on the planet knows how to read it. It is one property. It is not hard, it is not obscure, and it does not cost you anything visually.

The AI just does not do it, for a reason that makes total sense once you see it. The AI is building what the screen looks like. Blue means selected to a person looking at it, so the AI styles it blue and considers the job finished. There is a whole parallel layer underneath the visual one, the layer that says what each thing is and what state it is in, and that layer is the entire thing my screen reader reads. The AI is not writing it, because nobody can see it, and looking right is what the AI is optimizing for.

This is also why AI loves to build its own controls from scratch. Ask for a set of toggle buttons and it will happily construct them out of plain tappable boxes instead of using the real control the platform already gives you, the one that would have handed you the selected state, the keyboard behavior, and the screen reader support for free. It rebuilds the thing that already existed, minus everything that made it good.

And I want to be clear that these are not the only three. Not even close. I could sit here all day. Buttons with no name at all, so my screen reader just says button and I have to guess what it does. No headings anywhere on the screen, so I cannot jump around and I have to swipe through every single thing to get where I am going. Images and icons with nothing describing them. Sliders and pickers I cannot actually move. Something slides up from the bottom of the screen and never announces itself, so I do not even know it is there.

I picked these three because they are the ones I hit in almost every app I open, and because all three of them stop me from finishing what I came into your app to do. The rest of it makes your app annoying. These three make it impossible.

Why it is always these three

I want to say something about the pattern, because I think it explains more than the individual bugs do.

Look at what those three have in common. An error you can see. A focus position you can see. A selection you can see. Every one of them works perfectly if you are looking at the screen, and every one of them is completely missing underneath.

That is not the AI being sloppy. That is the AI doing exactly what it was asked. It was asked to make something that looks right, and it made something that looks right. It has never once used what it built. It does not get confused, it does not lose its place, it does not press a button three times wondering if the app is broken. It cannot, so it does not know to check.

And that is also why your tests all pass. The email field exists, so the test passes. The button responds, so the test passes. The chips render, so the test passes. Those tests are not wrong. They are just answering a completely different question than the one that matters, which is whether a person can finish the task.

Nobody has to be at fault here for this to be a real problem. Most people building this way were never taught any of it. It never came up. That is why I would rather write this down than complain about it.

So here is what to actually do

Alright, this is the part that matters most, and most of it is free and you can do it today.

Turn on VoiceOver on your own phone and use your own app. This is the single highest value twenty minutes you will spend. On an iPhone you can set the side button to toggle it, and you only need three gestures to get going: swipe right to move to the next thing, double tap anywhere to activate what you are on, and two finger swipe down to read from the top. That is enough.

Then go sign up for your own product with it on. Deliberately type a bad email and see whether anything on earth tells you what went wrong. Then press your main action button and just listen to where you end up. Then swipe across your filter row and count how many times you hear the word selected. You will not need me to interpret the results. You will hear it.

Use the real controls instead of letting the AI invent new ones. If the platform has a segmented control, a switch, a picker, an alert, use it. You get the state, the keyboard behavior, and the screen reader support for free, and free is a good price.

Put the accessibility review into how you already build. If you are coding with AI, you can get accessibility agents right into that workflow so the review happens as the code is written instead of never. A group of us built exactly that with Jeff Bishop and the Community Access folks, and they work with Claude Code, Copilot, Codex, and Claude Desktop. They are free and open source, because gatekeeping the fix would defeat the whole point. You can grab them at the accessibility agents on GitHub.

And know the ceiling on the automated stuff, including mine. A checker can tell you a button has no label. It cannot tell you that pressing your main button throws me to the bottom of the screen and I never find my way back, because getting lost is a human thing. A scanner does not get frustrated and delete your app. I do.

Where I come in

That last part is the whole reason I do teardowns.

A teardown is me taking your product and using it the way a blind customer actually would, with a screen reader, on a real device. I sign up, I log in, I do the main thing your app is for. Then I tell you in plain language where it works, where it falls apart, and what to fix first in priority order. Not a scan somebody ran. A real blind developer using your app, telling you what happened.

And while I am in there I write down the regular bugs too, the ones that have nothing to do with accessibility. The flow that takes eleven steps when it should take four. The button that does nothing. The thing that says it saved and did not. I always find some, because that is what happens when a person actually uses software instead of testing it. You get that either way.

If you have an iOS app, send me a public TestFlight link or the App Store link and I test it on a real device with VoiceOver, not a simulator. If you are on Android, send me a Play Store link or an internal testing link and I test it on a real device with TalkBack. Web apps, AI chatbots, whatever else, same deal.

Let me be straight about what it does not cover, because that honesty is the whole point of how I work. A teardown is the screen reader and keyboard experience. It is not a full WCAG audit and I am not going to pretend it is. The purely visual things, color contrast being the obvious one, are real accessibility problems that matter, and I am blind, so I am not the right person to judge whether your gray text is readable. A checker measures that precisely and a full audit covers it formally. Techopolis does those when you genuinely need one, and if that is what your situation calls for I will tell you that instead of selling you the wrong thing.

You also do not have to take my word for what you get, because I publish teardowns in the open. Go read my teardown of ActiveCampaign, my teardown of Codex, or my teardown of Xcode Intelligence. Yours looks exactly like that, except yours is private unless you decide otherwise.

Let me put the money in perspective, because this is where people freeze up. A written teardown is 75 dollars right now, down from 149, and you get the findings on your key flows plus the specific things to fix in priority order. A teardown with a recorded screen reader walkthrough is 175, down from 349, and honestly that recording is the one I would pick, because hearing your own app go silent on somebody is a lot more convincing to a team than reading about it. That is launch pricing for the first 20 teardowns, and there are only a few of those spots left, so if you have been meaning to do this, now is the moment.

For comparison, a traditional audit runs two to five thousand dollars and up. If what you actually need right now is to find out whether a real person can use the thing you built, you do not need to spend that yet. Start here, let it show you where the pain is, and spend the audit money later if it turns out you need to. You can book a teardown right here.

One last thing

I am not writing this to tell you not to build with AI. Build with AI. I do. The fact that you shipped something is the hard part and you already did it.

I just want you to know that there is a layer of your app you have never seen, and right now the tool you are building with is not writing it. Three things. Tell me what went wrong. Do not lose my place. Say which one is selected. Fix those three and you will be ahead of almost every AI-built app I have opened this year.

And if you are not sure where yours stands, just ask me. Tell me what you built and I will give you the truth about it, no pressure either way.

item.title: AI Finally Gave Some of Us a Level Playing Field. I Don't Want Watermarking to Take That Away.
item.description: AI Finally Gave Some of Us a Level Playing Field.
item.dc:creator: Taylor Arndt
item.content:encoded:
AI Finally Gave Some of Us a Level Playing Field. I Don’t Want Watermarking to Take That Away.

Yesterday I was browsing online like I normally do, reading about AI, and I found something that genuinely concerned me.

Taylor’s Substack is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

Anthropic is starting to put machine-readable marks into text generated by Claude.

Not just images.

Not just audio or video.

Text.

For supported Claude models, Anthropic says generated text will carry an embedded, imperceptible watermark. The company says those marks will apply across supported Claude products and wherever Claude is offered worldwide. Anthropic also says a detected mark only tells you that content may have been processed by Claude. It does not prove Claude was the original author, because people may use Claude to proofread, translate, summarize, or convert material. [1]

That immediately got my attention.

I live in the United States. The EU AI Act is not United States law. But here I am in the United States using products from companies that are changing how their systems work partly because of a European law.

That is exactly why I pay attention to technology policy outside this country.

And the more I read, the less this felt like a simple argument about AI labels.

It started to feel like an accessibility argument.

Before I go any further, I want to be clear about something.

I am not a lawyer.

This is not legal advice, and I am not pretending to give a definitive interpretation of the EU AI Act. I am looking at this as a blind person, an accessibility professional, a developer, and someone who builds and uses AI products.

I also know the EU guidance mentions accessibility. I am glad it does.

But anybody who has worked in accessibility for long enough knows that language in a policy document and an accessible product are not the same thing.

That gap is what I am worried about.

What Europe Actually Did

The EU AI Act is a broad legal framework for artificial intelligence. It does not treat every AI system the same. Different obligations apply depending on what a system does, how it is used, and the level of risk involved.

The part I am focused on here is Article 50, which contains transparency obligations for certain AI systems.

Article 50 started applying on August 2, 2026. Among other things, providers of generative AI systems that generate synthetic audio, image, video, or text content must make covered AI-generated or manipulated content detectable in a machine-readable format. There are also separate transparency rules for things such as direct interaction with AI systems, deepfakes, and certain AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest. [2]

That distinction is important.

The law is not simply saying: “You used AI. Put a giant AI warning on everything.”

There are different duties for providers and deployers, different kinds of content, different contexts, and exceptions.

But machine-readable marking of generated content is very real.

And major companies are already building around it.

The Standard Editing Exception Matters

There is an exception in the European Commission’s guidance that matters a lot for this discussion.

The Commission says the marking obligation does not apply when an AI system performs an assistive function for standard editing. [3]

I am glad that language exists.

It recognizes something important: AI touching a piece of text does not automatically mean AI created the underlying work.

But then my accessibility brain immediately asks a harder question:

What does “standard editing” mean for a disabled person?

If I type a sentence and ask AI to fix a spelling mistake, that seems easy.

What if I dictate three paragraphs and the transcription is full of false starts, missing punctuation, and words that dictation misunderstood?

What if someone with dyslexia has all of the ideas but uses AI to reorganize the writing into a structure that other people can follow?

What if somebody with limited dexterity dictates everything and has AI clean up the transcription because manually editing thousands of words is difficult?

What if somebody with a cognitive disability gives AI their own ideas and asks it to communicate those ideas more clearly?

At what point does assistive editing become generation?

I do not know the legal answer.

That is exactly why I am asking.

Anthropic Is Making This Global

Anthropic is one reason I do not think Americans can just dismiss this as an EU issue.

Anthropic has signed the EU Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content. Its current documentation says supported Claude models launched on or after August 2, 2026 will carry machine-readable marking, including embedded watermarks in generated text. Anthropic says those marks apply worldwide across supported Claude products, APIs, and partner platforms. [1]

So a European compliance regime can change the text produced by a model I use in the United States.

That is not a hypothetical.

It is happening now.

Anthropic also says something that I think should be printed in giant letters anywhere these marks are detected:

A detected mark does not prove Claude wrote the original material.

The company explicitly gives examples such as proofreading, translation, summarization, and file conversion. [1]

That distinction is basically the heart of this entire post.

“AI processed this” is not the same statement as “AI replaced the human who created this.”

Those are not equivalent.

Google Is Already Watermarking Text

Anthropic is not the first company doing this.

Google already uses SynthID for AI-generated text in the Gemini app and web experience. Google describes SynthID Text as changing token probabilities during generation so the resulting text carries an imperceptible signal that can later be detected. Google has also open-sourced a reference implementation of SynthID Text for developers. [4]

So we are already in a world where text can contain a machine-detectable indication that an AI system generated it.

This is not a future thought experiment.

OpenAI, Microsoft, and Meta Are Part of the Same Provenance Trend

OpenAI is taking a somewhat different approach right now.

OpenAI’s current public provenance work uses C2PA and SynthID for supported generated images, and it has also added SynthID watermarking to supported generated audio. Its public verification tooling currently focuses on those media types rather than ordinary ChatGPT text. [5]

That means all of these companies are not implementing the same thing in the same way.

But the direction is clear: provenance, detection, and some way to determine when AI was involved.

Microsoft is also adding watermarking and provenance features for AI-generated or AI-altered content in Microsoft 365. Its current tooling can add visible or audible watermarks to supported video and audio, and Microsoft adds provenance information to supported generated media. [6]

Meta has also used visible markers, invisible watermarks, and metadata for photorealistic images created with Meta AI, while building systems that can recognize industry-standard provenance signals from other companies. [7]

Again, I understand why companies are doing this.

Deepfakes are real. Fraud is real. Impersonation is real. Synthetic political content can be dangerous.

I am not arguing that provenance technology should disappear.

I am asking what happens when provenance becomes judgment.

Then There Are Open and Local Models

This conversation gets even more complicated when AI is not just a hosted chatbot.

Open and open-weight models can be downloaded and run locally. Qwen, for example, has released open-weight models under the Apache 2.0 license and explicitly recommends local runtimes including MLX, Ollama, LM Studio, and llama.cpp. [8]

Once the model is in the user’s hands, the relationship changes.

Maybe there is no cloud provider sitting between the user and the output.

Maybe the model is fine-tuned.

Maybe an app developer adds a different system prompt or safety layer.

Maybe several models process the same content.

Who is responsible for the provenance signal then?

The original model developer?

The app developer?

The inference framework?

The user?

There is no single answer that fits every local AI workflow.

This Is Very Real for Me Because of Perspective Intelligence

This is not just something I read about as an outside observer.

We build Perspective Intelligence around on-device AI.

The app includes local chat, vision, text recognition, and OCR. Its current App Store listing describes on-device processing and features for recognizing text and describing images. [9]

That matters to me because I do not think every accessibility task should have to leave the user’s device and go to a cloud server.

Sometimes I want to point my phone at a document and read it.

Sometimes I want a local model to describe an image.

Sometimes I want to use a model privately because the document itself contains sensitive information.

And sometimes an open or local model may simply work better for a particular accessibility task.

When I evaluate a model for that kind of use, I do not only care about benchmark scores.

Can a blind person use it to read something accurately?

Does the vision model hallucinate objects?

Does OCR invent words that are not there?

Does the model refuse harmless content because a safety system misunderstood the context?

Does it preserve the meaning of the original document?

Does it introduce bias?

Those are safety questions too.

China Makes the Europe Question Bigger

China came up in my conversation with my friends too.

We were talking about Chinese-developed models, local AI, model bias, and whether companies are releasing models so quickly that important kinds of testing can get missed.

I want to be precise here: it would be inaccurate to say China does not test AI models.

China has regulatory requirements around generative AI, including requirements aimed at discrimination, privacy, training-data quality, accuracy, and reliability. Certain generative AI services with public-opinion or social-mobilization capabilities must undergo security assessment and algorithm filing procedures. Chinese providers and model developers also conduct their own safety evaluations and red-team testing. [10]

DeepSeek, for example, has published internal safety evaluation results, and its disclosures describe model safety assessments and red-team testing. Qwen has released Qwen3Guard, an open safety model designed to evaluate prompts and responses across categories including violence, illegal activity, privacy, self-harm, copyright, jailbreaks, and politically sensitive topics. [11]

So the question is not: “Did anybody test the model?”

The better question is:

What did they test for?

That distinction matters because China’s regulatory definition of safe AI includes things that overlap with concerns in the United States and Europe, such as discrimination, privacy, reliability, and harmful content.

It also includes compliance with China’s political and information-control rules. [10]

A model can therefore be heavily tested for one definition of safety while still having weaknesses somewhere else.

Independent evaluation matters too.

NIST’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation evaluated several DeepSeek models and reported weaknesses in areas including agent hijacking and jailbreak resistance. NIST’s report is also clearly situated in U.S. strategic competition with China, so I would not treat every political conclusion in it as neutral. But the technical testing is still useful evidence that internal testing and independent testing are different things. [12]

And that lesson does not only apply to China.

If OpenAI says a model is safe, I still want independent testing.

If Anthropic says a model is safe, I still want independent testing.

If Google says a model is safe, I still want independent testing.

If we ship a model inside one of our own products, I want people other than us testing it too.

“Tested” is not a binary property.

China Has Its Own AI Labeling Rules

China also brings me directly back to Europe because it already has its own AI-generated-content labeling regime.

China’s Measures for Labeling AI-Generated Synthetic Content took effect on September 1, 2025. The rules cover text, images, audio, video, and virtual scenes. They distinguish between explicit labels that people can perceive and implicit labels such as metadata. The rules also encourage digital-watermark approaches in generated content. [13]

So now we have two enormous markets trying to answer a similar question:

How do we know when AI was involved?

China has one framework.

Europe has another.

The technical details are not identical, but the direction is similar: make synthetic content identifiable.

China Actually Brings Me Back to Europe

The more I looked at China, the more it brought me right back to the EU AI Act.

Because these rules do not stay neatly inside national borders.

I live in the United States.

China’s labeling rules are not U.S. law.

The EU AI Act is not U.S. law.

But the models do not live neatly inside one country either.

I can use Claude.

I can use Gemini.

I can use ChatGPT.

I can download a Chinese-developed Qwen model and run it locally on my Mac.

I can build an app around an open model.

Global AI companies then have to decide whether to maintain separate regional versions of their systems or build compliance mechanisms into products that are distributed much more broadly.

Anthropic’s worldwide text-marking approach is a perfect example of why a law passed in Europe can affect me in the United States. [1]

That is why I care.

Then I Talked About This With My Friends

Later yesterday, I was talking with Michael and some friends.

Our AI conversations tend to go everywhere.

We talked about how quickly new models appear.

We talked about whether companies can realistically test every important failure mode when releases keep moving this fast.

We talked about local AI.

We talked about Chinese models and the different kinds of bias and restrictions you can see depending on where a model is developed and how it is deployed.

And eventually we got into watermarking.

One of the points that came out of that conversation has stuck with me:

For a brief moment, AI has given some disabled people something closer to a level playing field.

If we are not careful, we could build a new system that pushes those same people back outside.

I Am Not Going to Apologize for Using AI

I use AI.

A lot.

I am not hiding it.

Technology has mediated my access to information my entire life.

I use a screen reader.

I use OCR.

I dictate.

I use text recognition.

I use image descriptions.

And now I use AI.

Sometimes it helps me organize a thought.

Sometimes it helps clean up dictation.

Sometimes it helps me understand visual information.

Sometimes it helps me get around something that was inaccessible in the first place.

That does not mean the human disappeared.

For Some People, AI Is Assistive Technology

For one person, AI is a novelty.

For another person, it is a productivity tool.

For somebody else, it can function as assistive technology.

A person with dyslexia may know exactly what they want to say but need help getting it into conventional written form.

A person with limited dexterity may dictate because typing and manually editing long documents is difficult.

A person with a cognitive disability may use AI to organize information or communicate their own thoughts more clearly.

A blind person may use a vision model because the image never had alt text.

Someone may run a terrible scan through an AI model because ordinary OCR could not make sense of it.

In all of those cases AI was involved.

But “AI was involved” tells you almost nothing about how much human thought, authorship, intention, or work went into the result.

Then Michael Asked About OCR

This was the point in the conversation where Michael made me stop.

He basically asked:

What happens if I am doing OCR?

Exactly.

Imagine I have a printed document.

I cannot see it.

Traditional OCR does a terrible job.

So I use a vision-language model.

The model looks at the image and produces readable text.

Maybe it infers a couple of words from context.

Maybe it fixes broken line structure.

Maybe it turns something completely inaccessible into something I can finally read.

What was I doing?

I was not asking AI to write an essay for me.

I was trying to read.

That is an accessibility task.

Now imagine that output contains a machine-readable AI signal.

What happens when it goes somewhere else?

Does a school detect it?

Does an employer flag it?

Does a publishing system label it?

Does some future automated process decide that the content is less trustworthy?

The detector may only know:

“AI processed this.”

A human or automated policy may interpret that as:

“This person did not do the work.”

Those are wildly different statements.

And Anthropic itself warns that a mark can survive content that Claude merely proofread, translated, summarized, or converted. [1]

That is why the downstream interpretation matters so much.

A Watermark Is a Technical Signal. Humans Turn Signals Into Judgments.

This is my biggest concern.

A provenance mark may legitimately tell you something about where content passed through.

It cannot tell you why the person used AI.

It cannot tell you that the original document was inaccessible.

It cannot tell you that someone has dyslexia.

It cannot tell you that somebody dictated the entire article themselves.

It cannot tell you whether the AI created the ideas or merely helped communicate them.

It cannot tell you whether the person was trying to deceive anybody.

But humans are very good at taking a technical signal and turning it into a social judgment.

AI detected.

Therefore cheating.

AI detected.

Therefore not authentic.

AI detected.

Therefore not human work.

That is the jump I am worried about.

I Know Accessibility Is in the Guidance

The European Commission does explicitly say that people who must be told they are interacting with an AI system should receive that notice clearly, distinguishably, and in accordance with accessibility requirements. [14]

I am glad that language is there.

But after working in accessibility for years, I know what happens in the real world.

A requirement can exist on paper.

A standard can explain exactly what developers should do.

A procurement document can require accessibility.

A company can have an accessibility policy.

And I can still open the finished product with a screen reader and find unlabeled buttons, inaccessible dialogs, keyboard traps, or information that is only communicated visually.

That is why I do not consider accessibility language in guidance the finish line.

Too Often Accessibility Becomes Urgent Only When There Is a Consequence

I wish guidance alone was enough.

Too often, accessibility becomes urgent when there is a procurement requirement, a formal complaint, a regulator, the possibility of a fine, a lawsuit, or a customer who is ready to walk away.

Then everybody suddenly wants to know how quickly the accessibility problems can be fixed.

That is backwards.

I do not want us to build AI-provenance infrastructure first and ask accessibility questions after somebody has already been harmed.

I want those questions asked while the system is being designed.

Because by the time enforcement becomes necessary, somebody has probably already encountered the barrier.

Article 50 has real enforcement behind it. The Commission says national market-surveillance authorities will mainly enforce the rules, and fines for violations can reach up to EUR 15 million or 3 percent of worldwide annual turnover, subject to the Act’s rules on proportionality. [15]

That kind of consequence gets companies’ attention.

Accessibility needs the same seriousness before something goes wrong.

What I Want Regulators to Answer

If you work for the European Commission, a national regulator, a standards body, or anyone involved in implementing these rules, I genuinely want you to answer this.

How are disabled people supposed to fit into this framework in practice?

What happens when AI is used for OCR?

What happens when a blind person uses a vision-language model to access a document they cannot see?

What happens when somebody with dyslexia uses AI to restructure their own writing?

What happens when someone with limited dexterity dictates everything and uses AI to clean up the transcription?

What happens when somebody with a cognitive disability uses AI to communicate their own thoughts more clearly?

Where exactly does standard editing end and generation begin in those cases?

And what protections are being built so that a machine-readable provenance signal is not later used against someone who was using AI as assistive technology?

I know accessibility is mentioned in the guidance.

I am asking what happens next.

How is it tested?

Who checks it?

What evidence do providers need?

Are disabled people participating in evaluation?

What happens when a technically compliant provenance system becomes part of a discriminatory downstream policy?

Who is responsible when a school, employer, publisher, or platform interprets “AI detected” as “human did not do the work”?

If the answer is already in the guidance, point me to it.

If regulators have already thought through OCR, dictation, disability-related writing support, and multimodal accessibility workflows, I genuinely want to read that work.

And if those things have not been considered deeply enough, disabled people need to be brought into this conversation now.

Do Not Wait for the Complaint, Fine, or Lawsuit

Not after somebody gets falsely accused of cheating.

Not after an employer builds a filter.

Not after a school adopts a blanket AI-detection policy.

Not after a platform creates an inaccessible disclosure.

Not after the first complaint.

Not after the first lawsuit.

Not after the first fine.

Now.

Because once this infrastructure becomes normal, it will be much harder to undo the assumptions built around it.

Transparency Is Not the Same Thing as Judgment

I am not asking Europe to abandon transparency.

I am not asking China to abandon every labeling rule.

I am not asking Google to remove SynthID.

I am not saying Anthropic is wrong to comply with a law.

I am not saying provenance has no legitimate purpose.

If somebody creates a fake video of a public figure saying something they never said, provenance matters.

If somebody clones a voice for fraud, provenance matters.

If a synthetic image is spreading during a breaking news event, provenance matters.

I understand the problem.

What I am asking is that we stop pretending provenance answers every human question about authorship.

“AI was involved” does not automatically mean “a human did not do the work.”

It does not automatically mean “this person cheated.”

It does not automatically mean “this is fake.”

And it definitely does not mean “this person’s work matters less.”

The technology may tell us provenance.

Humans decide what provenance means.

That second part is where disabled people need to be in the room.

The Question I Keep Coming Back To

Yesterday I started by browsing AI news.

Then I found Anthropic’s watermarking plans.

Then I read the EU guidance.

Then I looked at Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, Meta, open models, and China.

Then I started thinking about Perspective Intelligence.

Then Michael asked about OCR.

And that is where I keep landing:

What happens when AI is not replacing the person, but enabling the person?

That is the distinction I do not want regulators, schools, employers, AI companies, and developers to miss.

For some people, AI helps them work faster.

For some of us, AI can help us access something we could not access before.

Those are not always the same thing.

If the future of the internet is going to include technical signals telling machines that AI was involved, then the future also needs enough humanity to understand why it was involved.

Otherwise, something designed in the name of transparency can become another barrier.

And disabled people have enough of those already.

If You Are Building AI, Test It Before It Becomes a Problem

This is also where developers and product teams have responsibility.

Do not wait for a regulator or a lawsuit to tell you that your AI experience is inaccessible.

Turn on a screen reader.

Try the disclosure.

Try the provenance interface.

Try the workflow without a mouse.

Test the OCR output.

Test the AI-assisted writing flow.

Put disabled people into the evaluation process before launch.

Techopolis works with app and software teams on accessibility testing, QA, and remediation, including AI-powered experiences. If you are building AI features and want to know how they work for disabled users before they become a compliance or usability problem, reach out.

I would much rather help you find the problem while you are building the product than after somebody has already been excluded.

Sources and Further Reading

1. Anthropic - How Claude marks AI-generated content

2. European Commission - Guidelines on Transparency of AI-Generated Content

3. European Commission - Transparency obligations under Article 50 of the AI Act (FAQ)

4. Google DeepMind - SynthID

5. OpenAI - Advancing content provenance for a safer, more transparent AI ecosystem

6. Microsoft Learn - Add watermarks to content generated or altered by AI in Microsoft 365

7. Meta - Labeling AI-Generated Images on Facebook, Instagram and Threads

8. Qwen - Qwen3: Think Deeper, Act Faster

9. Apple App Store - Perspective Intelligence

10. Cyberspace Administration of China - Interim Measures for the Management of Generative AI Services

11. Qwen - Qwen3Guard; DeepSeek - V2.5 safety evaluation

12. NIST CAISI - Evaluation of DeepSeek AI Models

15. European Commission - Article 50 enforcement and fines in the transparency FAQ

Two Years at Techopolis, and Yeah, This Post Is Late

Okay so this post is late and I want to say why up front.

Taylor’s Substack is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

My two year anniversary at Techopolis was July 26. I didn’t write anything that day because that day I was in St. Louis, Missouri, standing in an exhibit hall at the American Council of the Blind conference and convention. The in-person part ran July 24 through the 31st at the Hyatt Regency at the Arch, and we were there as an exhibitor. So my anniversary just kind of went by while I was at a booth talking to people about the stuff we built.

Which, honestly? That’s probably the best way it could have happened. I just didn’t have a free minute to sit down and write about it.

So now I’m home, my voice is mostly back, and I want to actually talk about this. Two years. I can’t believe it.

This goes back further than two years

If you were here for last year’s post you know some of this, but I want to back all the way up, because the job is two years old and the relationship is not.

Michael Doise is my boss and the founder of Techopolis, and I met him in 2018 at the NFB convention in Orlando. In the deli at the hotel. That’s where this whole thing starts.

He was doing a drawing for a Google Home Mini, and I won it.

That’s it. That is the entire origin of my career. I won a Google Home Mini in a deli at a hotel in Orlando, and we’ve been friends ever since.

Then COVID happened, and that’s when we really got to know each other. I joined his Discord server and we just talked. A lot. For a long time. That was the thing about that stretch, everybody was stuck at home, and the people you talked to online turned into real friends in a way that probably wouldn’t have happened otherwise.

Then in 2022 I moved to Texas to live with him. And I am not making this up, the Google Home Mini kicked the bucket right around that move. It got me all the way to Texas and then it was done. Rest in peace to the little speaker that started all of this.

And this is the part I really want people to hear, because it’s the thing that changed my life more than any job title did.

Michael taught me iOS development.

I did not know how to build an app. He sat there and taught me. Swift, Xcode, how the whole thing fits together, how you actually ship something to the App Store instead of just having a project folder on your Mac. Every app I’ve put out has that in it somewhere.

So when you see my name on Perspective Transcribe, or on Start Testing, or on BITS Connect, understand that the reason I could build any of it is that somebody took the time to teach me. That’s not a small thing. A lot of blind people who want to code never get that, because the tutorials are inaccessible, or the tooling fights you, or nobody around you knows how to help.

I got that. It’s the whole reason I teach now.

So by the time the work stuff happened, we already knew each other well and I’d already learned most of what I know from him. That matters. I wasn’t a resume that showed up in an inbox.

And then a Chili’s

July 26, 2024. Michael and I sat down at our Chili’s, which is just what we did. That was the place we went to brainstorm and catch up. Nothing about that night was supposed to be a big deal.

I was already doing contract work for Techopolis at that point. I’d built parts of the website, helped plan projects, kicked around early ideas for services. So we’re sitting there talking about where the company should go, and it kind of dawned on both of us that we were describing the same company. His vision and mine had lined up more than either of us realized.

So he asked if I wanted to make it official. I said yes. That same night I started filling out the payroll paperwork.

That’s it. No offer letter, no interview panel, no three rounds of anything. Dinner, a conversation, and then it was real.

The other part I don’t bring up as much is what happened before that dinner. I lost my other job back in 2023, and that was not a fun stretch. So when I say this job means something to me, I don’t mean it in a LinkedIn way. I know exactly what the other version of my life looks like.

Okay but where does the name come from

I get asked this more than you’d think. Techopolis. What even is that.

So you have to understand something about Michael. He loves technology, obviously. But he also loves cities. Cityscapes, metropolises, the whole thing. Those are his two favorite things in the world.

And back in 2017 he was trying to come up with a good name for his Wi-Fi network. That’s the origin. He wanted his Wi-Fi to have a cool name. So he took his two favorite things and smashed them into one word. Technology plus metropolis. Techopolis.

I love that. There’s a whole company now, with apps and a platform and customers, and it’s named after a guy’s Wi-Fi network.

The tagline that came out of it is building community through technology, and that one still holds up. That’s genuinely what we’re doing.

Then in 2021 he actually formed Techopolis Online Solutions, LLC, and the reason was pretty boring. He’d had an individual Apple Developer account since 2011, but if you want to add other people to your projects, you need a real business entity. So he set one up.

And then the name kind of just sat there. It existed on paper and not much else. It wasn’t until 2024 that we started actually building things out and treating it like a real company.

So when somebody asks how long Techopolis has been around, the honest answer is a little complicated. The Wi-Fi network is nine years old. The paperwork is five. The company that actually ships things is two.

Honestly, I’m not sure I knew what I was brought in to do

I was brought in to do operations. That was the title. But if you’d asked me on day one what that actually meant day to day, I don’t know that I could have told you. The real answer, the one underneath the title, is that I was brought in to make this company grow.

Here’s what was going on. Michael had ideas. He’d had some of them for a very long time. Beyond The Gallery, the community for sharing Shortcuts. Perspective Intelligence, which back then was called Perspective AI. Real ideas, good ones, just sitting there.

And he didn’t really know how to implement them. He didn’t have the time. That’s not a knock on him at all, that’s just what happens when one person is doing everything.

So my job was to take the stuff that lived in Michael’s head and get it out into the world where people could actually use it.

I didn’t know if I could do that. I said this last year too. I didn’t know if I could be a manager, or handle operations and payroll and accounting and consulting and teaching all at once. Year one was me finding out whether I could. Year two was finding out what happens when the answer turns out to be yes.

Okay, so what did we actually ship

I sat down to write this list out and it got long enough that I went back and checked the dates twice, because some of this feels like it happened years ago. It all happened since last August.

Perspective Intelligence became a real product line

We launched Perspective Intelligence at the end of November, and then we just kept going. 1.4 in February. Then 1.5, which came out of what was genuinely the craziest week and a half I’ve had here. Then 1.6, where it went from AI that talks to you to AI that actually gets things done.

That’s the idea that was sitting in Michael’s head when I got here. It’s on people’s phones now. That still gets me a little.

Perspective Transcribe, which is the personal one

Perspective Transcribe is my first app and I use it constantly. It launched at the end of March, and by May it was really out, subscriptions and everything.

You know me. I’m blind and neurodivergent, and typing is not always the fastest way to get a thought out of my head. Being able to just talk, and then go chat with what I said later, changed how I work. A lot of these posts start in Transcribe. This one did.

Perspective Describe went into beta in June, and that one’s still in progress. Notify shipped for developers who need push notifications. Meetings keeps all my recurring meeting links in one spot. And I built Perspective Tasks because my ADHD brain fired every other task app I ever tried.

Beyond The Gallery is out too, which is the Shortcuts community app, and like I said, that’s one Michael had been carrying around for years.

All of it is at perspectiveapps.net, and the company side is techopolis.app. Go look around.

Start Testing

This is the big one and I’m not going to pretend it isn’t.

Start Testing went live July 16, and I really did almost quit building it. Three years of trying versions of this thing. About a year on the version that finally became Start Testing. So many late nights and early mornings where I’d go to bed thinking about a problem and wake up thinking about the same problem. And plenty of days where I’d look at how much was still left and think, what business does one developer on a two-person team have trying to build something this size.

It’s a QA and accessibility platform, but don’t let the name fool you, it’s also just a really good project management tool. Bugs, features, tasks, milestones, sprints, custom forms, public status pages, GitHub sync, crash reports and TestFlight feedback pulled straight in from App Store Connect, an API, an MCP server. And Lyra, the AI agent, who will take an hour of me rambling about bugs and turn it into actual usable issues. Not a hundred pieces of garbage. Good ones.

And it’s accessible because I use it every single day with VoiceOver. That was never something we bolted on at the end. I couldn’t have built it that way even if I wanted to.

Five days after launch we shipped attachments and launched Techopolis for Open Source, which is a cheap plan for people maintaining qualifying public open source projects. I use open source stuff other people built all the time, so being able to give something back there means a lot to me. I brought the idea to Michael and he said let’s do it, immediately.

The free plan is real, not a seven day trial that disappears on you. Put one actual project in it and see if it helps.

BITS Connect

Two days before Start Testing, BITS Connect shipped. It’s the official iPhone app for Blind Information Technology Solutions, an ACB affiliate, and it’s free. Voting and ballots, events, media with transcripts, the community directory, email lists, Siri Shortcuts, all of it in one accessible place.

Jeff Bishop and Michael were in that one with me, and the BITS folks tested it hard.

The agents, and giving stuff away

Back in February I got fed up with AI forgetting accessibility, so I built a team of agents that wouldn’t. Six agents on a Friday turned into forty-seven by Monday, and then fifty-five across three teams. They’re open source, free, go take them.

Perspective Server went open source in March.

And then there’s Quill, the screen-reader-first editor from BITS and Community Access. I got pulled into that as a tester, filed thirty-eight issues in about a day, and then ended up solving the wxPython web view problem that had been blocking blind developers for years. And we didn’t keep the fix. We pulled it out into its own library and gave it away, so anybody hitting that same wall can just install it and move on with their life.

That’s still my favorite thing I did all year. Not because it was clever. Because Becky finally got a working Markdown editor after four years of that problem stopping her, and Jeff about cried.

Plus everything else

I trained an LLM on my MacBook Neo and then wrote a book about the machine. I turned teardowns into something you can actually hire me for, and kept doing them: Xcode Intelligence, Codex, ActiveCampaign, LM Studio Bionic, and Nativ. Shipped version 2 of my custom GPTs. Finally got a personal website. And I started Learn to Code Tuesdays, which is free, every week, and still running.

All of that is on this Substack if you want to go dig.

And we finally got help with marketing

This is the one I should have done sooner.

For two years it’s been me and Michael doing everything, and marketing was always the thing that got whatever was left over at the end of the day. Which is usually nothing. I’d ship something I was proud of and then realize I hadn’t really told anybody about it, or I’d tell people once and move on to the next thing.

You can build the best platform in the world and it doesn’t matter if nobody knows it exists. I knew that, I just couldn’t get to it.

So this year we finally started getting real help with marketing instead of me squeezing it in at midnight. That changed things. Turns out telling people what you built is its own job, and it deserves somebody who actually has time for it. More on that at the end.

And then St. Louis

Okay, I have to point something out, because I went back and reread last year’s post while I was writing this one.

Last year we didn’t have our own booth. We shared one with the Laurel Wheeler Foundation and the Virtual Lions Club, and I debuted the Techopolis Creations 3D printed stuff there. And at the end of that post I wrote that we were already planning to have our own booth next year in Missouri.

And then this year, that’s exactly what happened. Our own booth. In Missouri. I wrote that down as a goal, forgot I’d written it, and then went and did it. That’s a strange feeling.

Here’s the thing about spending a whole year shipping software.

You build it, you push it, you write the post, and then you’re looking at numbers. Sign-ups, downloads, support tickets. It’s real, but it’s abstract. You’re staring at a dashboard, not at a person.

And then you go stand in an exhibit hall for a week and it stops being abstract really fast.

People came up to the booth and told me they use the apps. Not in a survey, not in an email. Standing right there in front of me. Some of them had feedback, and some of that feedback wasn’t comfortable to hear, and honestly that’s exactly what I wanted. You learn more in ten minutes with somebody who’s annoyed at your app than you do in a month of analytics.

And I got to explain Start Testing out loud, over and over, to people who’d never heard of it. That does something to you. You find out real quick which parts land and which parts you’ve been explaining wrong this whole time.

The other thing is just, that’s the community. That’s who we build for. BITS is an ACB affiliate, and BITS Connect shipped ten days before the convention started, so all of that landed in the same week, in the same building, with the same people. I didn’t plan it that way. It just happened. Convention week is long and loud and you come home wrecked, but it was the good kind of wrecked.

So yeah, that’s why this is late, and I’d make that trade again.

What I keep thinking about

A few things have been rattling around since I got back.

One is that you don’t need a big team to solve a real problem. You need to actually understand the problem, keep showing up, and be willing to throw away the parts that aren’t good enough. I threw away a lot of Start Testing over three years, and every time that was the right call, even when it hurt.

Another is that using your own tools is not optional. We run Techopolis on Start Testing. When Start Testing has an error, the logs go back into Start Testing and file an issue in our own project. We can’t hide from our own bad decisions, and that keeps it honest in a way nothing else does.

And accessibility at the end isn’t accessibility. I couldn’t build any of this and then come back at the end and ask if a blind person could use it, because I’m the blind person using it. That’s not a philosophy, that’s just Tuesday.

Year three

More apps. More Start Testing, and a lot of what’s coming there is coming straight out of conversations I had in St. Louis. More teaching. More conventions, because now I know what a week in an exhibit hall does for a product.

And we’re hiring a marketing intern.

I’m genuinely excited about that one. It’s the first time we’re bringing somebody in beyond the two of us, and it’s for the exact thing I know we need the most help with. If that sounds like you, or you know somebody in school who wants real work instead of fetching coffee, keep an eye out. I’ll post details.

And I’m gonna keep doing this out loud the way I have been. The wins and the parts that didn’t work.

Eight years ago I was in a deli in a hotel in Orlando winning a Google Home Mini off a guy I’d just met. Two years ago I was sitting in a Chili’s with that same guy, not knowing if I could do this job.

I still get nervous. I’m not going to pretend I don’t. But I’m not sitting there wondering anymore.

Thank you for reading this year. I mean that. Some of you have been here since this newsletter had a number instead of a name.

If you want to go look at any of it

  • Techopolis, and everything we make

  • The Perspective apps

  • Start Testing, free plan and all

  • My site

We Have a Return to Office Problem, and Disabled Workers Are Paying for It

I do not usually write posts like this.

Taylor’s Substack is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

I write about accessibility, apps, AI, the stuff I am building. That is my lane. But every once in a while something aggravates me enough that I have to say it out loud, and this is one of those times.

Return to office mandates keep landing. Three days a week. Four days a week. Badge swipes counted. It is happening across tech, across government, across a lot of places that spent five years doing perfectly fine work from people’s houses.

And almost nobody is talking about what it does to disabled workers.

That is the part I want to sit on for a minute, because it is not a small side effect. For a lot of people it is the whole job.

I actually get the argument

Let me be fair here, because I do understand where this comes from.

Downtowns took a hit. The restaurants, the coffee shops, the parking garages, the little sandwich place that lived off the lunch rush. Cities want that back. Politicians want that back. Companies with a lease on twelve floors of an office tower definitely want that back.

I get it. I want vibrant downtowns too. I like cities. I like the culture. That is not the part I am arguing with.

The part I am arguing with is who gets handed the bill.

Five years of proof, thrown out

Here is what bothers me the most.

For about five years, the same employees now being called back worked from home and did the job. Not barely got by. Did the job. Some of them were more productive than they had ever been, because they were not spending two hours a day fighting to get to a desk.

That is five years of evidence. Real evidence, from the actual employees, doing the actual work.

And now we are throwing it out. Not because the work got worse. Because a building is empty and somebody wants it full.

If the work is fine, the work is fine. You do not get to run a five year experiment, get the answer you did not want, and then pretend the experiment never happened.

What “just come in” actually means when you are disabled

This is the part that I do not think most people making these decisions have ever had to think about, so let me spell it out. I am blind. I do not drive. I have done the office commute, and I can tell you what it actually involves.

When you cannot drive, getting to work is not a fifteen minute commute. It is a logistics problem you have to solve again every single morning, and some mornings it does not have a good answer.

I have had to get to an office on a bus route that was not safe. Not inconvenient. Not annoying. Not safe. Crossings with no audible signal, where I am standing at a corner guessing at traffic. Stops on the wrong side of a road nobody should be walking across on foot. Sidewalks torn up for construction with no accessible way around, so the route I learned does not exist anymore and I am figuring it out live. That is real physical risk, and I was taking it so I could sit at a desk and do work I could have done from my house.

Then there is Uber. I have been denied rides. Drivers cancel. You are standing on a curb watching the car get close on the map and then the ride is just gone, and you have no idea if the next one does the same thing. When that happens on a Saturday it is a frustrating hour. When it happens on a workday it is you being late to a meeting for a reason you cannot control and probably do not want to explain to your boss again.

It is also money. A lot of money. When transit does not work for your route, you are paying for rides out of your own pocket, both directions, three or four days a week. Nobody reimburses that. It comes straight out of what you earn, and it is a cost your coworkers who drive to the same building simply do not have.

And that is before you get to the part where some people are managing pain, fatigue, chronic illness, or a body that does not give them the same amount of energy every day. Working from home was not a perk for those folks. It was the thing that made the job possible.

So when a policy says three days in the office, no exceptions, what it really says to a chunk of people is: figure it out or leave.

A lot of them are going to leave. Not because they cannot do the work. Because they cannot do the commute.

The accommodation process is not the safety net people think it is

Somebody is going to say, well, they can just request an accommodation.

Sure. In theory.

In practice that means disclosing your disability to your employer, filling out paperwork, getting a doctor involved, waiting, and then finding out whether your manager decides remote work is “reasonable” for a job you have been doing remotely since 2020. And doing all of that while everybody around you just gets to keep working the way they always did.

That is not a neutral process. That is an extra tax, paid only by the people who already have the least room in their day.

And here is the ugly part. The thing you are asking permission for is the exact thing the company let everybody do for five years without anybody filling out a single form.

What a decent policy actually looks like

I am not saying nobody should ever be in a room together. I am not anti office. In person time is genuinely good for some things.

I am saying be intentional about it instead of counting badge swipes.

Bring people in for the things that actually need a room. Kickoffs, planning, onboarding a new person, the messy conversation that dies over chat. Then let them go home and work.

Judge people on output. Did the work get done, was it good, did the team hit what it said it would hit. That is the measurement. Chairs occupied is not a measurement of anything except chairs.

Make flexibility the default instead of the exception, so nobody has to file paperwork and disclose a medical condition just to keep doing the job they were already doing well.

And if you are a leader reading this and you are about to roll out a mandate, ask one question first: who on my team is this going to quietly push out? Because somebody always is. You just may not hear about it until they are gone.

If you are a policymaker reading this

You are probably hearing from the people who benefit from full offices. Downtown business groups, commercial landlords, the folks with a revitalization plan and a slide deck. Those are organized voices and they show up to meetings.

You are almost certainly not hearing from the disabled employee who quietly gave notice in March because the commute stopped being survivable. That person does not have a lobbyist. That person is busy trying to find another job.

So I am asking you to go looking for that side of it before you sign off on the next mandate, or the next tax incentive tied to office occupancy.

Ask what it does to disabled workers in your city. Ask what your own paratransit system can actually absorb if thousands of people go back to fixed schedules at the same time. Ask whether the accessible transit you are counting on runs early enough, late enough, and often enough for a real work day.

And if you are writing incentives, tie them to something other than warm bodies in a building. Reward companies for hiring and keeping disabled workers. Fund the transit that would make a downtown genuinely reachable. Those things make a city more alive than a mandate ever will.

Right now this issue barely gets discussed at all. That is exactly why it is worth your attention.

Why I care

I care because the accessibility conversation usually stops at software. Screen readers, captions, contrast, alt text. That is most of my work and I will keep doing it.

But policy is accessibility too. You can ship the most accessible product in the world and still build a company that a disabled person cannot actually work at.

Remote work was one of the biggest accessibility wins disabled workers have gotten in my lifetime, and it did not come from a law or a task force. It came by accident, because everybody needed it at once. Now that everybody else does not need it anymore, it is getting taken back.

That is what makes this a crisis and not just an annoying office policy.

One thing you can do

If you made it this far, do one thing with it.

Send this to the person at your company who is writing the policy. Or bring it up the next time a mandate gets announced and everybody nods and moves on. Somebody in that meeting is doing the math on whether they can keep their job, and they are probably not going to say so out loud.

And if you have lived this, hit reply and tell me. I would like to know how common this is, because right now the people it happens to are mostly dealing with it alone.

If your team is working through this and you want help thinking it through, reach out. I do this work.
