item.content:encoded:
found something this morning and sent it to me.

Taylor’s Substack is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

That happens a lot. One of us finds a new AI tool, sends it to the other one, and then we start pulling it apart together. Not because we want it to fail. Usually it is the exact opposite. We see something promising and immediately start asking what it could become.

This one is called Nativ. There is no E on the end. It is a new, open-source Mac app for running AI models locally through MLX, Apple’s machine learning framework for Apple silicon.

Nativ was built by Prince Canuma, who goes by Blaizzy on GitHub. I have followed Prince’s work in the MLX community for a long time. He is behind projects including MLX-VLM and MLX-Audio, and he has done a lot to make powerful language, vision, and audio models run directly on Macs.

So when Michael told me Prince had built a native Mac app around this work, I paid attention.

Then we downloaded it and started testing.

This is a first look

I want to make something clear before I get into what worked and what did not.

Nativ is brand new. The first public release is version 0.0.1. This is an alpha, not a finished product that has spent years in the market.

I am not writing this to criticize Prince or to dunk on an early open-source project. I am writing it because this is the best time to give feedback. It is much easier to build accessibility into a product while it is young than to bolt it on after thousands of people depend on it.

That is why I do these teardowns.

I share the good because good work deserves to be recognized. I share the bad because vague feedback like “it is not accessible” does not give a developer anything useful to fix. And when I find something with real potential, I want the people building it involved in the conversation.

Prince, if you are reading this, Michael and I would genuinely love to collaborate with you on Nativ’s accessibility. The project is open source, you have already shown that you care about building in the open, and there is a lot here worth backing.

Michael and I tested it together

This was not just me sitting alone and running through an app.

Michael found Nativ that morning, and we reviewed it together. I used VoiceOver, the screen reader built into the Mac, and worked through the app from the keyboard. Michael compared what he was seeing visually and tested a different model.

That distinction matters when I talk about the model problems.

Michael downloaded the Gemma 4 31B model. I downloaded the 26B model. The 31B problem was Michael’s experience, not mine, and I do not want to blur the two together just because we were talking while we tested.

We were both forming first impressions in real time. At one point I said I already liked Nativ better than LM Studio Bionic. But this was still a first look, and I did not want to pretend a promising first impression was the same thing as extended use.

So this is exactly what it claims to be: our first pass through a very early app.

What Nativ is

Nativ brings several pieces of a local AI setup into one native Mac app.

You can discover and download compatible MLX models, chat with them, watch performance and token statistics, monitor memory pressure and thermal state, and start a local server. That server speaks both OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic-compatible APIs, which means other tools can connect to the model running on your Mac.

The integrations are one of the most interesting parts. Nativ can connect local models to Codex, Claude Code, Pi, Hermes, and OpenCode. That is not just another ChatGPT-style window. It can become the local model layer underneath tools people already use to code and work.

It also has menu bar controls, so I can check the server, see what model is loaded, and manage it without digging through the full app every time.

That is a strong idea.

Why the open-source part matters

Nativ is released under the MIT license, and the source is right there on GitHub.

That matters to me for more than price.

When I found accessibility problems in LM Studio Bionic, I could explain them publicly and hope the team listened. With Nativ, we can do more. We can file a precise issue. We can inspect the SwiftUI code. We can propose a fix. If Prince wants the help, we can work with him instead of shouting feedback across the internet and waiting.

Open source does not automatically make something accessible. Plenty of open-source apps are terrible with a screen reader. But it changes what can happen next. The distance between finding a problem and contributing to the solution gets much shorter.

That makes me more willing to back this project.

The first impression was better than Bionic

I recently did a teardown of LM Studio Bionic, another early product built around running open models and doing real work with them.

I like Bionic’s idea. I said that in the teardown. A private, local-first AI agent is exactly the kind of thing I want.

But Bionic felt like a web app inside a desktop wrapper, and I ran into basic accessibility problems almost immediately. Headings were missing through most of the app. Focus landed in the wrong places. Downloads and responses happened without useful announcements. Controls changed state without telling VoiceOver. The model could be doing good work and I would have no idea it had finished.

Nativ felt different immediately.

It is a real SwiftUI Mac app. The model discovery experience was easier to understand. I could find models faster than I could in Bionic. Between the two of us, we also checked the visual contrast, and that looked good.

The model downloader was simply a better first experience. I could move through the available models, get to Discover, and make a choice without the same amount of fighting.

That does not mean Nativ is accessible yet. It means the starting point felt better.

The sidebar needs work

Once I moved through the tutorial and got into the main app, VoiceOver’s description of the sidebar became messy.

I heard a string of things like buttons, sub-buttons, cells, and a table. The words were there, but the structure was not giving me a clean mental picture of the app.

A sidebar should be simple. VoiceOver should tell me that I am in a sidebar or navigation area, give each destination a clear name, and let me move through those destinations predictably. I should hear something like Dashboard, Models, Chat, Developer, and Settings. I should not have to untangle table cells and nested button language to work out where I am.

The good news is that I could move around. This was not a completely blocked interface.

The bad news is that navigation was noisier and more confusing than it needed to be. For a native SwiftUI app, this is fixable. The sidebar items need clean labels, appropriate traits, and a structure that VoiceOver can announce without exposing the implementation details.

Model discovery is one of the best parts

The Models area was the part that made both of us lean in.

Finding models was easier than it had been in Bionic. I did not have to know an exact repository name or go hunting through a separate site before I could get started. Nativ showed compatible MLX models and let us begin downloading from inside the app.

This is important because local AI has a learning curve before you ever type a prompt. People have to understand parameters, quantization, available memory, model formats, and whether a particular model will even run on their Mac.

Nativ cannot make those technical limits disappear, but it can keep users from having to assemble the whole stack themselves.

I also liked that it surfaces memory pressure. On a Mac, the question is not just whether a model exists. The question is whether that model, at that precision, can fit into the unified memory you actually have available while macOS and the rest of your apps are running.

Putting that information in the app is useful. It helps turn “why is this frozen?” into something a person can reason about.

The 31B model did not go smoothly

This is where Michael hit the biggest ordinary product problem in our first pass.

He selected the Gemma 4 31B model. The download or load did not complete correctly, and the app appeared to sit there without giving us a clear explanation of what was happening.

At one point it looked like the model was stuck loading or unloading. We knew something was wrong, but the interface did not make the recovery path obvious.

Michael eventually had to delete the model and download it again.

That is an alpha bug, but it also has an accessibility layer. When a download fails, a model cannot load, or the app changes from loading to unloading, that state has to be exposed clearly to VoiceOver. It needs a real status message and a useful error. “The model download is incomplete. Delete and download it again” would have saved us a lot of guessing.

A spinner is not an explanation. A state change that only makes sense visually is not an explanation either.

Michael’s 31B problem should not be confused with my test. I downloaded the Gemma 4 26B model. That was the model path I was trying on my Mac while we compared what each of us was getting.

This is also why I am not making a sweeping claim that Nativ cannot download Gemma 4. We tried two different model sizes and had different experiences. The honest finding is narrower: the 31B path failed during Michael’s test, recovery required deleting and downloading again, and the app did not explain the failure well enough.

There are feature gaps too

Nativ does not currently support everything I would ultimately want from an all-in-one local AI app.

One of the things I noticed was the lack of Apple Foundation Models support. That is something I would like to explore with Prince. Nativ is built around MLX models, and that is already a large and useful ecosystem, but Apple’s own on-device model could be another valuable option for tasks where it fits.

The project also says dedicated audio-only and image-generation-only model support is still coming.

Those are not accessibility failures. They are early-product gaps, and there is a difference.

I do not want to take every feature that is missing from version 0.0.1 and turn it into a complaint. The point of an alpha is that the product is not done.

What is good

There is a lot I like here.

The app is native to the Mac. Model discovery is easier than it was in Bionic. The visual contrast looked good in our first pass. The menu bar controls are useful. Memory pressure, token usage, time to first token, and model performance are not buried in a log somewhere. They are part of the product.

The local server is also a big deal. Being able to connect Codex, Claude Code, Pi, Hermes, or OpenCode directly to a model running on my own Mac gives Nativ a reason to exist beyond its chat window.

And the whole thing is open source.

That last part matters because I do not just want to point at the sidebar and say it is confusing. I want to help make the sidebar better. I do not just want to complain when VoiceOver misses a state change. I want the state change fixed at the source so the next blind person never has to think about it.

What needs work

The VoiceOver structure in the sidebar needs to be cleaned up. Navigation should sound like navigation, not a collection of nested table cells and button implementation details.

Model download and loading states need clear, spoken feedback. If something fails, the error and the recovery step should be available to VoiceOver immediately.

The 31B download and load path needs another look because Michael’s model did not complete cleanly and had to be removed and downloaded again.

And the app needs more time under real use. A promising first experience is not the same thing as a dependable daily tool.

Where this leaves me

I am excited about Nativ.

That is my honest answer.

It is not finished. There are accessibility issues. There are ordinary alpha bugs. One of the two model paths we tried failed badly enough that we had to start the download over. The sidebar needs work with VoiceOver, and the app needs to communicate loading and error states much more clearly.

But I would back this project more strongly than I would have expected from such an early build.

The model discovery is better. The native Mac foundation is better. The integrations are ambitious in a useful way. The performance information is actually helpful. And because it is open source, there is a real path from feedback to a fix.

This is not us attacking Prince’s work. It is us saying: there is something good here, we want blind people included while it grows, and we would love to collaborate and help make that happen.

I am going to keep testing Nativ. Michael will too. As we use it longer, try more models, and connect it to tools like Hermes and Codex, I will report back on what holds up and what does not.

If you are using Nativ already, tell me what you have tried. And if you know Prince or work in the MLX community, share this with him. I want this to be a conversation, not a drive-by review.

Want a teardown of your own?

This is one of my public teardowns. I found something interesting, used it the way I actually work, and shared the results in the open.

But you do not have to wait for me or Michael to stumble across your product.

You can hire me to do this for your app, website, or software. I go through the key flows with a screen reader and keyboard, show you where a blind customer succeeds and where they get stuck, and give you the specific things to fix first.

A written teardown is normally 149 dollars, and the current launch price is 75. A teardown with a recorded screen reader walkthrough is normally 349 dollars, and the launch price is 175. The recording lets your team hear what a blind customer hears while using your product, including the silence, clutter, and confusing focus changes that are difficult to understand from a checklist.

A teardown is not a full legal accessibility audit. It is a practical, human first look at the real customer experience. If you need a formal audit, I will tell you that plainly instead of selling you the wrong thing.

You can get your own Taylor’s Teardown here.

If this teardown gave you a better understanding of how a blind person experiences an early product, share it with a developer. And if there is a tool you want Michael and me to try next, leave it in the comments.

Start Testing Is More Than Testing, and Now It’s More Reachable Too

What Start Testing Is

If you haven’t run into it yet: Start Testing is a QA and project tracking platform. You track bugs, features, tasks, and milestones, all in one place, across as many projects as your plan allows. You can bring in a custom form so people can submit issues without needing an account, put up a public status page so people can see what’s being worked on, connect it to GitHub so issues sync automatically, and pull in crash reports and TestFlight feedback straight from App Store Connect if you’re shipping an iOS app. And it’s built to be fully accessible, because I use it myself, every day, with VoiceOver.

Launch Week

Ever since Start Testing launched last Wednesday, the reaction has been amazing. People have been sharing all the ways they’re using it in their daily lives, and personally, I’m thrilled. If you’ve seen the earlier Start Testing posts, you know this has been a dream of mine for a long time. Watching people actually pick it up and use it, in ways I didn’t even plan for, is exactly why I do this. You all gave us so many ideas yesterday, and I wanted to take those to heart right away.

Attachments Are Here

Start Testing now supports attachments. You can upload photos and videos directly to your bugs, features, tasks, and milestones. If a picture or a screen recording explains the problem faster than a paragraph does, now you don’t have to choose.

Start Testing Is Not Just a Testing Tool

I want to clear up a myth, even though it’s baked into the name. Start Testing is not only a testing platform. It can be, if that’s what you need. But people are already using it for general task tracking and full project management, and that’s not an accident. Bugs, features, tasks, milestones: everything lives in Start Testing. If you want one place to run a project from start to finish, this is built to be that place.

Introducing Techopolis for Open Source

A lot of you have told us you want to use Start Testing to run your open source projects. For me, that means a lot. I use open source projects other people built all the time, and being able to give back and help make them even better is something I’ve wanted to do for a long time. When I brought this idea to Michael yesterday, his reaction was immediate: let’s do it.

So we built Techopolis for Open Source, a plan for people maintaining a qualifying public open source project. It’s $3 a month, or $30 a year if you want to save a little.

Here’s exactly what it includes:

  • 3 public open source projects

  • 5 custom forms and 5 public submission or status pages

  • 3 API keys

  • 3 Start Testing users total, including you as the owner

  • 1 GB of attachment storage

  • GitHub import and issue sync

  • Optional AI credit add-ons, same as every other plan

That “3 users” limit is about Start Testing seats, the people actually working inside the platform. It has nothing to do with your GitHub contributors. Your project’s actual contributor base on GitHub is unlimited. Anyone can open an issue, submit a pull request, or use your project’s public pages without needing a Start Testing seat at all. The plan is generous with the part that costs us money, hosting and storage, and unrestricted on the part that doesn’t, your open source community.

To qualify: your project needs to connect to a public GitHub repository, carry a “Tested with Start Testing” README badge, and be non-commercial. Every application goes through review by our team, no exceptions. I look at every single one myself. Fill out the quick form on the pricing page, add the badge to your README, and we typically get back to you within twelve to twenty-four hours.

Once you’re approved, you’ll be able to buy the plan right from your org settings, and it becomes active as soon as you do. You’re not paying up front and hoping it goes through. Approval comes first, then the plan is yours to activate.

If your open source project needs more than the plan offers, contact support and we’ll see what we can do. We want open source projects, and every project on Start Testing, to actually thrive, not just get by.

Where This Fits in the Lineup

Techopolis for Open Source sits right above the Free plan. Free gets you one project to try Start Testing out. Techopolis for Open Source gets you three, five times the storage, and GitHub issue sync, for $3 a month, as long as your project qualifies.

If you’re not running an open source project but still want more room, Individual is $5 a month for two projects, and Individual Pro is $10 a month for three projects plus App Store Connect crash and TestFlight sync and email intake. From there it scales up through Organization Starter, Organization Studio, Agency, and Enterprise for teams and agencies managing client work. Every plan, from Free to Enterprise, starts with 10 welcome AI credits and can add more as an optional add-on. AI was never bundled into the base price on any plan, and it isn’t here either.

Why This Matters to Me

That commitment to feedback isn’t limited to this one plan. Whether you’re on Individual or any other plan, we take your feedback seriously, and customer service is a priority here, not an afterthought. Being transparent about that is just how we operate at Techopolis.

At Techopolis, I come into work every day to make a difference in people’s lives, whether that’s through our apps, our services, or our SaaS products. When people tell me they want to make a difference too, through their own open source work, we want to support that. Better project management, better testing, and all of it fully accessible: that’s a win-win, and it’s the kind of thing that makes the world a little better.

If you’ve been putting off getting real organization around your project, this is a good time to stop putting it off. Go apply, and if you have any questions, concerns, or feedback along the way, head to the Support and Feedback page and let us know. The more you tell us what you think, the better we can help you.

item.description: Well, Michael Doise told me about something cool a few days ago that he found online while he was browsing.
item.dc:creator: Taylor Arndt
item.content:encoded:
Well, told me about something cool a few days ago that he found online while he was browsing. And I decided I wanted to cover it, because it seemed like a really cool concept.

The thing is called LM Studio Bionic, and it came out a few days ago. So the minute I heard about it, I did what I always do. I sat down with my screen reader and my keyboard and I tried to actually use it, not read about it. Here is what I found.

Taylor’s Substack is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

What Bionic is

If you have not run into it, LM Studio is the tool a lot of people use to run open AI models right on their own computer, on their own hardware, instead of sending everything off to some company in the cloud. Bionic is their new thing, and it goes further than just chatting with a model. It is billed as an AI agent for open models, so it is meant to help you with coding, research, and real work with documents and files. It has a voice keyboard that transcribes what you say locally on the device, it can run models locally, and it can also reach out to bigger open models in the cloud when you need more power.

So the concept is genuinely great. A private, local first AI agent that keeps your data on your machine is exactly the kind of thing I want to root for. That is a big part of why I wanted to do this one.

I do want to be fair up front, and Bionic tells you this itself. It is a technical preview. It is early. So I am not tearing this down like it is a finished, shipped product that has had years to get things right. I am giving you an honest first look at where a blind person gets stuck today, in the hope that the team fixes it before this thing gets big. Because it could get big.

How I am testing this

I am running this on my Mac with VoiceOver, which is the built in screen reader on the Mac, and my keyboard. Bionic has the feel of a web based app running in a desktop wrapper, and that matters, because a lot of what I hit is the kind of thing you see when web accessibility basics get skipped.

I go through the flows a real person would go through. Signing up, getting set up, downloading a model, chatting with it, poking around the settings, starting a project. And I tell you where it works and where it falls apart.

Signing up, and a sign up flow that felt off

Let me start at the very beginning, with creating an account.

The first problem is there are no headings on the create account screen for Bionic. And that is not ideal, because headings are how I move around a page fast. On a web style app like this, I expect to be able to pull up a list of headings and jump straight to what I need. Here there was nothing to navigate by.

Then the sign up itself felt strange. It emails you a link, then there is a step that is something like verify your sign up, and then a separate complete login step. So it is this multi part thing where I am bouncing between an email link and the app, trying to work out which step I am actually on. I was not happy with that flow. It is confusing enough for a sighted person, and with a screen reader, when the structure is not there to tell me where I am, it gets harder.

Getting set up, and focus that goes nowhere

Once I got in, there is a setup step. I clicked on it, and my focus landed at the bottom of the page instead of on whatever I had just opened. That is a focus management problem, and it is one of the most common ones I hit. When you open something, my focus should move to the thing that opened, not get dumped somewhere random. On the onboarding screen it just was not handled.

The download that would not tell me how close it was

Part of getting set up is downloading a model, and this is where it got frustrating.

It started downloading, and it was showing a percentage, which is great in theory. The problem is it never told me how close it was to being done. As a screen reader user, a percentage that only updates silently on screen does me no good. Nothing announced the progress, so I was sitting there with no idea whether I was at ten percent or ninety. Then it moved to a finalizing step, and again, my focus was not where it should have been, and there was no status update telling me what was happening.

Eventually it finished, and the good news is the model worked. That was a genuine positive. But the entire way there, I was guessing.

When it announced, and when it did not

Here is the part that really gets me. Later on, when I downloaded another model, the Gemma download actually did announce its progress. It told me where it was. So Bionic clearly has the ability to do this right, it just does not do it everywhere.

There are two different download components in this app, and one of them reads its progress bar and the other one does not. That inconsistency is its own problem. When the same app announces a download in one place and stays silent in another, I never know what I am going to get, and I cannot trust it. Pick the one that works and use it everywhere.

The voice keyboard, and a good idea that talks over me

Bionic has a voice keyboard, where you dictate and it transcribes locally. I like that button. I like the whole idea, especially that the transcription happens right on the device.

But here is what makes it rough for me. When my focus is in the prompt box and I dictate, every chunk of text it transcribes gets read back to me as it lands in the box. So I am talking, and the screen reader is reading my own words back at me the whole time, on top of everything else. It is a constant stream of noise while I am just trying to get my thought out. It should not do that. My words landing in the box do not need to be announced back to me piece by piece. That one small behavior turns a feature I want to love into something tiring to use.

The chat, where I cannot tell when it answered

This is the one that disappoints me the most, because I actually like the AI part.

The good news first. I can press Enter to send my message, which is exactly what I want. That works.

But once I send a message, there is no way for me to know when the assistant has responded. Nothing announces it. There is no live region, which is the normal way you get a screen reader to read new content out loud the moment it arrives. There are no status alerts, no notification, no sound, nothing. I send my question, and then I am just sitting there, having to go hunt around to find out whether an answer even came back.

I will be honest, this is slightly worse than something like Codex, because at least Codex makes a sound when it is done. Bionic gives me silence. I did eventually get a model responding and doing real work, which is great, but the fact that I had to keep manually checking to find out it had finished is a real problem for the main thing this app is for.

What should happen is simple and well understood. When a new response comes in, it gets announced through a live region, so I hear it arrive. And even a simple sound when a long task finishes would go a long way.

Credits and context, where I am flying blind

When you use the cloud models, there are inference credits involved, and you cannot use those for free. That is fine, that is their business. But I would really like the app to tell me where I stand. How many credits am I burning, how much do I have left, how much context am I using. I would love for it to just tell me, something like I am at 4.8k of context, here is what you have left. Right now I do not get that, so I am using something with real limits attached and I cannot see the meter.

I also ran into a spot where, once I picked a model, I could not seem to change it. So choosing a model felt like a one way door, which it should not be.

Settings, where it actually gets better

Now let me give some credit, because the settings were noticeably better.

In the settings, there are actually headings. I could move through by heading and get the lay of the land, the way I am supposed to. That was a real positive, and I said so out loud when I hit it. The problem is that the headings basically only live here. Everywhere else in the app, they are missing. So the settings prove the team knows how to structure a page. They just have not carried it through the rest of Bionic.

A couple of specific things in here, though.

There is a label that reads something like app, back to app. I do not need to hear the word app twice. That is the kind of redundant label that should just say back to app, cleanly, once.

There is also a local models category in the settings, and there is content that sits underneath it. That category should be a heading. If it were a heading, I could jump to it and then step down into what is below it, which is exactly how I would want to navigate this. Right now it is not, so that structure is missing.

The engine picker that never told me it opened

The settings also let you dig into the engine and runtime side of things, which is really the heart of what LM Studio does, running these open models locally. I went to expand one of those sections, and I had to go all the way to the bottom to find things, and my focus did not move to what opened. Worse, nothing told me that anything had expanded at all. I activated the control, and the app just did not tell me the state changed.

This is what the aria-expanded attribute is for. You put it on the control that opens something, and it announces expanded or collapsed, so I actually know whether the thing is open or closed. Without it, I am left guessing whether I opened it, and then hunting around to find whatever appeared. And there were no headings on that model list either, so once it was open, there was nothing to navigate by.

An image sitting in front of the button

As I moved through, I hit an image on one of the cards, sitting right before the download button. If that image is decoration, it should be hidden from the screen reader so it does not get announced. If it means something, it needs real alt text that describes what it is. An unlabeled image just sitting in my path is extra noise on the way to the button I actually want.

Projects, and the folder I did not know I needed

To really use Bionic you create a project, so I went and made one. And this part was confusing.

I found the new project flow and made a test project. Along the way there was some kind of code or tag involved that I did not fully understand, and projects show up as closeable tabs, which is fine, but the whole setup left me unsure of what I had actually done. I expected that creating the project would ask me to pick a folder to work in, and it did not, so I was left thinking I would have to sort that out later.

And that is exactly what tripped me up. I went to send my first message in the project, and the send would not go through. Now, I want to give real credit here, because the send button was dimmed. It was disabled. And that is actually great, because a disabled control at least tells me I cannot send yet, instead of letting me fire off a message into nothing. That is the right instinct.

The problem is it never told me why. The reason the button was disabled is that I had not selected a folder for the project. But nothing on the screen made that obvious, so I was sitting there with a dimmed send button and no idea what I was missing. The fix is simple. If a folder is required before I can send, the app should make me pick that folder first, right in the flow, and it should tell me plainly that the folder is what is holding me up. A disabled button is a good start, but a disabled button with no explanation just leaves me stuck.

That is the theme across a lot of Bionic. When something cannot happen, the app needs to tell me why, out loud, through a proper announcement. Right now too much of it happens in silence.

What they actually got right

I want to be fair, because it is not all bad, and the good parts are the whole reason a teardown like this is worth doing.

The settings page has real headings and real structure. When I hit the new chat button, my focus moved correctly, which is exactly what should happen. I can press Enter to send a message in the chat. The Gemma download announced its progress properly. And the models, once I got them going, actually did the work. So the building blocks of an accessible app are in here. They are just not applied evenly yet.

Why this matters

Here is what I want people to take away. It would be easy to read a list like this and think it is a pile of small technical complaints. It is not.

Every one of these is the difference between me being able to use this tool and not. I could not tell how far along my download was. I could not tell when the AI had answered me. I could not tell whether a menu had opened. Those are not edge cases. That is a blind person trying to do normal work and getting stopped, over and over, in silence.

And I want to say clearly, I am rooting for this one. A private, local first AI agent is exactly the kind of thing I would use all day. If LM Studio gave me a good way to use this, especially something I could drive from a terminal, I would be all over it. The concept is that good. Which is exactly why I want the accessibility to catch up before this thing takes off.

Where this leaves me

So that is my first real pass through LM Studio Bionic, on the Mac with VoiceOver.

The honest summary is that the idea is excellent and the execution, on accessibility, has a long way to go. There are real bright spots. The settings headings, the focus that moves right when you start a new chat, the download that does announce itself, the model work that genuinely happens. And then there is a lot that is rough. No headings across most of the app, focus that lands in the wrong place, a chat that never tells me when it answered, download progress I cannot hear, an expand control that does not announce its state, and a voice keyboard that reads my own words back at me while I talk.

Remember, this is a technical preview, and I am holding it to that standard. This is not a finished product I am dunking on. It is an early one I am hopeful about. So if anyone at LM Studio is reading this, I would genuinely love to talk. I will happily walk you through every one of these, control by control, and help you get Bionic to a place where someone like me can actually use it. That is the whole reason I do these.

I am going to keep exploring Bionic, because I think it is worth it, and I will report back as it grows up.

Want a teardown of your own?

This one is a free teardown, the kind I do when I run into something worth talking about. If you want to see another example, you can read my ActiveCampaign teardown to get a feel for what one looks like.

But you do not have to wait for me to stumble onto your product. You can hire me to tear down your own. It is the same thing you just read, a real blind person actually using your product with a screen reader and a keyboard, telling you in plain terms where a customer like me gets stuck. You get the specific findings, what should happen versus what is actually happening, and the things to fix.

A written teardown is normally 149 dollars, and right now the launch price is 75. A teardown with a recorded screen reader walkthrough, me narrating as I go, is normally 349 dollars, and right now it is 175. That recording is the thing you hand to your team, because hearing your product get stuck is a lot more convincing than reading about it.

I only have very few spots left at the launch price, so if you have been meaning to do this, get one now. You can grab yours on Taylor’s Teardowns. And if you are not sure whether a teardown or a full audit is what you need, just ask me, I am always happy to be straight with you about it.

item.description: START TESTING IS LIVE
item.dc:creator: Taylor Arndt
item.content:encoded:
START TESTING IS LIVE

I Almost Quit Building Start Testing. Now It Is Live.

Taylor’s Substack is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

Start Testing is live. I have been trying to get to that sentence for years. There were days I wanted to quit. There were days I was not confident at all. I looked at everything this platform needed to do and thought, honestly, I do not know if I can pull this off.

Platforms like this are normally built by huge teams. Product managers. Designers. Frontend and backend engineers. QA teams. Accessibility teams. Support teams. Techopolis is a team of two, but I am the developer who built Start Testing. One developer took this from an idea to a real platform that people can sign up for and use today. Our two-person team got it across the finish line, and I am proud of that. But I did not build Start Testing just to prove that we could. I built it because I needed it.

I knew what good felt like

Years ago, I worked as an accessibility tester at a company that had a real platform for the work. The project was there. The issues were there. The assignments, comments, history, and fixes were all in one place. I did not have to spend my day figuring out where the work went. I could test. Then I left, and I lost access to that platform. Suddenly I was back in documents and spreadsheets. Every project had its own pile of files. I was trying to remember what I found, what I told the client, what had been fixed, and what was still sitting there waiting for somebody.

I hated it. I was doing real accessibility and QA work, but too much of my time was going into managing the mess around the work. I tried other tools. I tried other ways of organizing it. Nothing fit the way I actually worked. So I started building the platform I wanted to use.

Getting here was not easy

I wish I could tell you I had one great idea, built it once, and everything worked. That is not what happened. There have been a lot of late nights and a lot of early mornings. I would go to bed thinking about a problem, wake up thinking about the same problem, and get right back to work. I wanted to make this as close to perfect as I could before I asked other people to trust it with their work.

I spent about three years trying versions of this. I built things I thought I would love, used them for real work, and threw them away. This version took about a year to become Start Testing. Some days it felt like we were making real progress. Other days I would look at how much was still left and wonder whether one developer on a two-person team had any business attempting something this big. I was not always confident. I did not always think I could do it. But we kept going.

We use Start Testing every day. It is where we track the work at Techopolis, so we cannot hide from bad decisions. If something is confusing or slow, we have to live with it too, and then I have to fix it. Start Testing even tracks its own problems. When the platform has an error, the logs go back into Start Testing and an issue is filed in our project. The platform tells us when something has gone wrong inside the platform itself, and that problem enters the same workflow our customers use.

I love that. We are not guessing how Start Testing works under pressure. We are using it to build Start Testing. That is how I know this is not just a collection of features that looked good on a sales page. It is a platform built inside real development work.

Do not let the name fool you

Start Testing is a QA and accessibility platform, but do not let the name fool you. It is also a great project management tool. You do not have to run a testing department to get real value from it. Create projects and tasks, assign the work, set priorities and due dates, organize everything into milestones and sprints, track feature ideas, and see what is finished and what is still waiting to be done. If you are trying to keep a team, a client project, or even your own work organized, Start Testing can do that too.

And when testing is part of the work, you do not need to move everything into another platform. You can track bugs, features, milestones, reviews, and releases in the same place as your everyday tasks. You can bring in crash reports and TestFlight feedback from App Store Connect. You can connect GitHub, collect reports through forms, assign the work, review it, and follow it all the way from open to resolved.

The built-in AI can help group duplicate reports, suggest priorities, and summarize what a report is actually about. It is there to help with the repetitive parts. The people doing the testing and making the decisions are still in control. If you are a developer, there is also an API and an MCP server. Start Testing does not have to sit in one browser tab by itself. You can connect it to the tools and workflows you already use.

This is not only for accessibility or QA teams. It is for the solo developer trying to ship an app without losing feedback. It is for the consultant keeping client work organized. It is for the small business or nonprofit that needs one place for projects, tasks, deadlines, and ideas. It is for the agency managing work across clients. It is for the product team that is tired of copying the same work between an inbox, a spreadsheet, a project manager, and a bug tracker. If your work feels scattered right now, I built Start Testing for you too.

Meet Lyra

Oh my gosh, I love Lyra. Lyra is the AI agent inside Start Testing. Not just a chat box that gives you a paragraph and sends you back to do the work yourself. You tell Lyra what you need in plain language, Lyra finds the right projects, people, items, and milestones, and then proposes a plan. Before Lyra changes anything, you approve that plan. Anything destructive requires another clear confirmation. You stay in control, but you do not have to click through ten different screens to get the work done.

Here is the example that made me realize how useful Lyra could be. One day I was testing Start Testing and finding bugs as I went. Instead of stopping every few minutes to write a formal report, I dictated my thoughts. This link is broken. This flow is confusing. This needs to become an issue. Then I kept testing. By the time I finished, I had about an hour of transcript. I pasted the whole thing into Lyra. She created more than a hundred separate issues from it.

And the number was not even the part that surprised me most. Anybody can generate a hundred bad issues. These were good, usable issues. Lyra understood where one problem ended and another one started. She turned my dictated thoughts into work I could actually review, organize, and fix. I was very, very surprised. That saved me from going back through an hour-long transcript, pulling every problem out by hand, and writing more than a hundred reports one at a time. Issues are useful. Good-quality issues are what actually move a project forward.

I have also had Lyra categorize problems so I did not have to open every issue and sort them one at a time. I have had her remove issues I no longer wanted. When I ask her to remove something, she does not quietly delete it and hope for the best. She shows me what she plans to remove and asks me to approve it. I get the speed of an AI agent without giving up control of my project. You can also ask Lyra to set up a milestone, invite somebody to the organization, organize work, or help you understand what is happening across a project. When Lyra finishes, you get a summary of what changed, and those changes are already there in Start Testing.

The name came from Michael. Lyra started as the name of Michael’s agent in Hermes, and we decided to bring that personality into Start Testing. The Star Trek energy is Michael’s. I am not really the Star Trek person in this partnership. But I do love that Lyra has a personality. Software does not have to feel like it was designed by a committee with no personality. Lyra feels like part of the team. That is the point.

Every organization gets 10 free Lyra credits. I want you to be able to give Lyra real work and see what she can do before you pay for an AI add-on. The Start Testing plan and the AI credits are separate on purpose. Your main plan pays for the platform, its project capacity, integrations, and collaboration features. AI credits pay for Lyra and the other AI work. I did not want every customer paying for AI they might never use. AI also has a real operating cost, especially when somebody gives Lyra an hour-long transcript and asks her to create more than a hundred issues. Keeping the credits separate means you can use Start Testing without AI, try Lyra with the 10 credits we give you, and then add more only when the time she saves is worth it to you. AI credits also power things like summaries, duplicate checks, accessibility explanations, and the heavier automation. If you want Start Testing to do more than store the work—if you want it to help move the work forward—this is where the platform really opens up.

Accessibility was never an add-on

I am blind. I use a screen reader every day. I could not build a platform like this and then come back at the end and ask whether a blind tester could use it. I had to be able to use it from the beginning. That changed how we made decisions. Headings have to mean something. Buttons have to say what they do. The workflow has to make sense when you are moving through it with a keyboard and listening to the interface instead of looking at it.

Accessibility is not a badge we added to the website. It is part of the baseline. And yes, that matters for accessibility teams. It should not be normal for somebody to need an inaccessible tool to do accessibility work. But it also makes the platform better for everybody. Clear structure, clear labels, and predictable workflows are just good software.

Start free, then pay for what saves you time

One of the things I kept coming back to was cost. Taking control of your testing should not require a $5,000 contract. You should not need a giant company budget just to stop drowning in spreadsheets. The Individual plan is free. You can use it for one real project and get your bugs, tasks, features, milestones, forms, integrations, and exports organized. The free plan is there so you can prove that Start Testing works for you. It is not a stripped-down demo that disappears after seven days. Put one real project in it. Connect one real source. Use it when actual feedback comes in. Then, if it saves you time, pay for the parts that let it do more.

If you are a solo developer with a few active apps, Individual Pro is $9 a month. That gives you more projects and more integrations, including the workflows that pull work in from GitHub, App Store Connect, and email. Organization plans start at $29 a month when the work no longer belongs to one person. That is where roles, assignments, shared workflows, and team collaboration start to matter. Organization Studio is $79 a month when you need client management, approval flows, accessibility reviews, sprints, and release tracking. There are larger Agency and Enterprise plans when you are managing many client programs or need unlimited project space.

Every organization starts with 10 free Lyra credits. After you use those, AI Starter is $10 a month for 100 monthly credits. AI Plus is $29 a month for 500. AI Scale is $99 a month for 2,500 and the heavier automation and self-healing work. If you would rather pay OpenAI directly, Custom AI Key is $5 a month. You securely connect your organization’s own OpenAI key, and work done through that key does not use Start Testing credits. Do not buy AI credits just because AI is popular. Add them when Lyra can give you back real time. I am not excited because I spent credits. I am excited because I did not have to write more than a hundred issues by hand.

Why pay for any of it? Because losing one important crash report costs you time. Copying issues between three tools costs you time. Manually building the same client report every week costs you time. Hunting through a project to figure out what is stale costs you time. If Start Testing gives some of that time back, the plan is doing its job. You can see the current details on the Start Testing plans and pricing page. Start small. Use it on real work. See whether it gives you back some control and some of your time. That is exactly why the free plan exists.

We could not have done this alone

Look, we could not have done this alone. There are a lot of people I need to thank, and I am probably going to miss a few, so forgive me. The people at Blind Information Technology Solutions put Start Testing through it. Jeff, Michael Babcock, Kayla, Larry, Shane, Doug, and the whole BITS crew: thank you.

You tested it. You broke it. You found the big issues before customers did. You told us when something was confusing, unreliable, or just did not work. Without you, this platform would be a buggy mess of oblivion. I mean that. Start Testing is as reliable as it is today because you were willing to get in there and find the problems. And to everybody who believed in me and signed up for the waiting list, thank you. You supported this before you could even use it. We really appreciate that, and we do not take it lightly. We want to make Start Testing the best platform it can be, and your belief in us helped get it here.

If something goes wrong, tell us

We built a real Start Testing support and feedback page because we want to help you and we want to hear what would make the platform better. Choose Support request when you need help with your account, organization, billing, projects, integrations, Lyra, accessibility, security, privacy, performance, or reliability. Choose Feedback when you have a feature idea, an accessibility or workflow improvement, a Lyra suggestion, an integration request, thoughts about pricing, or something we need to explain better in the documentation.

Every message is recorded in Start Testing and reviewed by the Techopolis team. You receive a reference number, and we normally send a confirmation email so you know we received it. If you are signed in, you can connect the request to your organization. When a problem is hard to reproduce, an organization administrator can also choose to give Techopolis temporary support access. That access is optional, recorded, and ends automatically after 72 hours. Please do not send us passwords, API keys, or other secrets. But if something is broken, confusing, inaccessible, or simply not working the way you need it to, tell us. We cannot promise the platform will never have a bug. We can promise that we want to know about it and make it better.

I want you to feel what I felt

I remember what it felt like to have a platform that held the work together. I also remember the dread of going back to spreadsheets after it was gone. Start Testing is about getting out of that dread. It is about opening one place and knowing what came in, what matters, who owns it, and what needs to happen next. It is about spending more time testing and building, and less time acting like a filing clerk for your own work. And on a personal level, this launch means something else to me too.

There were so many reasons this should have been too much for one developer on a two-person team. There were so many moments when I could have stopped. I did not. If you are building something right now and wondering whether you are capable of finishing it, I understand that feeling. You do not need to have a huge team before you are allowed to solve a real problem. You need to understand the problem, keep showing up, and be willing to rebuild the parts that are not good enough. We did that. Now Start Testing is here.

Try Start Testing now

This is not a waitlist. You do not have to give me your email and hope that someday you get invited. You can create your Start Testing account now.

If you are an individual, start with the free plan and bring in one real project. If you run a company, create your account and set up your organization. If your team is already using Start Testing, ask your manager for an invitation. Do not wait until the spreadsheet gets worse. Do not wait until another crash report disappears, another client asks for an update you have to assemble by hand, or another bug falls through the cracks.

Come try the platform we spent years building. Take control of your testing work. Sign up for Start Testing.

item.content:encoded:
bits-connect-substack-post.docx

BITS Connect is out. That is the simple version.

Taylor’s Substack is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

The more honest version is that I am sitting here looking at the App Store listing and thinking about all the times I wondered whether we were actually going to pull this off. BITS Connect is the new official app from Blind Information Technology Solutions, an affiliate of the American Council of the Blind. It brings the BITS community together in one accessible place on the iPhone, and I got to help build it.

I am very happy that BITS trusted me enough to let me be one of the developers on this app. I do not take that lightly. Building something for an organization is one thing. Building something for a community I am part of, full of blind and low-vision people who are going to use it with the same screen reader I use every day, is something else.

There were moments when I knew exactly what I wanted the app to do, and there were moments of innovation when an idea came together and I thought, yes, this is why we are building it this way. And then there were plenty of moments when I thought, I have no idea how all of this is going to work together. Sometimes getting WordPress and the iPhone app to cooperate felt like climbing a mountain that kept getting taller while I was on it. I would solve one part, get a little farther up, and find another problem waiting for me. But we kept climbing.

Now BITS Connect version 1.0 is on the App Store, and I want to tell you what we built, what it took to make it work, and why the voting experience is still my favorite part of the entire app.

BITS trusted me with something that mattered

BITS stands for Blind Information Technology Solutions. It is a community built around accessible technology, education, and connection for blind and low-vision people. That meant this app could not just be a website placed inside an app-shaped box. It had to feel like a real iPhone app, work naturally with VoiceOver, and make announcements, events, presentations, ballots, courses, email lists, contacts, and community resources easier to reach, not harder.

It also had to understand the difference between a guest, a signed-in user, an active member, and somebody who had already completed something like a ballot. The app needed to know what each person was allowed to see without turning the experience into a maze of errors and inaccessible web pages.

And I did not build this alone. This was a team effort with Jeff Bishop, Michael Doise, BITS leadership, our testers, and the people who kept giving us real feedback. Every round of testing showed us something else that needed attention. Sometimes it was a large system problem. Sometimes it was one VoiceOver announcement, one button label, or one screen that did not move focus where it should. Those small things matter. If you are blind, one small focus problem can be the difference between completing a task independently and getting stuck.

The mountain between WordPress and the app

The BITS website already held so much of the organization’s information. News, member information, media, events, forms, and other resources lived in WordPress. The easy answer would have been to duplicate all of that inside the app, and that would also have been the wrong answer.

If a Zoom link changed, BITS should not need to submit a new version of the app to Apple. If a ballot opened, nobody should have to hard-code it into an iPhone release. If an email list, support address, website link, event, or presentation changed, the app needed to learn about that from the website. So WordPress became the control room behind BITS Connect.

The app asks the BITS website what is current and then turns that information into a native, accessible iPhone experience. That sounds simple when I put it in one sentence. It was not simple.

The app and WordPress had to agree about authentication, memberships, public and private content, forms, notifications, links, dates, media files, and what should happen after somebody finished a ballot. Then caching got involved. Then member access got involved. Then we had to make sure a guest could not see a private ballot or a protected Zoom link. Then we had to make sure somebody who had already voted did not keep seeing a button asking them to vote again.

There were days when I would fix the iPhone side and discover that WordPress needed a change too. Other days, the website returned the right information but the app still had an old copy saved. A feature could look finished until I tried it as a guest, as a member, after signing back in, or after submitting the same test form again. That was the mountain.

But it was also one of the most important decisions we made. BITS can manage the information where it already lives, and the app can stay current without waiting for another App Store release every time something changes.

Voting is my favorite part

Okay, I have to talk about the ballots, because this is the part I love the most. You do not know how many test ballots I have completed while working on this app. Honestly, I do not know how many test ballots I have completed. It has been a lot, and I still enjoy it every time.

When an eligible ballot is active, it can appear right on the Home screen. You open it, move through the choices with VoiceOver, select the people or options you want, and submit it in the app.

The choices are real native controls. VoiceOver tells you the question, the choice, and whether it is selected. If a ballot says to choose no more than a certain number of candidates, the app understands that limit. If a required question is missing, the app explains the error and moves focus back to the first place that needs attention. Then you submit the ballot and get a clear confirmation. That is already a much better experience than fighting with a form that was never designed for a screen reader, but we went farther than that.

The WordPress side checks whether the person has an active membership and is actually eligible to vote. It also checks whether that member has already submitted the ballot. We added protection against duplicate submissions. We handled the already-submitted state. We fixed cases where an old cached ballot could keep appearing. Finally, we made the ballot disappear from Home after the vote is complete.

There is even a Siri shortcut for opening the current BITS ballot or special event. I know voting may sound like one feature in a very large app, but to me it represents the whole point of BITS Connect. It takes something that can be frustrating and turns it into a task I can complete independently, quickly, and with confidence. That is why I love it.

The Home screen is actually useful

When you open BITS Connect, the Home screen gives you a personalized greeting if you are signed in, along with the latest BITS news and whatever is most important right now. That might be a new announcement. It might be an active ballot, a registration, or another special event. It might be time to join BITS Chat.

The quick actions can take you straight to the active special event, BITS Chat, Events, or support. The important thing is that these are not permanent buttons pointing to stale information. WordPress can tell the app what is available right now.

You can open an article in a clean reader, share it, save it for later, or have it read aloud. On supported devices, the app can also create an on-device summary. Public announcements can appear in Spotlight search too, so BITS information is not trapped inside the app. You can also choose to continue as a guest. Public announcements, media, events, and resources are still available without forcing somebody to create an account first. Signing in opens the member content that is available to that person, and returning users can use Face ID after they have signed in.

The Content tab became a real media experience

BITS has years of useful presentations and resources, and we did not want the app to show them as a giant pile of links. The Content tab lets you browse the BITS media library by category and search what is available. It can include audio, video, transcripts, PDFs, Word documents, presentations, spreadsheets, text files, and other supported resources.

For audio and video, you can play, pause, seek, change the playback speed, set a sleep timer, and continue from where you left off. There is a mini player and a full Now Playing screen. Playback works with lock-screen and headphone controls, and VoiceOver users can use the two-finger Magic Tap to play or pause.

You can build a queue, reorder it, shuffle it, replay items, and keep the queue around instead of watching it disappear every time something finishes. You can download supported media for offline listening too. Transcripts have their own reading experience. You can read them as paragraphs, copy text, open links, use Read Aloud, and create an on-device summary on supported hardware. Documents can open in a native reader or a safe preview instead of automatically throwing you into an inaccessible browser view.

A lot of those details came directly from testing. Media players are full of tiny states that can go wrong. The wrong item can show as current. A queue can remove something too soon. A login can expire. A search can become slow. Audio can stop behaving when the app goes into the background. We worked through those things because the media library needed to feel like a place people would actually use, not a feature we could check off a list.

Events should not require digging through email

The Events tab gives you both an accessible month view and a linear list. You can move between months, hear the full selected date and event count with VoiceOver, filter by category, and open an event for the details. If the event has an authorized Zoom link, you can join from the app. You can add it to your personal calendar, share it, or set a reminder.

And the reminders are smarter than just reminding you about one date. When you set one, the app can ask whether you want a reminder for only this event or for all future events like it. So if you want to be reminded about this board meeting, you can do that. But if you know you want to attend every board meeting, you can say, basically, yes, remind me about all board meetings. Then when another matching meeting comes up, you are covered without having to set the same reminder all over again. I really like that because it works the way people actually think about recurring events.

BITS Chat is a good example of why the WordPress connection matters. The recurring Friday and Saturday sessions can appear as events, but the current Zoom link is managed on the website. If that link changes, the app does not need to change with it.

You can also subscribe to the BITS calendar through Apple Calendar, Google Calendar, or Outlook when those feeds are available, and the app can keep its reminder records in sync through iCloud when iCloud is available. The goal is simple: when it is time for something, you should not have to search through old email messages to find out where to go.

The community part is more than a name

BITS Connect is not only about consuming information. It is about participating in BITS. The Community tab includes the BITS contact directory, with email and phone actions for the people listed there. Active members can browse the available BITS email lists and compose a subscribe or unsubscribe request without hunting for the right instructions. The app also brings together current courses and community resources.

This is another place where keeping information on the website matters. Email lists and links can change. The app fetches what BITS currently offers instead of freezing an old list inside the code. And because special events and registrations use the same native form system as ballots, the work we put into accessible voting helps with more than elections. The form system supports text fields, email and phone fields, radio buttons, checkboxes, dates, times, consent choices, addresses, selection limits, required fields, and conditional questions. It can even fill matching contact information from the Contacts app when that makes sense.

Siri and Shortcuts are part of the experience

BITS Connect also has App Shortcuts. You can ask Siri to play your BITS media, play the latest presentation, pause or resume, skip forward or backward, join BITS Chat, open the current ballot, open Events, or tell you the latest announcement headline.

This took more work than adding a few phrases. A shortcut has to do the right thing even if the app is not already open. It may have to launch the app, wait for onboarding or sign-in, and then finish taking you to the right place. That is the kind of feature people usually notice only when it fails. I am proud that we worked on the handoff instead of pretending the app would always already be sitting in the perfect state.

Accessibility was not the last step

You know me. I am a blind developer and a VoiceOver user. Accessibility was never going to be something we added at the end. The app uses real buttons, links, headings, labels, values, hints, and accessible focus. List rows have to be semantic controls, not invisible tap gestures that a screen reader has to guess about. VoiceOver custom actions make it possible to save, share, summarize, and work with items without wandering through unnecessary screens.

The onboarding tutorial explains the main parts of the app, Siri actions, VoiceOver behavior, and display choices. Reduce Motion and Dynamic Type are part of the design. Loading, empty, offline, permission, and error states need to tell people what is happening and, when possible, give them a way forward.

Did we get every detail perfect the first time? Absolutely not. We changed focus behavior. We rewrote labels. We fixed forms. We fixed media. We fixed Home and Community. We changed how the tutorial worked. We listened to beta feedback and kept going.

That is what accessibility work actually looks like. It is not one audit at the end. It is using the app, finding where the experience breaks, fixing it, and then testing it again in the states you did not think about the first time.

What building BITS Connect taught me

The biggest thing I learned is that the hard part is rarely making one screen. The hard part is making all the systems tell the same truth.

If WordPress says a ballot is over, the app has to stop showing it. If a person has already voted, the Home screen, the quick action, the form, and the cached data all need to handle that correctly. If a link changes, every path that uses that link needs the new one. If content is for members, the server and the app both need to protect it.

That is where so many of my moments of doubt came from. I could see every individual piece, but I was not always sure how we were going to make them move together. Then there were the moments of innovation. The moment a ballot felt genuinely easy with VoiceOver. The moment a WordPress setting changed what the app showed without a new build. The moment a Siri phrase reached the right screen. The moment a submitted ballot finally disappeared exactly when it should. Those moments kept me going.

I am grateful to BITS for letting me be a developer on this project. I am grateful to the people who built it with me, the people who tested it, and the people who trusted us with honest feedback. I really enjoyed working on this app, even when it felt impossible. Maybe especially then.

Go try BITS Connect

BITS Connect version 1.0 is available now on the App Store. It is free and requires iOS 26 or later. If you are already part of BITS, I hope it makes the community easier to reach. If you are not a member yet, you can still continue as a guest and explore the public announcements, media, events, and resources. You can also learn more about BITS from the organization’s website.

And if you are eligible when the next ballot opens, try voting in the app. I have tested that experience more times than I can count, and I still love it.

Download BITS Connect on the App Store

Visit the BITS website

Seriously, just join BITS

And honestly, if you like the content, if you like the app, or if you have been showing up to BITS events and getting something out of them, seriously, just join BITS. A regular annual membership is $20 a year. If you are a student, it is $10 a year. If you are under 18, it is $5 a year. ACB lifetime members can join for $15 a year, and a lifetime BITS membership is $200. There is even a free Friend of BITS level if you just want to start getting connected, although that one is non-voting.

Twenty dollars a year for the community, the courses, the presentations, the members-only content, the conversations, and now this app is really not a lot. So if you like what BITS is doing, do not just sit there thinking about it. Join. Your membership supports the organization and helps BITS keep building things like this.

Join BITS

item.dc:creator: Taylor Arndt
item.content:encoded:
I Spent Three Years Building the Accessibility Testing Platform I Always Wanted. Start Testing Is Almost Here.

I want to tell you about something I have been building for a long time, why it exists, what it actually does, and why, if you do accessibility work or QA work or you are just tired of losing track of your own projects, you are going to want to be on the waiting list before this thing opens up.
