It is called Start Testing. It is at starttesting.net. And right now it is waiting list only, so you cannot just go sign up and start using it today. You get on the list, and when we let you off the list, that is when you are in. I will walk you through exactly how that works, and I promise it is a better deal than it sounds. But first I have to tell you the story, because honestly the story is the whole reason this thing is any good.

Where this started, and why I got so spoiled

So years ago, before I ran accessibility for the studio I run it for now, I worked as an accessibility tester at another company. And that company had a real platform for the work. Like a real one. You would open it up and everything was just there. The project, the issues, who was assigned to what, the whole history of everything we had already found and everything we had already fixed. I never once had to think about where something went. I just did the testing, and the platform held all of it together for me.

And here is the thing. I did not even realize how good I had it until I left.

Because the second I went out on my own and started doing this work myself, running accessibility for a studio, doing my teardowns, testing products the way a blind person actually uses them, I had nothing. No platform. It was just me and a screen reader and a giant pile of documents and spreadsheets, trying to keep track of what I found, what I told the client, what got fixed, what did not. Every single project was its own little mess of files. And I was sitting there spending my actual time being a filing clerk instead of doing the accessibility work I am actually good at.

And I hated it. I mean it. I had been spoiled, and now I was doing all of it by hand, and every day it felt like a step backward.

So I did the thing I always do when something bugs me enough. I sat down and started building.

Three years, a lot of stuff I threw away, and finally one I actually like

Let me be straight with you about the timeline, because I think it matters. I have been at this for about three years now. And most of those three years was me building something, using it for real, deciding nope, this is not it, and starting over. There were versions I was genuinely excited about that I threw straight in the trash. There were ideas that sounded amazing right up until I tried to do real work in them and they fell apart. That is just what it looks like when you build a tool you personally have to live in every day. You find out fast what does not work, because you are the one stuck using it.

This last version, the one that turned into Start Testing, I have been building for about a year, me and AI together. And I will tell you, this is the first one I actually like. Not put up with. Like. It is the first version where I open it up and it just does the thing my brain already wanted it to do. And that took three years of getting it wrong to figure out. I am not going to pretend it came to me in a weekend, because it did not.

And here is the part I care about the most, because of who I am. I am a blind developer. I am on a screen reader all day, every day. So this whole thing was built accessible from the very first line, because I literally could not use it otherwise. And if you run an accessibility company, just sit with that for a second, right? Think about how many of the tools they hand you to do accessibility work are themselves not accessible. It is almost a joke at this point. Start Testing is built to WCAG AA by a blind woman who has to get around it with a screen reader to get anything done at all. That is not a line on a website. That is just the only way this thing was ever going to get built.

So what even is Start Testing

Alright, so here is the simplest way I can say it. Start Testing is a project management platform for testing work. That is the core of it.

And I want to be really clear about something, because people hear “testing” and they think, oh, it is a bug tracker. No. It is way more than that. Yes, it tracks bugs. But it also runs your whole project. Tasks, features, milestones, sprints, the actual work of shipping something, not just the broken stuff. You can genuinely run a project in here start to finish. So if you are picturing a little list of bugs, throw that picture out. This is the place your work lives.

The way I think about it, it does the three things that normally live in three totally separate tools that never talk to each other. Accessibility scanning. QA and issue tracking. And catching bugs and crashes and feedback from your real users. Normally you are paying for a scanner over here, a bug tracker over there, and some feedback tool in a third place, and you spend half your life copying stuff between them like a machine. Start Testing is the one spot where a finding becomes an issue becomes a fixed thing, and you are not the messenger anymore.

And there is one more piece that I do not want to bury, because it is a big deal. You can build this into your own applications. There is a real API, and there is a full MCP server, so you are not stuck only working inside my website. You can wire Start Testing right into your own product, your own tools, your own workflow. If you are a developer or an agency, that means the testing and issue tracking can live inside the app you already ship, not off in some other tab you keep forgetting about. I will come back to that, but I wanted it on the table early, because a lot of platforms lock you in their box and this one does not.

Let me actually walk you through what is in it.

What is actually in it

I am going to go through this the way I would explain it to someone who does this work, not the way an engineer would rattle it off.

The accessibility scanning is the part I am proudest of, so let me start there. You point it at a site and it crawls the thing. Follows the links, reads the sitemap, audits the pages. And not just web pages, it does PDFs and documents too, which is the part everybody always forgets about, right, because half your compliance problems are hiding in a PDF nobody looked at. Every finding it turns up gets mapped to the actual WCAG success criterion it breaks, with an impact level, so you are not sitting there guessing whether something is minor or serious. It can scan behind a login. It can run on a schedule, daily, weekly, monthly, so you are not the one remembering to go re-check things. And here is the piece that makes it click: a finding from a scan can turn straight into a tracked issue on your board, with an owner and a status. It does not just die in some report nobody ever opens.

Then the issue and work tracking, which like I said is a real project system, not a glorified to-do list. Bugs, features, tasks, all in one place. Every item has the stuff you actually need. Steps to reproduce, expected behavior, actual behavior, priority, status, who it is on. When I am doing manual testing I can map an item straight to the WCAG criteria myself. There is AI that will analyze an item for you if you want it. There is duplicate detection, so you are not tracking the same bug five different times, and if a couple slip through you just merge them.

For the human testing side, the manual work I am doing all the time, there is a whole reviews and approvals flow. A review queue, and you can hand a review to a specific person, or just toss it into a pool and let somebody grab it. That is how an actual testing team works, not how a solo hobby project works.

Now the reporting, this is where the agencies are going to perk up. There is a custom report engine. You can save your report setups. And you can schedule reports to just get emailed out automatically, so your client gets their update and you did not have to lift a finger. You can export to CSV, JSON, Markdown, whatever, because the data is yours and it should go wherever you need it to go.

And if you run an agency or a consultancy, there is client management built right in. Real client records tied to your projects. So when you are running accessibility programs for a dozen different clients at once, they are actually separated and organized instead of all mashed together and you praying you did not mix two of them up.

Then there is all the stuff that makes it a team tool and not a lonely one. Organizations, members, roles and permissions, so people only touch what they are supposed to touch. Invites, and collaboration links so you can pull somebody in fast without a whole big setup. Comments with at-mentions right on the items. Notifications so nothing quietly falls through the cracks. Public pages where your clients or your users can submit issues straight to you through a form you built. Public roadmap and ideas boards with upvoting, if you want your users actually voting on what matters to them.

It also grabs work from where it is already happening, so you are not chasing it. It pulls in crash reports and TestFlight feedback from App Store Connect for the mobile people. It does two-way GitHub sync, so your issues and your repo stay in step. It hooks into Todoist and Notion. And you can just email an issue in and it becomes a real ticket on the other end.

And then, back to what I said earlier, the API and the MCP server. This is the part I am genuinely excited about for developers. You can plug Start Testing into your own applications and your own workflow. And if you are working with AI coding agents, and more and more of us are every day, they can actually reach into your testing platform directly, through around a hundred and eighty tools. It even runs its own OAuth, so it can connect into things like OpenAI Apps. That connects right up to the accessibility agents work a lot of you already know me for. The whole idea is that this is not a walled garden. It talks to the tools you already use, and you can build it into the tools you make.

There is AI woven through it for the spots where it actually helps. Triage, summaries, catching duplicates, a support chat. And I am going to be honest about AI the same way I always am with you. It is a helper, not the expert. It is there to save you time on the boring mechanical stuff, not to replace the human who does the real testing. You can bring your own key, or you add AI credits on the side, and I will get to how that works when I talk pricing. Point is, you are in control of it.

Okay, that is a lot, so let me be honest with you

I know that is a lot of features. Believe me, I know. When I list it all out like that even I go, wow, okay. So let me just say the thing plainly.

This is not only an accessibility testing platform. I lead with accessibility because that is who I am and that is a huge part of why I built it, but the truth is you can run real app development work through this thing. At Techopolis we track all of our bugs and all of our tasks through Start Testing. Not accessibility bugs, all of it, our whole build. It is the tool we actually use to ship our own apps. So when I tell you it holds a project together, that is not a hopeful guess, it is me telling you what my own team does with it every single day.

And I will admit something a little silly, because I want you to know the personality of this thing. It is gamified. There are achievements, there are levels, there is a leaderboard. And I love the achievements. I do. There is something genuinely good about the boring work of clearing out bugs and closing out tasks actually feeling like you are getting somewhere, instead of it just being this endless grind that never rewards you for anything. I built it in because testing and bug work can be a slog, and a little bit of “hey, you did the thing” goes a long way when you are deep in it.

So yeah. Accessibility testing, sure. But also QA, also your actual product development, also the day-to-day of running a team, and yes, with achievements you can chase if that is your kind of fun.

Yes, there is real documentation

I know exactly how this usually goes, right. A tool shows up with a hundred features and zero real docs, and you end up never learning half of what you paid for. That is not this. There is a full guide built right into the product, around twenty-two sections of it. Getting started, the AI agent, organizations and members, roles and permissions, billing and plans, forms, public pages, projects, reports, integrations, the MCP server and API keys, a full API reference, items, reviews, comments, all of it. It is right there while you are working. You are not going to be sitting there guessing how something works.

Let me walk you through the plans

Okay, let me talk money, because you should know exactly what you are looking at before you get on the list. I am going to walk these through like I am sitting here explaining them to you, so you can figure out which one is you. And one thing up front: billing is per workspace, per organization, not per seat. I did that on purpose, because I did not want growing your team to feel like a punishment.

So the free one is just called Individual, and it is actually free, not free-with-a-catch. You get one project, one form, one public page, one integration, one API key. Manual tracking of your bugs and tasks and features and milestones, and CSV import and export. This is a real free tier for a solo person who just wants to finally get organized. No team stuff, no client management, no bundled AI, but it genuinely works.

Individual Pro is nine dollars a month, or ninety for the year. Three projects, five forms, five public pages, three integrations, three API keys. This is where the integrations open up, so GitHub sync, App Store Connect crash and TestFlight feedback, email intake, project dashboards. This is your plan if you are a solo developer who actually ships things and wants the automation without needing a whole team around you.

Organization Starter is twenty-nine a month, or two ninety a year. Ten projects, twenty forms, twenty public pages, five integrations, five API keys. This is the first real team plan. You get team roles and permissions, the collaboration and assignment workflows, the public submission pages, and organization reporting. This is for a small product team that has outgrown one person holding it all in their head.

Organization Studio is seventy-nine a month, or seven ninety a year. Twenty-five projects, fifty forms, fifty public pages, ten integrations, ten API keys, twenty-five accessibility scan runs a month, and twenty-five client records. And this is the important one, because this is the first plan where the accessibility review workflows turn on, and the first one with client management. You also get review approvals, sprints, release tracking, and priority email support. So if you are a growing team that does accessibility work and juggles clients, this is your plan right here.

Agency is a hundred and forty-nine a month, or fourteen ninety a year. Seventy-five projects, two hundred forms, two hundred public pages, twenty-five integrations, twenty-five API keys, a hundred accessibility scan runs a month, a hundred client records. On top of everything in Studio you get cross-organization collaboration, advanced reporting and exports, the bigger integration allowance, and priority support with onboarding. This is the one I built for people who do what I do. Agencies and consultants running accessibility and QA across a whole bunch of clients. If that is you, this is the plan.

And then Enterprise starts at two hundred and fifty a month and it is custom from there. Everything is unlimited or set to whatever you need. Projects, forms, pages, integrations, API keys, scan runs, clients, all of it. You get a security and procurement review, priority onboarding, custom AI planning, custom billing terms. This one is not instant, you talk to us at Techopolis and we quote it, because that is just how enterprise actually has to work in the real world.

Now, AI. I kept AI as a separate add-on completely on purpose, so you only pay for it if you want it, and none of the plans force it on you. AI Starter is ten a month for a hundred credits, good for light reports and duplicate checks. AI Plus is twenty-nine a month for five hundred credits, for your regular summaries and support chat. AI Scale is ninety-nine a month for twenty-five hundred credits, for heavy automation. Or, honestly, bring your own AI key for five bucks a month and use your own provider. You are the one in control of the AI spend, not me.

Here is the part that should make this easy

This is the piece I really want to make sure you hear, because it is exactly why I am telling you to get on the list now instead of later.

Getting on the waiting list costs you nothing. You put in your name, your email, your company, and boom, you are on it. That is the whole thing. You are not putting in a card. You are not committing to a plan. You are not paying a single dollar to wait.

You only pick a plan and pay for it after we let you off the list and you are actually in there setting up your workspace. And free access is always sitting right there if that is what fits you. But even if you are an accessibility company or a web agency and you already know you want Studio or Agency, you are still not paying anything today. You pay when you are in and using it. Not while you are waiting.

So genuinely, there is no reason not to hop on the list right now. The downside is zero. The upside is that when we start letting people in, you are near the front of the line.

So here is what I am asking you

If you do accessibility testing, if you run a web agency, if you are a QA team sick of duct-taping three tools together, or honestly even if you are just a solo developer who wants to stop losing track of your own bugs and your own tasks, go to starttesting.net and get on the waiting list. It costs nothing, it commits you to nothing, and it puts you in line for the thing I have spent three years trying to get right.

I am not going to oversell this to you, because that is not how I do things. It is not open yet. We are close, and I am being careful about how we let people in, because I want it to actually be good when you get there. But look, I have been on the other side of this. I know exactly what it is like to do this work without a real platform, by hand, drowning in documents. And I know what it is like to have a good one and never want to go back. I built the good one. And I built it accessible, because I had no choice, which means it is one of the very few tools in this whole space that the blind testers on your team can actually use.

And one more thing before you go. If you know somebody who could use this, send it their way. Maybe it is a whole company or an agency that does this work. Or maybe it is just one developer you know who is drowning in files and spreadsheets the exact way I was. Either way, forward this to them. Getting them on the list costs them nothing either, and it might be the thing that finally gets them organized.

Come get on the list. Tell me what you are building and what you test, and when that door opens, I will make sure you are one of the first people through it.

item.title: When Color Is the Only Thing Telling You What’s Going On
item.description: When Color Is the Only Thing Telling You What’s Going On
item.dc:creator: Taylor Arndt
item.content:encoded:
When Color Is the Only Thing Telling You What’s Going On

I keep running into the same thing lately, and it is starting to drive me up the wall, so I want to talk about it. I will be using something, an app, a website, a dashboard, and the only way it tells me what is happening is with color. Something gets selected, and the only difference is that it turned blue. There is an instruction that says “click the box outlined in red.” A field is wrong, and the only sign is that it went red. A toggle is on, and the only difference between on and off is the shade.

Here is the problem with all of that. I am blind. There is no color for me. None. So every one of those signals is just gone. I am sitting there with a screen reader, and the thing the designer was sure they made obvious might as well not exist.

And I am seeing it more and more, not less. So I want to do what I always try to do here, which is teach you something real first, something you can use whether or not you ever hire me for a thing. Then at the end I will tell you how I can help, because this is genuinely the kind of problem I get paid to catch.

What “color alone” actually means

The plain version is this. You are conveying information using only color, with nothing else backing it up. The meaning lives entirely in whether something is red or green or blue, and there is no second signal, no text, no icon, no shape, no announced state, that carries the same meaning a different way.

This is not some new, exotic rule either. It is one of the oldest and most basic accessibility requirements there is. In the web accessibility guidelines it is success criterion 1.4.1, called Use of Color, and it sits at Level A, which is the floor. Level A is the stuff that is supposed to be table stakes, the things you do before you do anything fancy. The rule does not say do not use color. Color is great, use all the color you want. It says color cannot be the only way you communicate something. There has to be another way to get the same information.

That is the whole idea. Use color as much as you like, just never make it the only messenger.

Why this matters, and it is not just me

Here is the part people miss. When I bring this up, folks assume it only matters to a blind guy like me. It does not.

Start with color blindness. Roughly 8 percent of men have some form of color vision deficiency, which is about 1 in 12. Worldwide that is somewhere around 300 million people. These are sighted people, looking right at your screen, who genuinely cannot tell your red from your green. So when your only error indicator is “the field turned red,” a big chunk of your users are staring at a field that looks the same as all the others and wondering what they did wrong.

Then there is me, and everybody else using a screen reader. For us it is even more total. A colorblind person at least sees that something changed, they just cannot name the color. I get nothing at all. If the only thing that happened when I selected an item is that it changed color, and that selected state was never actually exposed to the screen reader, then as far as my computer is concerned, nothing happened. I do not know it is selected. I do not know which one is active. I am guessing.

So this one rule, this little Level A thing people skip, quietly locks out colorblind users and screen reader users at the same time. That is a lot of people for something that is genuinely easy to fix.

The one that gets me the most: forms and quizzes

I want to sit on a specific example, because this is the one I hit constantly and it makes my point better than anything. Picture a quiz, or a form you are filling out, where you submit an answer and the field changes color. Green means you got it right, red means you got it wrong. Maybe the button itself changes color too. For a sighted person it is instant, they see green and feel good, they see red and try again.

Now do it as me. I submit my answer. The field turns red. I hear nothing. There was no text, no announcement, nothing added to the page that my screen reader can read. So I am sitting there having no idea whether I got it right or wrong, while the page is, to a sighted person, screaming the answer at them in color. The whole point of the quiz, the feedback, the thing it exists to tell me, never reached me. That is color alone in its purest, most frustrating form.

How you actually fix it on the web, and yes, this is the ARIA part

Everybody loves to talk about ARIA, so let me tell you what it is actually for here, because this is exactly the job it was built for. ARIA is the set of attributes that lets you tell the screen reader things the visuals alone cannot. So instead of “the field turned red and a sighted person understands,” you make the page literally say “incorrect” in words, and you make sure the screen reader announces it.

For that quiz, when the answer is wrong, put the word “Incorrect” on the page as real text, and put it in a live region, which is an ARIA feature, with aria-live, or use role equals alert, so the moment it appears the screen reader reads it out without me having to go hunting. When the answer is right, do the same with “Correct.” Now the color can stay, green and red all you want, but the meaning also arrives in words, the second it happens, for everyone. That is the fix. The color tells the sighted user, the announced text tells me, and we both get the same information at the same time.

And here is the thing I really want developers to take away, because this is where ARIA earns its keep. ARIA is not magic and it does not change a single pixel on the screen. All it does is change what the screen reader is told. So for almost every color alone problem, there is a specific, named attribute whose entire job is to carry the meaning the color was carrying. You are not inventing anything. You are using the right attribute. Let me name the real ones, because “look, it turned red” is never the answer.

For form errors, do not just turn the field red. Put the error in text, and then wire it up properly. Set aria-invalid to true on the field that is wrong, so the screen reader actually announces the field as invalid when I land on it. Connect the error text to the field with aria-describedby, or better, aria-errormessage, which points the field at the exact element holding the error so I hear the label and the specific problem together. Then drop that error text into a live region or give it role equals alert so it speaks the moment it appears. Now the red field also says, out loud, “Email, invalid, please enter a valid email address.” The color stays. The meaning arrives.

For required fields, this one drives me up the wall, because the browser already gives you the answer for free. Put the actual required attribute on the input. That is native HTML, it is one word, and every screen reader announces the field as required without you doing anything else. If you are building a custom control where you cannot use the native attribute, then aria-required equals true does the same job. Either way the requirement lives in the field itself, not in the fact that the label happens to be red.

For anything with a selected or active state, and this is the big one for color alone, the web has the same idea the phone does, it just has more attributes for it. A selected tab or list item uses aria-selected. A toggle button that is on or off uses aria-pressed. A checkbox or radio uses aria-checked. The current page in your navigation, the one you are showing as highlighted, uses aria-current equals page. A menu or accordion that is open uses aria-expanded. Every one of those makes the screen reader say the state out loud, selected, pressed, checked, current, expanded, instead of leaving that meaning trapped in a color. If you are highlighting the active thing only with a background color and you did not set the matching state attribute, I cannot tell which one is active. Set the attribute, and suddenly I can.

For links inside a paragraph, do not rely on the link just being a different color than the text around it. Underline it, or give it some other visible treatment, so it reads as a link to someone who cannot see the color difference. This is the classic one. A blue word in a sea of black words is invisible to a lot of people.

For a status dot, a green dot for online, a red dot for down, a colored tag for a category, give it a text label too. “Online.” “Down.” The color can stay. It just cannot be alone.

The pattern is always the same. Whatever the color is saying, say it a second way, and on the web the right ARIA attribute is usually how you make the screen reader actually say it.

How to catch this yourself, in ten minutes

Here is the part I really want you to take away, because you do not need me for this. There are two quick tests you can run on your own product right now, today, and between them they will find almost every color alone problem you have.

The first one is the grayscale test, and it is the fastest accessibility check in the world. Turn your whole screen black and white. On a Mac it is in the accessibility settings under Display, there is a Color Filters option with a grayscale mode. On Windows it is a setting too, and on iPhone and Android it is right in the accessibility menu. Flip it on, then go use your product. Every place where you suddenly cannot tell what is going on, the selected tab you can no longer find, the error you can no longer spot, the required field that now looks like every other field, that is a color alone problem, full stop. If the information survives in black and white, you are fine. If it disappears, you have work to do. This is the same test for color blindness, by the way, because you just simulated the most extreme version of it.

The second test is to turn on the screen reader and actually listen. On a Mac press Command F5 to start VoiceOver, on iPhone you can triple click the side button once you set it up, and on Android it is TalkBack. Then put the mouse down and move through your product with the keyboard or the swipe gestures, and just listen to what it tells you. When you land on that selected tab, does it say the word “selected,” or does it only read the label and leave you guessing. When you trigger an error, do you actually hear the error text, or only silence. You will learn more in five minutes of listening to your own product than a scanner will tell you in an hour, and it costs nothing.

Do those two things and you have caught the things that matter most. Fix them with the second-signal trick from above, the text label, the icon, the underline, the selected trait, and you have genuinely made your product better for a lot of people, all by yourself.

The mobile version of this, and the selected trait

Now I want to get specific about phones and tablets, because this is where I see the cleanest example of the problem, and the cleanest fix, and almost nobody uses it.

Picture a row of filter chips, or a set of tabs, or a little segmented control. You tap one and it highlights. Sighted users see which one is active because it is a different color. Great. But here is what happens with a screen reader if all you did was change the color. I swipe over to that chip and VoiceOver just reads me the label. It does not say it is the selected one. There is nothing in there telling me this is the active tab. So I cannot tell which filter is on. The information is on the screen, in the color, and it never made it to me.

The thing that kills me about this one is that the platform hands you the fix for free, and it is one line.

On iOS, every accessible element has a set of traits, and one of those traits is the selected trait. In SwiftUI you literally add it based on your state, something like accessibilityAddTraits with isSelected when the item is selected. The moment you do that, VoiceOver reads the label and then says the word “selected” right after it. That is it. Now I know exactly which tab is active, the same way a sighted person knows from the color. The state finally made it into the accessibility tree where my screen reader can find it.

Android has the same idea. In Jetpack Compose you set the selected state in the semantics, or you set a state description, and TalkBack announces “selected” the same way. Same concept, same one-liner, same payoff.

This is what I mean when I say color alone is usually not a hard fix. The operating system already built the proper, native way to expose “this thing is selected.” The designers leaned on color, the developers never added the trait, and now the state is trapped in the visuals. You do not invent anything. You use the control the platform already gave you, the real one, the way it was meant to be used. That is the whole job.

If you want a human to find the ones you missed

Everything above you can do yourself, and I genuinely hope you do. But I will be honest about where the do-it-yourself version runs out, because that is where I come in, and only if you want me.

The grayscale test and listening to your own screen reader will catch the obvious color alone problems. What they will not catch is the stuff you do not know to look for, the flow you do not realize is broken because you know your own product too well to get lost in it. An automated scanner is even worse at this. A tool can sometimes flag a contrast number, but it cannot tell that the only reason you know a tab is selected is that it turned blue. It does not know what the color was supposed to mean. You need a human who has never seen your product, actually using it, going “wait, which one of these is on right now, because my screen reader will not tell me.” That is me.

I do something called a teardown. I take your product, your website, your web app, your iOS app, even an AI chatbot, and I use it the way a blind customer actually would, with a real screen reader and a keyboard. VoiceOver on the Mac and iPhone, NVDA on Windows. I go through the real flows, signing up, logging in, doing the main thing your product is for, and I tell you in plain terms where it works and where it falls apart. Color alone shows up constantly. The selected tab nobody can find. The error that is just a red glow. The status that is only a colored dot. I catch those because I hit them, not because a tool guessed.

And I am open about what a teardown is and is not, because honesty is the whole point. A teardown is the screen reader and keyboard experience, the human layer. It is not a full legal audit, and it does not cover the purely visual side like contrast ratios, because I am blind and I am not the right person to judge whether your gray text is readable for someone with low vision. A scanner measures that, and a full audit covers it formally. If you need the legal-grade document for an ADA concern or a compliance contract, that is an audit, and I will tell you that straight and point you to it. A teardown is the fast, affordable, human first look. Most teams should start there and let it show them where the real pain is.

You do not have to take my word for what you get, either, because I publish these in the open. Go read my teardown of ActiveCampaign, my teardown of Codex, or my teardown of Xcode Intelligence. That is the exact kind of clear, specific, prioritized read you get for your own product, and yours is private by default unless you want it public to show your customers you actually care.

A few ways we can work together

Let me lay out who this is for, because it is more than just companies wanting their own product checked.

If you run a company or a product, the straightforward one. Hire me to tear it down and I will show you where real users get stuck, in priority order, with the specific things to fix. If it turns out you need the full audit, I will tell you and help you get the right one.

If you are an accessibility vendor or consultancy, here is one people do not always think of. You probably do great work on the standards and the testing side, but you may not always have a blind developer with lived experience on call to actually use the product and tell you what it feels like from the inside. That is a thing I can be for you. Bring me in as a partner for the human, real-user layer, the part the tools and the checklists cannot feel.

If you are a web agency or a dev shop with clients, your clients are increasingly asking about accessibility, and you may not have someone in house who actually uses this stuff every day. I can be your accessibility partner behind the scenes. You keep the client relationship, I help make sure what you ship actually works for disabled users, and you get to offer something real instead of a badge in the footer.

If you are a disabled person yourself, and there is an app or a site you fight with every day, you can hire me to tear it down and you get a report you can send straight to the company that makes it. It is a way to put real, specific, credible feedback in front of the people who can fix it, instead of just being frustrated on your own.

If you want a teardown

Let me put the money in perspective, because this is where people freeze. A full audit runs a few thousand dollars. A demand letter, the kind small businesses are getting hit with right now, asks for five to twenty-five thousand to settle. Against either of those, a teardown is almost nothing.

Right now it is half off as a launch, no code to enter. A written teardown is 75 dollars instead of 149, and you get the findings on your key flows and the specific things to fix, in priority order. A teardown with a recorded screen reader walkthrough, me narrating your own product getting stuck, is 175 instead of 349, and that recording is the thing you hand your team, because hearing your product get stuck is a lot more convincing than reading about it. The launch price is only for the first 20 teardowns, and only a few of those spots are left, so if you have been meaning to do this, now is the moment.

When you are ready, you can book a teardown right here on Gumroad. If you want to partner with me as a vendor or an agency, or you just have a question, message me right here on Substack or find me on LinkedIn and tell me what you are working on. I will have a proper form for all of this before long, but for now a message is the fastest way to reach me. And if you want the full picture of where this whole industry stands in 2026, I wrote that up in the state of accessibility and AI.

One last thing

Color alone is such a good example of the bigger point I keep coming back to. It is not hard. It is not expensive. The platform usually built the fix for you already. The only thing missing is somebody deciding it mattered before they shipped, and then somebody actually using the product the way a disabled person would, to catch the spot where the meaning got trapped in the paint.

I have spent eight years proving accessibility is a basic, not a luxury. Stop making color do a job it cannot do for everyone, give every signal a second voice, and if you want a real blind developer to come find the places you missed, that is exactly what I am here for. Tell me what you are building, and I will give you the truth about where it stands, no pressure either way.

item.description: Everybody Is Vibe Coding.
item.dc:creator: Taylor Arndt

Everybody Is Vibe Coding. Here Is What That Does to Accessibility, and What to Actually Do About It.

Okay, so I want to talk about something that has been on my mind constantly, and I want to do it the way I would if you and I were just sitting down and talking it through. No lecture, no scolding, no 200-page report. Just the truth about where we are, from someone who lives in this every single day.

Taylor’s Substack is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

I am a blind developer. I have been doing accessibility for eight years, since 2017. In that time I have tested products, trained teams, consulted, and built the tools, and I have done this work inside some of the biggest names in the field as well as at the small studio I run accessibility for now. I also build apps for Apple platforms for a living, accessible from the first line, so I am not just talking about this from the sidelines. I ship it. And I use a screen reader all day, every day, still in the weeds doing screen reader testing every single week. So when I tell you the ground is shifting under all of this, that is not a hot take. It is what I am watching happen in real time, from the inside.

I am also going to be on Main Menu, ACB Media’s technology show, talking about vibe coding with some friends. So I figured it was time to write the whole thing down in one place. What vibe coding even is, what it is doing to accessibility, everything I have built to deal with it, and most importantly, what you can actually do about it. Because that last part is the whole point. I do not want you walking away from this just feeling bad. I want you walking away knowing what to do.

First, what even is vibe coding

Let me back up, because not everybody knows the term, and that is fine.

Vibe coding is a name Andrej Karpathy coined in early 2025. It means building software by describing what you want in plain language and letting the AI write the code for you. You guide it by prompting and testing instead of reading every line yourself. In the fuller version of it, people do not read the code at all. If there is an error, they paste it back into the AI and it fixes it. They go off the vibes.

And honestly, I think it is amazing. I really do. People who could never ship software before are shipping real things now. A few years ago, making an app meant getting out Xcode and writing every line by hand, and it took forever. Now somebody can put an app together in an afternoon. That is a genuinely good thing, and I am not here to dunk on it or gatekeep it.

I will say clearly, I am not a vibe coder myself. I use AI to write my code, and then I actually review it, because I know what good looks like and I know what breaks. But that is me. The wave of new builders coming in does not work that way, and we have to deal with the world as it actually is.

Here is the problem nobody wants to say out loud

Accessibility is not a strength of AI. At all.

This is the part I really need you to hear, because a lot of people are quietly acting like accessibility matters less now, when the truth is the exact opposite. It matters more than it ever has.

The research on this is blunt. Large language models produce inaccessible code by default, and the newer, fancier models did not fix it. Study after study in 2025 found the same pattern: the interfaces these models generate ship with multiple WCAG violations right out of the box, the kind that stop a screen reader cold. AI is decent at a couple of things, like color contrast and basic semantic HTML. But it misuses ARIA, it misses anything dynamic, and it has no idea what it is actually like to use the thing with a screen reader. AI is not your accessibility expert. It was never trained to be.

So put the two pieces together. We have more people shipping more software faster than ever before, using a tool that does not prioritize accessibility in what it produces. Which means, day by day, the apps and sites we all rely on are getting less accessible, not more, even as there are more of them. And this is not just websites. It is mobile apps, it is all the AI experiences everyone is bolting on right now, all of it. If a real person uses it, it counts, and most of it was never checked by anyone who navigates the world the way I do.

What actually breaks, in plain terms

Let me make this real, because “inaccessible” is a vague word until you have lived it. Here is what I hit over and over in vibe-coded apps.

Buttons with no name. The AI throws an icon on something clickable and never labels it. A sighted person sees a little trash can. My screen reader just says “button,” and I have no idea what it does.

Everything is a generic box. Instead of a real button or a real heading, the whole interface gets built out of plain containers styled to look right. On screen it looks fine. To my screen reader there is no structure at all, no headings to jump between, nothing that announces what it is.

Focus that goes nowhere. You tap something and a dialog opens. Obvious if you can see it. But focus never moves there, so as far as my screen reader knows, nothing happened. Sometimes focus gets trapped and I cannot get back out.

Color as the only signal. The form field turns red to show an error, with no text and no announcement. So I submit the same broken form three times, because nothing ever told me what was wrong.

Custom controls that reinvent the wheel. The AI builds its own dropdown or slider from scratch instead of using the one the platform already gives you for free, and the homemade one has none of the keyboard and screen reader behavior the real one would have had.

None of this is exotic. This is the sign up, the login, the main thing the app is for. And none of it is hard to get right if somebody who knows what they are doing is in the loop. That is the whole catch. Somebody has to be in the loop.

The other half of the problem: the industry priced out the people who need it most

Here is the part that really bothers me, and it was a problem long before AI showed up.

Accessibility, as an industry, was never built for everybody. It was built for big companies with budgets. A full audit usually runs a few thousand dollars, commonly between 2,500 and 10,000. The services that put a real disabled person in front of your product run well into the thousands and are aimed at enterprises. If you are a solo developer or a small business, that is just out of reach. So you do nothing. Not because you do not care, but because the front door costs more than you have.

And doing nothing is getting more dangerous, not less. In just the first half of 2025, website accessibility lawsuits jumped about 37 percent over the same stretch the year before, with more than 2,000 filed, and most of them hit small businesses and e-commerce. There is no small business exemption. The demand letters alone ask for five to twenty-five thousand dollars to settle. So the people who cannot afford a 5,000 dollar audit are the exact same people getting hit with a 15,000 dollar demand letter. That is backwards, and it is cruel.

Now add the vibe coding wave to that. A whole new group of builders, most of whom have never used a screen reader and have no idea what one even is, shipping fast with a tool that does not do accessibility for them. They are not bad people. Nobody ever taught them. So if we hand them a 200-page WCAG document and a five-figure invoice, of course they are going to skip it. We have to meet them where they are.

What I built about it, because I got tired of waiting

So I stopped waiting for the industry to fix this and started building. I built it in two halves on purpose, because you genuinely need both.

The AI side: a team of accessibility agents

Since AI will not prioritize accessibility on its own, a group of us decided to make it. Together with Jeff Bishop and the Community Access folks, I helped build a team of accessibility agents that plug right into the AI coding tools people already use, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Codex, and Claude Desktop. They review the interface as it is being written.

The idea is that the accessibility work happens while you build, by agents that actually know what good looks like, instead of being something you bolt on at the end or after you get sued. Accessibility is not one thing, so it is not one agent. There is a lead that looks at your task and pulls in the right specialists, somebody for ARIA, somebody for keyboard behavior, somebody for contrast, for forms, for modals, for headings and structure, and more. The lead coordinates them, sorts out the findings, and gives you a real review right there in your workflow.

And here is the part I care about most: they are open source. Gatekeeping the fix would defeat the entire point. You can grab them and read exactly how they work at the accessibility agents on GitHub.

I will be honest with you about what this is and is not, because I always try to be. The agents are fantastic at catching the mechanical stuff while you build, the missing labels, the bad ARIA, the structure problems. That is real, and it is the part AI tools skip. But an automated check, even a smart one, still catches only a slice of what actually matters. It can tell you a button has no label. It cannot tell you that your whole checkout flow is impossible to finish with a keyboard, because finishing a flow is a human thing. A scanner does not get frustrated and close the tab. A real person does. Which brings me to the other half.

The human side: teardowns

The second half is the one I am most excited about, and it is the human part.

Years ago I really sat with something I had known for a long time from doing this work. Accessibility had become long, expensive, arduous, and intimidating, and that is exactly why people avoided it. It had quietly turned into a thing you only do when a lawyer makes you. That is not how it should feel.

I think accessibility should be personal, it should be effective, and it should be easy enough for somebody who genuinely wants to do right by their users but has no clue where to start. So that is what a teardown is. I take your product and I use it the way a blind customer actually would, with a screen reader, signing up, logging in, doing the main thing it is for. Then I tell you in plain terms where it works and where it falls apart, and the specific things to fix first. Not a scan a tool spits out. A real blind developer, using your product, showing you what happens.

It does not have to be a website either. I can tear down web apps, iOS apps, even AI chatbots and AI experiences. If you have an iOS app, you send me a public TestFlight link or the App Store link and I test it on a real device. If real people use it, I can use it the way they would.

And here is the part that should make this an easy yes. You do not have to take my word for what you are getting, because I publish teardowns in the open. You can read exactly what one looks like before you spend a dollar. Go see my teardown of ActiveCampaign, my teardown of Codex, or my teardown of Xcode Intelligence. That is the exact kind of clear, specific, prioritized read you get for your own product, except yours is private by default. If you want yours public to show your customers you actually care about access, that is your call, and we can talk about it up front.

Now let me be straight about what a teardown does and does not cover, because honesty is the entire point of this. A teardown is the screen reader and keyboard experience. It is me, a blind person, actually trying to use your product, so I catch the things that wreck that experience, the unlabeled buttons, the focus that goes nowhere, the flow you cannot finish without a mouse. What it does not cover is the purely visual stuff. Color contrast is the obvious example. I am blind, so I am not the right person to tell you whether your gray text on a white background is readable for someone with low vision. That is a real accessibility issue, it matters, and it is exactly the kind of thing a tool can measure precisely and a full audit will check. The accessibility agents I mentioned catch contrast while you build, automated checkers catch it, and an audit covers it formally. A teardown is the human layer on top of all that, the part the tools cannot feel. The trick is knowing what each one is for, and I will always tell you straight which one you actually need.

So here is what to actually do

Alright, this is the part that matters most. If you build things, here is the honest playbook, from the cheapest thing to the most formal.

Start by caring on purpose. The single biggest predictor of whether something is accessible is whether anybody decided it mattered before they shipped. The best accessible software I have ever worked on was built accessible from the first line, by people who chose to. That is always easier and cheaper than fixing it later.

Put accessibility into the way you already build. If you are coding with AI, get the accessibility agents into your workflow so the review happens as the code gets written. They are free and open source. There is no reason not to.

Use the automated tools, but know their ceiling. Run a scanner. Just understand it catches maybe a third of what matters, and the third it catches is the easy third. Do not let a green checkmark convince you a blind person can actually use your product.

Get a real human to use it. This is the step almost everybody skips, and it is the one that actually tells you the truth. That is what a teardown is for. It is the fast, affordable way to find out where real users are struggling, without a five-figure invoice.

Know when you genuinely need an audit. If you want full legal compliance, this is the one. An ADA concern, a compliance requirement, a contract where you have to prove conformance, all of that means you need a full audit, the formal report, every screen, every checkpoint, including the visual things a teardown does not cover. I will tell you that straight, and I will point you to it rather than sell you the wrong thing. A teardown is the smart, affordable first look. An audit is the legal-grade document. They are not the same, and most teams should start with the teardown and let it show them where the real pain is before they spend audit money.

If you want a teardown

Let me put the money in perspective, because this is where people freeze up. A full audit runs a few thousand dollars. A demand letter, the kind small businesses are getting hit with right now, asks for five to twenty-five thousand to settle. Against either of those numbers, a teardown is almost nothing.

Right now it is half off as a launch, no code to enter. A written teardown is 75 dollars instead of 149, and you get the findings on your key flows and the specific things to fix, in priority order. A teardown with a recorded screen reader walkthrough, me narrating your own product getting stuck, is 175 instead of 349, and that recording is the thing you hand your team, because hearing your product get stuck is a lot more convincing than reading about it. The launch price is only for the first 20 teardowns, and only a few of those spots are left, so if you have been meaning to do this, now is the moment.

So here is the one thing I would ask. Stop treating accessibility as the thing you will get to someday, because the someday version is the lawsuit version, and it is the most expensive and least kind version there is. You do not have to become an expert, and you do not have to do it alone. You just have to start small. When you are ready, you can book a teardown right here on Gumroad. And if you want the full picture of where this whole industry stands in 2026, I wrote that up in the state of accessibility and AI.

One last thing

I am not trying to corner a market here. I am trying to open one up. In an AI economy where anybody can build anything, I want everybody to succeed, the builders and the disabled people who deserve to use what they build. Those are not competing goals. They are the same goal.

The industry priced accessibility like a luxury. I have spent eight years proving it is a basic, and I am building it that way. If that is the kind of accessibility you believe in, come build it with me. And if you are not sure where you stand, just ask me. Tell me what you are building, and I will give you the truth about where it stands, no pressure either way.

There is even a name for it, vibe coding, a term Andrej Karpathy coined in early 2025 for building software by describing what you want in plain language and letting the AI write the code, guiding it by prompting and testing instead of reading every line. And honestly, it is amazing. People who could never ship software before are shipping real things now. I love that.

But here is what I need people to hear. Accessibility is more important now than it has ever been, even though a lot of people are quietly acting like it matters less. And the reason is simple: accessibility is not a strength of AI.

The research is pretty blunt about this. Large language models produce inaccessible code by default, and the newest models did not fix it. In one recent benchmark, models passed accessibility checks only a few percent of the time, with several WCAG failures in a single sample, and the hardest pages failed completely. AI is good at some pieces, like contrast and basic semantic HTML, but it misuses ARIA, it misses anything dynamic, and it has no idea what it is actually like to use the thing with a screen reader. AI is not your accessibility expert.

So put it together. We have more people shipping more code faster than ever, using a tool that does not prioritize accessibility in what it produces. Which means, day by day, the things we all rely on are getting less accessible, not more, even as there are more of them. And this is not just websites. It is mobile apps, it is the AI experiences everyone is bolting on right now, it is all of it. If a real person uses it, it is in scope, and most of it was never checked by anyone who actually navigates the world the way I do. That is the trend I keep seeing, and it is the one nobody wants to talk about.

And the field already agrees, even if the hype does not

I want to be clear that I am not out on a limb here. If you read what the serious people in accessibility are saying about 2026, the consensus is remarkably consistent. AI helps when you pair it with knowledgeable human reviewers, and it hurts when you let it replace them. One industry roundup put it perfectly: teams that expect AI to do accessibility for them will keep missing the real barriers, just faster than before. Another expert was blunter, that in the right hands AI is a genuinely useful tool, and in the wrong hands it is how snake oil salesmen swindle people who do not know any better.

That is exactly the line I walk, and it is why I built things in two halves. You need the tool inside the workflow, and you need a real human who lives this to catch what the tool never will. Not one or the other. Both. The whole industry is converging on that answer. The only thing missing is making it reach the people who are not big enough to afford a seat at that table.

What the industry actually needs to do

I think we need to go back to the basics of accessibility, and we need to help a whole new group of people who never had to think about this before.

The vibe coder shipping their first app is not a bad person. They just do not know what a screen reader is, and nobody ever taught them. Most of the indie developers I talk to every single day have never used one. So if we want them to care, we cannot hand them a 200-page WCAG document and a five-figure invoice. We have to meet them where they are.

That means two things have to change. The tools have to bring accessibility into the way people actually build now, which is with AI. And the services have to become something a normal person can both afford and understand. Self-serve options exist, but they mostly assume you already know the vocabulary. The big firms are all chasing big businesses. Almost nobody is thinking about how you make accessibility affordable and approachable for everybody else.

This is why I built what I built

So I stopped waiting for the industry to fix it and started building.

The first piece is on the AI side. Since AI will not prioritize accessibility on its own, a group of us built something that makes it. Together with Jeff Bishop and the Community Access folks, I helped build a team of accessibility agents that plug into the AI coding tools people already use, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, and Claude Desktop, and review the interface as it is being written. The accessibility work happens while you build, by agents that actually know what good looks like, instead of being something you bolt on at the end or after you get sued. They are open source, because gatekeeping the fix would defeat the entire point. You can find them here: the accessibility agents on GitHub.

The second piece is the human side, and it is the one I am most excited about. Back in 2021, I really sat with something I had known for years from doing this work: accessibility was long, arduous, expensive, and intimidating, and that is exactly why people avoided it. It had quietly become a thing you only do when a lawyer makes you. That is not how it should feel.

I think accessibility should be personal. It should be effective. And it should be easy enough for someone who genuinely wants to do right by their users but has no idea where to start. That is what my teardowns are. I actually use your product the way a blind customer would, with a screen reader, and I tell you in plain terms where it works and where it falls apart, for a price a small business can actually say yes to. No 200-page report, no five-figure invoice, no lawsuit required.

This is bigger than me, and it takes all of us

I want to be clear about something. I am not trying to corner a market here. I am trying to open one up.

Accessibility has to be democratized. Right now it sits behind big budgets and big firms, and the knowledge sits with a small group of specialists, and that has to change. The people building the future, the indie developers, the small teams, the founders vibe coding their first product, need to be let in, not priced out and not talked down to. That means spreading awareness, sharing what we know instead of guarding it, and making the on-ramps cheap and human instead of expensive and intimidating.

And no one person does this alone. The accessibility community is small. But we are mighty, and we always have been, because we are the people who actually live this every day. So this is a genuine call to everyone in this field, and to everyone building with AI right now. Let’s work together. Let’s stop locking accessibility behind five-figure invoices and start treating it like the basic right it is. Let’s meet this new wave of builders where they are and bring them in instead of shutting them out.

Because here is what I actually want. In an AI economy where anyone can build anything, I want everyone to succeed, the builders and the disabled people who deserve to use what they build. Those are not competing goals. They are the same goal. We just have to decide, together, as an industry, to build it that way.

How to actually start

If you build things, here is the one thing I would ask. Stop treating accessibility as the thing you will get to someday. The someday version is the lawsuit version, and it is the most expensive and least kind version there is.

You do not have to become an expert overnight, and you do not have to do it alone. You just have to start small. That is what my teardowns are for. I use your product the way a blind customer would, on real screen readers, and I give you a clear, honest, prioritized read on where it actually stands and what to fix, for a price a small business can say yes to without flinching. I publish them in public too, so you can see exactly what you are getting before you spend a dollar. When you want one of your own, it is right here: book a teardown.

And if you are not sure where you stand, or you just want to talk it through, my door is always open. I am always available, for a teardown, for a bigger review down the road, or honestly just to point you in the right direction. Tell me what you are building, and I will give you the truth about where it stands, no pressure either way.

The industry priced accessibility like a luxury. I have spent eight years proving it is a basic, and I am building it that way. If that is the kind of accessibility you believe in, come build it with me.

How My Teardowns Work, and the New One You Can Hire Me For

Right now, a blind person could be trying to use your product and quietly giving up. They will not file a bug. They will not email your support team. They will just leave, and you will never know they were there, or that you lost them. I know this because I am that person more often than I would like to be.

Taylor’s Substack is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

So let me tell you about something I do that catches this before it costs you, and the new version of it you can now hire me for. I also want to be clear about what it is and what it is not.

A teardown is a simplified version of an audit. I go through the flows that a normal user would go through, and I attempt to use your product the way a real customer would. That is the whole idea. I am not crawling through every single screen and every checkbox. I use your product like a person trying to get something done, and I tell you where it works and where it falls apart.

What a teardown actually is

When I do a teardown, I am using your product the way I use anything, with a screen reader and a keyboard. On the Mac that is VoiceOver, and on Windows that is NVDA. I go to the parts a customer actually touches, signing up, logging in, the main thing your product is for, and I try to get it done.

And that is the part that makes a teardown valuable. It is not a checklist. It is a real person, who is blind, actually trying to use your product and showing you what happens. You get to hear, in plain terms, where a customer like me gets stuck.

This is not just for websites either. I can tear down web apps and mobile apps too. If you have an iOS app, you just send me a public TestFlight link, or if it is already on the App Store, the App Store link, and I will test it the same way, with VoiceOver on a real device.

And it goes well beyond websites and apps. I am a developer myself, so I can test just about anything, including AI chatbots and AI experiences. If real people use it, I can use it the way they would and show you where it breaks down for someone who cannot see the screen.

The free teardowns

I have been doing free teardowns for a while. Those are the ones where I am trying to use a product, it is not accessible, and I decide to write it up. I go through the things I wanted to do as a customer, and I show what got in my way. My recent one on ActiveCampaign is exactly that. We switched our marketing over to it, I hit problem after problem just trying to log in and get around, and I wrote the whole thing down. You can read my ActiveCampaign teardown to see exactly what one looks like.

I will keep doing those whenever I run into something worth talking about. That is not going away.

The new thing: paid teardowns

Here is what is new. I am now offering paid teardowns, where a company or an individual hires me to do this on their product.

It is the same idea. You pay me, and I go through the flows I would want to use as a customer, on real screen readers, and I tell you what I find. And this is genuinely useful, because you get to see from a usability standpoint what is actually happening when somebody who cannot see the screen tries to use your product. Not a scan that a tool spits out. A human, using it.

And here is another way to use this. It does not have to be your own product. If there is an app or a site you use every day that is a pain with a screen reader, you can hire me to tear it down, and you get a report you can send straight to the company that makes it. It is a way to put real, specific, credible feedback in front of the people who can actually fix it, instead of just being frustrated on your own.

A teardown is not an audit, and I want to be clear about that

I need to say this plainly, because it matters. A teardown is not a replacement for a full accessibility audit.

A full audit goes through everything, every screen, every WCAG checkpoint, with a formal report. That is the thing you need if you are worried about legal compliance, ADA lawsuits, that kind of pressure. A teardown does not cover that. I am not going through every page, and I am not handing you a compliance document you can hold up in court.

What a teardown is, is a way to get your feet wet in accessibility for a little money. It is the fast, affordable way to find out where real users are actually struggling, and to start fixing the things that matter most. If you need the full legal-grade thing, get an audit. If you want a real, human first look without spending audit money, that is what a teardown is for.

What an audit actually costs

To put the money in perspective. A full accessibility audit usually runs a few thousand dollars, commonly somewhere in the 2,500 to 10,000 range depending on the provider and the size of your product. That is real money, and for a lot of indie developers and small businesses it puts real, human accessibility help out of reach.

That is the gap a teardown fills. You get a blind person actually using your product, for a tiny fraction of what an audit costs. And to be clear, if you do want a full audit, you can absolutely get one. Just get in touch with me and we will talk about what you actually need, whether that is a teardown to start with, a full audit, or me pointing you to the right thing.

Teardowns can also be a marketing engine

Here is something people do not always think about. A teardown can work for you, not just on you.

Because these can be public. If you are proud of where your product is, or you want to show your customers that you actually care about access, I can do a teardown that we publish. That shows real commitment to accessibility, out in the open, with a real blind user putting your product through its paces, instead of a badge in your footer that does not mean anything. It is good for your users and it is good for your reputation.

And to be clear, that is your call. A paid teardown is private by default. If you want it public, we make it public, and that is something we can talk about up front.

What it costs

Here is the pricing, and right now it is half off as a launch, no code needed.

A written teardown is normally 149 dollars, and right now it is 75. I go through your key flows and you get the findings, what should happen versus what is actually happening, and the specific things to fix.

A teardown with a recording is normally 349 dollars, and right now it is 175. You get all of that, plus a recorded screen reader walkthrough of your own product, with me narrating it. That recording is the thing you can hand to your team, because hearing your product get stuck is a lot more convincing than reading about it.

The launch price is just the price right now, there is nothing to enter. But it is only for the first 20 teardowns, so if you have been meaning to do this, now is a good time.

One more time, so it is clear

A teardown is not an audit. It will not cover you for compliance or lawsuits. What it will do is show you, fast and affordably, where a real blind customer struggles with your product, and give you real things to fix. It is the way to get started, and for a lot of people, getting started is the hardest part.

If you want to see what one looks like first, read my ActiveCampaign teardown. And if you want one of your own, you can grab it on Taylor’s Teardowns on Gumroad. If you are not sure whether a teardown or a full audit is right for you, just ask, I am happy to be straight with you about it.

item.dc:creator: Taylor Arndt
