Taylor’s Teardowns: ActiveCampaign

So yesterday Techopolis switched our marketing over to ActiveCampaign, and I thought, what a great time to do an accessibility teardown.

Taylor’s Substack is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

That is kind of how I am. The minute I start using a new tool for real, I am paying attention to how it actually works with VoiceOver and a keyboard, not how the marketing says it works. So here are my thoughts on ActiveCampaign so far.

What ActiveCampaign is

If you have not run into it, ActiveCampaign is a marketing automation platform. It is email marketing, automations, and a sales CRM all in one place, and it has gotten kind of known for having one of the most powerful automation builders out there. You build out these customer journeys, you send email and SMS, you track what people do, that kind of thing. They say it serves something like 185,000 businesses, so it is not a small player. And lately they have been leaning hard into AI, this whole idea of AI agents that help run your marketing for you. That is honestly part of why I am interested.

How I am testing this

I want to be clear about how I am doing this, because it matters for what I find.

I am running the teardown on both Mac and Windows. On the Mac I am using VoiceOver with Safari. On Windows I am using NVDA, which stands for NonVisual Desktop Access, with Chrome. And when something behaves differently between the two, I am going to tell you exactly what the difference is, because that happens more than people think, and it is useful to know.

So I sat down to go through the functions of ActiveCampaign. Part of that is because Michael wanted to see how accessible it is, and part of it is just me, because I really like all the AI stuff and I wanted to see how usable it actually is when you cannot rely on the screen.

The first major issue, and I had not even logged in

I had not even gotten to the login yet. Before I could, a modal popped up telling me I could book a demo with one of their experts.

That is a pretty normal thing for a marketing tool to do, so no complaints about the offer itself. The problem is closing it.

When a modal opens, you expect the Escape key to close it. That is just how modals work, and it is the first thing I reach for. This one did not. I pressed Escape and nothing happened. I tried pressing Escape twice and looking for some other key combination, and even then I could not reliably get it to go away.

And here is where it goes from annoying to a real problem. Every time I refresh the page, the modal comes right back, like it is following me around. It would show up after about three or four seconds on the page, every time, which was honestly kind of fascinating to watch it just keep doing that. So I am sitting here trying to log in, and I cannot, because this thing keeps planting itself in front of me and I cannot escape out of it.

What finally got me past it was figuring out that the login form on the main site was not actually what I needed. I had to go straight to our Techopolis instance of ActiveCampaign through the address bar. That is what got me in. But I want to be honest about how I got there, which is a lot of frustration and a lot of messing around before it clicked.

That is the first major issue. It is not a cosmetic popup I can shrug off. It got in the way of me actually logging in, and I only got past it because I worked out a route around it, not because the modal ever behaved the way it should.

The login page is basic, but there is still an issue

Once I got to the actual login page for our instance, the one you reach by going to your own ActiveCampaign address in the address bar, it was really basic. And I mean that as a compliment. It is a straightforward login page, the standard fields and a button, nothing fancy fighting my screen reader. So compared to that modal, this was already a relief.

But I take back saying it was totally clean, because there is an issue. When I tab to the password field, it reads “eight characters.” It does not actually read the label. What it is reading is some kind of placeholder or hint, not the real name of the field. So the field is technically unlabeled.

Now, I know it is the password field. From context it is obvious. But that is not the point. A screen reader should land on that field and tell me it is the password field, by its actual label, not read me a hint about how many characters it wants. Sighted people get a visible label there. I should get one too.

So it is a small thing next to the modal, but it is still the kind of thing that should not be there on a login page.

Then it asked me for a code

After I put in my password, it asked me for a verification code. And this step had two problems.

First, the code field was unlabeled, same as the password field. What should happen is the field carries a real label, so the screen reader lands on it and tells me this is where the verification code goes. What actually happens is I land on a field that does not announce what it is, and I am left working it out from context.

The bigger one is the error handling. I tried to enter a code, and when there was an error, it did not read the error message and it did not move my focus to the field with the problem. What should happen here is well established: when a form has an error, the error needs to be announced, and focus should move to the field that has the issue, so I know what went wrong and I am taken right to where I fix it. What actually happens is the page stays quiet and leaves my focus wherever it was, so I am stuck guessing that something even went wrong. On the step standing between me and my account, that is a real problem, not a nitpick.

First thing I noticed once I was in

Once I was actually logged in, the first issue is that there is no skip to main content link, no skip link to get past the header at all.

What should happen is simple and it is a basic expectation. The first thing I tab to should be a skip link that lets me jump straight to the main content, so I am not forced through the entire header every single time. What actually happens is there is nothing, so I am dropped into the top of the page with no quick way past the navigation.

And it goes a little deeper than that. I cannot even tell where the header begins or where it ends. That tells me the landmarks are probably not set up right, because if the header and the main content were marked up properly, I would be able to move between those regions and know exactly where I am. Right now I cannot.

I will also say there is probably some kind of reading order or focus order issue going on for screen reader users, but I want to be honest and careful here. I cannot confirm that visually, for obvious reasons. It has the feel of it, but I am not going to state it as fact until I can verify it. What should happen is the reading order and the focus order match the logical order of the page, so tabbing through and reading through both make sense. Whether that is actually true here is something I still need to pin down.

The header feels like two navigations stacked together

It gets worse than just the missing skip link. Once I started moving through the header, the first thing that hit me is that it feels like there are two navigations, not one. A lot of things are clickable, and the same items keep showing up more than once.

Let me give you a real example. As I move through it, VoiceOver reads “Return home, group,” and then separately “Return home, clickable, image.” And I genuinely have no idea what either of those is supposed to do. Return home group versus return home clickable image. For one thing, it is an image, not a link, so it is not even clear what kind of control it is or what happens if I activate it. What should happen is that going home is a single, clearly labeled link, something like “ActiveCampaign home,” so I know exactly what it does. What actually happens is I get this two part, vaguely named thing and I am left guessing.

And that is the pattern up there. There are not a lot of the standard links, buttons, and controls I am used to. I see a few buttons and a few headings, but a lot of what is in that header is not marked up as anything I can recognize. There is one item that reads as “link, image, Help,” sitting in a list by itself, so I cannot even tell where the navigation starts and where it ends. And that matters, because the whole way screen reader users move around a page depends on those standard pieces actually being there.

A quick word on how I actually navigate

Let me explain something here, because I want to educate, not just complain.

When you use a screen reader, you rarely read a page top to bottom. Instead you pull up a list. On the Mac with VoiceOver I can open a rotor of all the links, or all the headings, or all the form controls. On Windows, JAWS has a links list and NVDA has an elements list. Same idea. You bring up every link on the page in one list and jump straight to the one you want. It is one of the main ways we get around fast.

But that list is only as good as the labels behind it. If half the entries say “clickable image” or “button” with no name, the list is useless, because I am reading a column of items that do not tell me what they are. So when I say a control is unlabeled, I am not nitpicking wording. I am telling you the main tool I use to navigate just broke.

And on top of that, things are duplicated. As I move element by element with VoiceOver left and right, I keep landing on the same thing twice. For example, “link, image, Settings,” and then again “link, image, Settings.” Same with Help, same with View support tickets. So even the items that do have a name show up two times, which clutters that list even more. These are my Mac and VoiceOver observations, by the way. I am going to run the same passes on Windows with NVDA and tell you exactly where they differ.

Unlabeled button roulette

Here is where it gets really rough. The tab order is not always doing what it should either. When I am on Settings and I press Tab, it moves to the next element, which is fine, that is what Tab is for. The problem is the next element literally just says “button.” No name. So I am playing what I call unlabeled button roulette, where I have to go activate a button just to find out what it even does.

What should happen is one of the most basic things in all of accessibility: every button has a label, so I know what it does before I press it. What actually happens is I am guessing.

So I went ahead and played the roulette, and the punchline is that the unlabeled button was actually a navigation menu, and a pretty important one. Inside it were things like Apps, an account upgrade item that VoiceOver read as “account upgrade icon, clickable, image,” and sending limits. This is not some throwaway control. A vital part of the site was sitting behind a button with no name, and I would not have found it at all if I had just skipped past that button. For a function that important to be unlabeled is a huge issue.

I do want to give credit where it is due. Once I got into that menu, the Billing and upgrade link is fine. It is a real link, it is labeled, it is accessible. So they can clearly do it right, which honestly makes the unlabeled stuff more frustrating, not less.

Why “a screen reader might figure it out” is not an excuse

Now, somebody is going to say, well, JAWS would probably guess a label for that button. And that is partly true, so let me explain it.

JAWS does try to make up for missing labels. It has heuristics where it will look at things like a title attribute, nearby text, or even the image filename to come up with a guess, and it even has an auto graphics labeler you can trigger to take a swing at unlabeled graphics. NVDA and VoiceOver do a little of this too. But everyone who works on this, including Freedom Scientific who makes JAWS, is clear that this is a workaround for bad code, not something you design around. The guess is often wrong, it is inconsistent from one screen reader to the next, and it puts the work on me instead of the developer. So no, the fact that a screen reader might paper over a missing label is not a reason to ship an unlabeled control.

Duplicate clutter, like the logout button

The logout situation is a perfect example of clutter that nobody needs. As I move through, I hit “account logout icon, clickable, image,” and then right below it there is a real logout link that works fine.

So why do we have both? The clickable image adds nothing. It is not properly accessible, and the actual logout link right under it already does the job. What should happen is there is one accessible logout link, and that is it.

And if that icon is just there for looks, there are clean ways to handle it. You can hide a decorative icon from screen readers with aria-hidden on the icon, which takes it out of the accessibility tree so I never hear it, while it still shows on screen. That is the right tool here, since the icon is purely visual and is sitting right next to a text link. The flip side, just so people know the difference, is the visually hidden or “sr-only” technique, which hides something on the screen but keeps it for screen readers, for when you want to give us extra context. Two different tools for two different jobs. The point is there is no reason to leave a meaningless clickable image sitting in my way. Every one of these duplicates adds verbosity, and verbosity is exactly what makes a screen reader experience slow and tiring to move through.

The mystery scrollable content regions

As I move through the page, VoiceOver announces a “scrollable content region.” Let me break down what that even is.

That is an ARIA region, which is a kind of landmark. Landmarks are meant to be helpful. They mark the major parts of a page, like the banner, the navigation, and the main content, so I can jump between them and always know where I am. Used well, they are great.

The problem is these should not be here, and there is more than one. At one point VoiceOver said “end of scrollable content region, 2 of 4,” which tells me there are four of these stacked on this single page. And it was announcing it twice on top of that, so I am hearing the same thing over and over. I see this a lot in AI generated code. It loves to sprinkle in extra ARIA regions for no real reason. But a region that does not mark anything meaningful does not help me at all, it just becomes one more thing VoiceOver has to announce as I pass through. Four of them, doubled up, on a page that is already this noisy, is the opposite of helpful.

Headings, or the lack of them

Here is one I almost missed. There is a heading on this page at level 6, sitting on the Apps item, and it has no business being there. So let me give the quick lecture on headings, because they matter more than people realize.

Headings are the skeleton of a page for a screen reader user. We navigate by them constantly, jumping heading to heading to get the lay of the land. The rules are simple. One H1 that names the page, then you go down in order, H2, H3, and so on, without skipping levels and without picking a level just because of how it looks. A heading level is structure, not styling.

What I have here is the opposite. There is a stray level 6 heading off on its own, which tells me somebody chose the number for looks instead of structure. And meanwhile the things that should be headings are not. There is a section that says “Automate your success” that should clearly be a heading, and it is not one. So the one heading on the page is the wrong level in the wrong place, and the real sections have no headings at all. What should happen is a clean, logical heading outline I can move through. What actually happens is there is basically nothing to navigate by.

The navigation menu I cannot collapse, and that should not be a landmark

Remember that important navigation menu I found hiding behind the unlabeled button? There is more wrong with it.

First, I cannot collapse it. If something expands, I should be able to collapse it again, and as a screen reader user I should be told what state it is in. That is exactly what the ARIA attribute aria-expanded is for. You put it on the control, set it to true or false, and now VoiceOver announces “expanded” or “collapsed” so I know whether the thing is open, and aria-controls can even tie the button to the menu it opens. None of that is happening here, so I cannot tell if it is open or closed, and I cannot reliably collapse it.

Second, and this one is a little more technical, this menu is being exposed as a landmark, and it should not be. Landmarks are for the big structural regions of a page, the banner, the navigation area, the main content. They are signposts, not controls. An interactive menu like this should be a proper navigation menu or a disclosure, a button that opens and closes a list, with the right roles and states. Turning it into a landmark mixes up two completely different things: a signpost you jump to versus a control you operate. And the frustrating part is this menu is honestly the main thing that helps me get around the platform, so it being this broken really hurts.

And while I was in there, I hit a wall I could not get past at all. I cannot get to the contact and sending limits with VoiceOver. It is just not exposed. For something that vital, the number that tells me where I stand on my plan, to simply not be reachable with a screen reader, there is no real way for me to get to it. That is not a small thing.

These links are fine, but why the image

I want to be fair, because not everything here is broken. A lot of the actual links, like Contacts, Business Goals, and Email, SMS, WhatsApp, are fine. They are real links with real names, and I can use them.

My only critique is the same one from before. Every one of them comes with an image, so VoiceOver reads “link, image, Contacts” instead of just “link, Contacts.” I already know it is a link, and the image is not telling me anything useful. If the design wants an icon next to the link, great, keep it on screen, but hide it from the screen reader with aria-hidden so it does not get announced. Like I said earlier, there are clean ways to keep an image for sighted users while keeping it out of my way, or the other direction with the visually hidden technique when you actually do want screen reader only text. Here it is just extra verbosity riding along on every single link.

The AI chat is the one that disappoints me most

This is the one that really gets me, because I actually like the AI, and I wanted this part to be good.

Start with the input. The text entry box for the chat is not labeled at all. VoiceOver just reads it as a text area with no name, so nothing tells me this is where I type my question to the assistant. What should happen is the input has a clear label, something like “Ask a question.”

Then I used it. I asked it how many contacts I have, and I pressed Enter. Now, I will be fair, chatbots are a little tricky to get right for screen readers, so let me say what I actually expect. When a new response comes in, it should be announced. The normal way to do that is an ARIA live region on the chat, so the assistant’s reply gets read aloud automatically the moment it arrives. That did not happen. I got an answer, the answer was correct and I liked what it said, but I had no idea it had arrived and I had to go hunting for it.

On top of that, there is no structure inside the conversation. Each message, mine and the assistant’s, should be a heading, so I can jump message to message and tell who said what. There is none of that here. No headings, no landmarks, no real navigation in the chat at all. So I am left with content I like, trapped in a window I cannot move around or keep up with.

And then I could not get out of it. There was no clear way to close the AI chat. I could not find a labeled close button, and Escape did not get me out. What I ended up doing was hitting Return home, which, remember, I never even knew what it did, just to escape. And while the chat was open it was actually covering up the menu I needed, so I was stuck inside a thing I could not close, blocking the thing I wanted. A panel like this needs an obvious, labeled close control, it should respond to Escape, and focus should move sensibly when it opens and when it closes. None of that is here, and it needs to be.

Something they actually got right

Let me give credit where it is due, because credit matters. When I went to connect MCP services, that whole flow is actually nice. It is a menu popup, there is a Manage connectors option, and for a change everything in there is a standard, properly labeled button. It just worked, the way it is supposed to. So they are clearly capable of building accessible controls. That is exactly why the rest of this is worth pointing out, because I know they can do it.

The email section, where I will actually live

I am not going to go through every single thing in here, but I went into the email section, because realistically that is where I am going to spend most of my time. And it is a real mix, which honestly sums up this whole platform.

First, the inconsistency. Looking at that list of options, contacts, automation, SMS, WhatsApp, and so on, some of them read twice as I move with VoiceOver left and right, and some of them do not. So the duplication problem I have been hitting all over ActiveCampaign is not even consistent. Some items double up, some are clean, and I cannot tell you why. That kind of inconsistency is its own problem, because I never know what I am going to get.

Then there is a heading that says Manage. A heading there is good, I am glad it exists, but it should really be an H1, and it is not. So the structure is close, but not right.

Here is the part I genuinely liked, though. The content area, with Content, Campaign templates, Message variables, and Archive, is built as a real native list of links. And that changes everything. Because it is a proper list, I can pull up my links list and just use it. Every item is fully labeled, and not one of them reads twice. This was the cleanest part of ActiveCampaign I hit, and it is not an accident. This is exactly why native controls, real lists and real links, beat custom in-house controls every time. When you use the built in stuff, you get the accessibility for free. When you roll your own, you have to remember to add it all back, and as we have seen across the platform, that often just does not happen.

I also like that there is a Reports heading. Small thing, but a real heading on a real section is what I want more of.

The campaign designer

The campaign designer is back to the mix. There is a heading level 2 that says “Welcome to the campaign designer,” and it is out of order. You should not be dropping to an H2 without the proper structure above it. Headings are supposed to form an outline, and an out of order one breaks that outline.

The AI feature in here is, once again, not labeled, which is a shame given how central they are making the AI to this whole product.

There are also list items for things like Personalization and Segmentation, and again each one has an image stuck in front of it, so VoiceOver reads the image and then the item. Same fix as everywhere else: if the icon is decoration, hide it from the screen reader.

And here is a classic one. There is an image whose name VoiceOver read out as “f3hphtrux_new-campaign-editor-screenshot.png.” That is the raw filename being used as the alternative text. What should happen is the alt text describes what the image actually shows, in plain words, or if it is purely decorative, it is hidden. A jumble of letters and a file name tells me nothing. That is exactly what you get when no real alt text was ever written and the system just falls back to the file name.

The rest of the email area is more of the same, some parts that are genuinely great and some that are genuinely not.

The settings page was the best part of ActiveCampaign

I want to give them real credit here, because they earned it. The settings were actually really good. Honestly, the best accessibility I saw anywhere in ActiveCampaign.

The headings were there and they were in order. There was a proper heading level 1, and everything stepped down logically from there. The list of categories was an actual list. The items were real links, not those duplicated link image combos I had been fighting everywhere else. So I could land on the settings, understand the structure, and move through it the way I am supposed to. This is what the whole platform should feel like.

The only critique, and it is a small one, is that down at the very bottom there were a couple of items, a language link and some other bits, that seemed to be invisible or only partly exposed to the screen reader. So not perfect. But compared to everything else, the settings page shows they absolutely know how to do this right. Which, again, is the whole point of a teardown like this. The good parts prove the bad parts are fixable.

The Windows pass with NVDA

This is exactly why I test on both Mac and Windows, because you find things you would never catch on one alone. So I went back through ActiveCampaign on Windows with NVDA in Chrome, and here is what I found.

For the most part, it is the same story. The same things that were broken on the Mac are broken on Windows. The errors on the code step still do not work. The code field is still not labeled. When I land in the AI area it still says “Customize your AI,” and the AI field is still not labeled. Same issues, same broken pieces, right across both platforms.

But there was one genuinely strange difference, and I cannot explain it. The password field on the login screen, the one that was unlabeled with VoiceOver on the Mac, is actually fully labeled with NVDA on Windows. Same page, same field, two different results depending on the screen reader. I do not have a clean explanation for that, and I am not going to pretend I do. It is a perfect example of why you cannot test on one platform and call something accessible. What reads fine in one screen reader can fall apart in another, and the only way to know is to actually try both.

Why this actually matters

Here is what I want people to take away, because it would be easy to read a list like this and think it is just a pile of technical nitpicks. It is not.

Every one of these is the difference between me being able to run my business and not. A company can check a box and say, yes, we have a modal, yes, you can close it, yes, we support a verification code. And technically all of that is true. But the option existing is not the same as it actually working. I could not close the demo modal. I could not read the AI’s answer. I could not even find out my own sending limits. Those are not edge cases. That is a blind person trying to do normal, everyday work and getting stopped at the door.

And this is not some niche problem. There are a lot of us, running real businesses, paying for these same tools, who just want to get our work done like everybody else. When accessibility is done in some places and skipped in others, what it really tells us, in a hundred small ways, is that we were an afterthought. That is the part I want you to feel, because it is the part that actually costs people.

Where this leaves me

So that is my first real pass through ActiveCampaign, on both the Mac and Windows.

And here is the honest summary. There are genuinely great parts. The settings page, the native list of links in the email section, the MCP connectors, the billing and upgrade link. Those show that the people building this know exactly how to do accessibility right. And then there are the parts that are genuinely rough. A demo modal I could not escape and that blocked me from logging in. Unlabeled fields, unlabeled buttons, a vital navigation menu hiding behind a button with no name. Duplicated controls everywhere, images cluttering up every link, missing and out of order headings, extra ARIA regions adding noise, and an AI chat whose answers I like but cannot really read, navigate, or even close.

That gap is the whole point. When the same product can give me a clean, well structured settings page and then a login modal I cannot get out of, it tells me accessibility was done in some places and skipped in others. The fix is not a mystery. They already proved they can do it on their own settings page. They just have to bring the rest of the platform up to the level of their own best work.

We are running our marketing on ActiveCampaign now, so I am going to keep living in it, especially the email section, and I will report back as I go. And if anyone at ActiveCampaign is reading this, I am genuinely happy to walk you through every single one of these, control by control. That is the whole reason I do these teardowns. Not to dunk on anybody, but to get these tools to a place where people like me can actually use them.

If this opened your eyes a little, share it with someone who builds software, because this is exactly the stuff that gets missed. And if you have hit walls like this in tools you use, drop it in the comments.
